You only need the five primary cell lines (HFF, H1hESC, GM12878, IMR90, HCT116) already distributed in the benchmark's Contact Map Prediction deposit Your task is one of the other DNALONGBENCH tasks (enhancer-target gene, eQTL, regulatory sequence activity, transcription initiation) that do not use Hi-C contact maps http://edamontology.org/topic_3912 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Retrieves raw Hi-C data for additional cell types (e.g., HAP1, HeLa, HepG2, K562) from the 4DN data portal and processes it into DNALONGBENCH-format 448x448 binned contact map targets using the Akita processing pipeline. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-65077-4
skills.summary: Retrieves raw Hi-C data for additional cell types (e.g., HAP1, HeLa, HepG2, K562) from the 4DN data portal and processes it into DNALONGBENCH-format 448x448 binned contact map targets using the Akita processing pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need the five primary cell lines (HFF, H1hESC, GM12878, IMR90, HCT116) already distributed in the benchmark's Contact Map Prediction deposit Your task is one of the other DNALONGBENCH tasks (enhancer-target gene, eQTL, regulatory sequence activity, transcription initiation) that do not use Hi-C contact maps

skills.description: Use when a multi-input deep learning model combines two feature extractors (e.g. dna2vec and motif features) and you must quantify whether fusion outperforms each module trained alone across multiple cell lines.
skills.name: ablation-study-performance-comparison
skills.search_text: ablation-study-performance-comparison Use when a multi-input deep learning model combines two feature extractors (e.g. dna2vec and motif features) and you must quantify whether fusion outperforms each module trained alone across multiple cell lines. Input is already an extracted feature table — this skill covers the full extraction (dna2vec_code.py, motif_find.py), training, and evaluation pipeline The goal is cross-cell-line prediction via transfer learning or motif interpretation via SHAP.py rather than module-ablation performance comparison Only a single feature type is available (e.g. no HOCOMOCO PWMs or pre-trained dna2vec vectors), so the dna2vec-only vs motif-only vs combined contrast cannot be constructed http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Reproduce a module-combination ablation for Enhancer-MDLF: train dna2vec-only, motif-only, and combined multi-input variants per cell line and compare all reported metrics on independent test sets to quantify the benefit of feature fusion for cell-specific enhancer prediction. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbae083
skills.summary: Reproduce a module-combination ablation for Enhancer-MDLF: train dna2vec-only, motif-only, and combined multi-input variants per cell line and compare all reported metrics on independent test sets to quantify the benefit of feature fusion for cell-specific enhancer prediction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an extracted feature table — this skill covers the full extraction (dna2vec_code.py, motif_find.py), training, and evaluation pipeline The goal is cross-cell-line prediction via transfer learning or motif interpretation via SHAP.py rather than module-ablation performance comparison Only a single feature type is available (e.g. no HOCOMOCO PWMs or pre-trained dna2vec vectors), so the dna2vec-only vs motif-only vs combined contrast cannot be constructed

skills.description: Use when raw FASTQ reads (single- or pair-ended NGS data, e.g. ChIP-seq/RNA-seq/ATAC-seq) must be cleaned of adapters, low-quality bases, and short or poorly mapping reads before alignment and downstream peak calling, differential expression, or nucleosome positioning.
skills.name: adapter-trimming-quality-filtering
skills.search_text: adapter-trimming-quality-filtering Use when raw FASTQ reads (single- or pair-ended NGS data, e.g. ChIP-seq/RNA-seq/ATAC-seq) must be cleaned of adapters, low-quality bases, and short or poorly mapping reads before alignment and downstream peak calling, differential expression, or nucleosome positioning. The workflow file must not mix single-ended and pair-ended data in the same CONFIG file — CIPHER does not handle that use-case (split them into separate runs). Only a single downstream tool (e.g. just a mapper or just a peak caller) is wanted — CIPHER currently only runs entire workflows, not subsets of tools. Input reads are already adapter-trimmed and quality-filtered by another tool; re-running trimming would be redundant. http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 The CIPHER pre-processing stage that evaluates raw reads (FastQC), trims adapters and removes low-quality or too-short reads (BBDuk, dropping reads with mapq < 20 or length < 10 during/after mapping with BBMap), and aggregates quality control (MultiQC) before any dataset-type-specific downstream analysis. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-017-1770-1
skills.summary: The CIPHER pre-processing stage that evaluates raw reads (FastQC), trims adapters and removes low-quality or too-short reads (BBDuk, dropping reads with mapq < 20 or length < 10 during/after mapping with BBMap), and aggregates quality control (MultiQC) before any dataset-type-specific downstream analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The workflow file must not mix single-ended and pair-ended data in the same CONFIG file — CIPHER does not handle that use-case (split them into separate runs). Only a single downstream tool (e.g. just a mapper or just a peak caller) is wanted — CIPHER currently only runs entire workflows, not subsets of tools. Input reads are already adapter-trimmed and quality-filtered by another tool; re-running trimming would be redundant.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a motif-based classifier (e.g., BOM) against a pretrained sequence model on binary or multiclass distal-CRE classification across cell types, and Enformer must be fine-tuned on identical train/test partitions.
skills.name: adaptive-head-transfer-learning-enformer
skills.search_text: adaptive-head-transfer-learning-enformer Use when benchmarking a motif-based classifier (e.g., BOM) against a pretrained sequence model on binary or multiclass distal-CRE classification across cell types, and Enformer must be fine-tuned on identical train/test partitions. Enhancer activity depends on open chromatin, histone marks, or sequence context beyond the cropped CRE window, which BOM/Enformer-style cis-only models cannot capture The goal is direct motif-level interpretability of a regulatory vocabulary from motif counts — use BOM (XGBoost + SHAP) instead of fine-tuning a deep model Training data for the cell state is too limited, since sequence-based deep learning performance is linked to the limited amount of data available per cell state http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Adapts the pretrained Enformer transformer to a new cell-type-specific CRE classification task by attaching an adaptive head of two fully connected linear layers, re-cropping Enformer's input to focus precisely on each CRE of interest, and exploring the hyperparameter space — used as a deep-learning baseline to benchmark BOM. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-65362-2
skills.summary: Adapts the pretrained Enformer transformer to a new cell-type-specific CRE classification task by attaching an adaptive head of two fully connected linear layers, re-cropping Enformer's input to focus precisely on each CRE of interest, and exploring the hyperparameter space — used as a deep-learning baseline to benchmark BOM.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Enhancer activity depends on open chromatin, histone marks, or sequence context beyond the cropped CRE window, which BOM/Enformer-style cis-only models cannot capture The goal is direct motif-level interpretability of a regulatory vocabulary from motif counts — use BOM (XGBoost + SHAP) instead of fine-tuning a deep model Training data for the cell state is too limited, since sequence-based deep learning performance is linked to the limited amount of data available per cell state

skills.description: Use when two cluster label vectors cover the same set of cells and you need a chance-corrected score of clustering stability, e.g. before vs. after removing CNV-harboring chromosome peaks from a scATAC accessibility matrix.
skills.name: adjusted-mutual-information-comparison
skills.search_text: adjusted-mutual-information-comparison Use when two cluster label vectors cover the same set of cells and you need a chance-corrected score of clustering stability, e.g. before vs. after removing CNV-harboring chromosome peaks from a scATAC accessibility matrix. The two cluster assignments cover different sets of cells — AMI must be computed on the shared cell set only You need to compare partitions of different cardinality or with unpaired labels rather than per-cell matched assignments The goal is assessing CNV inference quality itself rather than stability of downstream cell clustering http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Quantifies concordance between two cluster assignments of the same cells using adjusted mutual information (AMI), as used in Copy-scAT to test whether removing CNV-bearing peaks changes scATAC clustering structure (reported AMI = 0.634, Fig. 4I). epigenomics/v2 10.1126/sciadv.abg6045
skills.summary: Quantifies concordance between two cluster assignments of the same cells using adjusted mutual information (AMI), as used in Copy-scAT to test whether removing CNV-bearing peaks changes scATAC clustering structure (reported AMI = 0.634, Fig. 4I).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The two cluster assignments cover different sets of cells — AMI must be computed on the shared cell set only You need to compare partitions of different cardinality or with unpaired labels rather than per-cell matched assignments The goal is assessing CNV inference quality itself rather than stability of downstream cell clustering

skills.description: Use when comparing TLD/TAD partitions predicted by multiple algorithms (e.g., deDoc2, deTOKI, scHiCluster, Higashi) on downsampled, simulated, or single-cell Hi-C matrices at 40 kb binsize and you need an accuracy ranking.
skills.name: adjusted-mutual-information-evaluation
skills.search_text: adjusted-mutual-information-evaluation Use when comparing TLD/TAD partitions predicted by multiple algorithms (e.g., deDoc2, deTOKI, scHiCluster, Higashi) on downsampled, simulated, or single-cell Hi-C matrices at 40 kb binsize and you need an accuracy ranking. The task is TLD prediction itself rather than benchmarking — use deDoc2.w/deDoc2.s directly on the contact matrix instead of computing comparison metrics Predictions and references come from different genomic regions or binsizes (e.g., mixing 40 kb with other resolutions), making the bin-level partition comparison invalid No reference (raw-data or ground-truth) TLD partition exists — AMI/WS are undefined without a reference partition in K http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Benchmark protocol for scoring TAD-like domain (TLD) predictions from sparse or single-cell Hi-C by computing adjusted mutual information (AMI) between predicted and reference partitions, complemented by weighted similarity (WS) against raw-data TLDs. epigenomics/v2 10.1002/advs.202300366
skills.summary: Benchmark protocol for scoring TAD-like domain (TLD) predictions from sparse or single-cell Hi-C by computing adjusted mutual information (AMI) between predicted and reference partitions, complemented by weighted similarity (WS) against raw-data TLDs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is TLD prediction itself rather than benchmarking — use deDoc2.w/deDoc2.s directly on the contact matrix instead of computing comparison metrics Predictions and references come from different genomic regions or binsizes (e.g., mixing 40 kb with other resolutions), making the bin-level partition comparison invalid No reference (raw-data or ground-truth) TLD partition exists — AMI/WS are undefined without a reference partition in K

skills.description: Use when comparing two genome partition/TLD call sets — e.g., predictions from noise-perturbed vs. original downsampled Hi-C matrices — to measure how much domain structure is preserved.
skills.name: adjusted-mutual-information-partition-comparison
skills.search_text: adjusted-mutual-information-partition-comparison Use when comparing two genome partition/TLD call sets — e.g., predictions from noise-perturbed vs. original downsampled Hi-C matrices — to measure how much domain structure is preserved. When comparing raw contact matrices rather than discrete partition/domain predictions — AMI operates on bin-level partition labels, not contact frequencies When the two call sets come from different bin sizes or genomic coordinates, since bins cannot be aligned into comparable partition vectors When you need boundary-level accuracy rather than partition-level agreement; the article's WS excludes intermediate windows of domains, and boundary-specific metrics would be a different analysis http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Quantifies agreement between two sets of genomic partition predictions (e.g., TLDs predicted from noisy vs. original downsampled Hi-C matrices) using adjusted mutual information (AMI) from scikit-learn, complemented by weighted similarity (WS), to assess robustness of TLD predictors such as deDoc2 to data noise. epigenomics/v2 10.1002/advs.202300366
skills.summary: Quantifies agreement between two sets of genomic partition predictions (e.g., TLDs predicted from noisy vs. original downsampled Hi-C matrices) using adjusted mutual information (AMI) from scikit-learn, complemented by weighted similarity (WS), to assess robustness of TLD predictors such as deDoc2 to data noise.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When comparing raw contact matrices rather than discrete partition/domain predictions — AMI operates on bin-level partition labels, not contact frequencies When the two call sets come from different bin sizes or genomic coordinates, since bins cannot be aligned into comparable partition vectors When you need boundary-level accuracy rather than partition-level agreement; the article's WS excludes intermediate windows of domains, and boundary-specific metrics would be a different analysis

skills.description: Use when scoring clustering quality of single-cell epigenomic methods against known ground-truth cell labels (e.g. sorted cell lines), comparing methods such as ChromSCape, SnapATAC, CisTopic, Cusanovich2018 and EpiScanpy on a shared dataset.
skills.name: adjusted-rand-index-computation
skills.search_text: adjusted-rand-index-computation Use when scoring clustering quality of single-cell epigenomic methods against known ground-truth cell labels (e.g. sorted cell lines), comparing methods such as ChromSCape, SnapATAC, CisTopic, Cusanovich2018 and EpiScanpy on a shared dataset. Cells have no known ground-truth labels (e.g. real tissue without sorted populations) — ARI against a reference partition cannot be computed. Input is a raw count matrix with no clustering or reduced feature space yet — this skill scores partitions; it does not cluster or reduce dimensions itself. Assessing continuous embeddings or pairwise cell similarities rather than agreement between two discrete partitions. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Computes the adjusted Rand index (ARI) between hierarchical-cluster assignments on each method's reduced feature space and known ground-truth cell-line labels, used to benchmark ChromSCape (ARI 0.998) against Cusanovich2018, SnapATAC, CisTopic and EpiScanpy on an in-silico H3K27me3 four-cell-type scChIP-seq mix. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-19542-x
skills.summary: Computes the adjusted Rand index (ARI) between hierarchical-cluster assignments on each method's reduced feature space and known ground-truth cell-line labels, used to benchmark ChromSCape (ARI 0.998) against Cusanovich2018, SnapATAC, CisTopic and EpiScanpy on an in-silico H3K27me3 four-cell-type scChIP-seq mix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Cells have no known ground-truth labels (e.g. real tissue without sorted populations) — ARI against a reference partition cannot be computed. Input is a raw count matrix with no clustering or reduced feature space yet — this skill scores partitions; it does not cluster or reduce dimensions itself. Assessing continuous embeddings or pairwise cell similarities rather than agreement between two discrete partitions.

skills.description: Use when you have age-ordered omics or feature trajectories (e.g., PBMC aging series from ATAC-seq/RNA-seq of adults aged 22-93) and need to detect abrupt age windows of rapid epigenomic or transcriptomic change rather than assuming gradual accumulation.
skills.name: age-breakpoint-detection-in-temporal-omics
skills.search_text: age-breakpoint-detection-in-temporal-omics Use when you have age-ordered omics or feature trajectories (e.g., PBMC aging series from ATAC-seq/RNA-seq of adults aged 22-93) and need to detect abrupt age windows of rapid epigenomic or transcriptomic change rather than assuming gradual accumulation. The data are cross-sectional samples without an ordered age axis, so no before/after age windows can be compared The goal is cell-type-resolved or single-cell sex-difference testing — the source study notes its bulk PBMC annotation approach 'is prone to biases in references' and that sex differences have not yet been described at single-cell resolution You expect strictly gradual change and only need a regression/trajectory fit; the moving-window MANOVA is designed to flag abrupt spikes, not model smooth trends http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 A moving-window breakpoint analysis that tests whether age-related changes in temporal omics series (e.g., PBMC ATAC-seq/RNA-seq aging trajectories) accumulate gradually or spike abruptly at specific ages, using MANOVA on PCA-reduced windows, LOESS-smoothed p-values combined by Fisher's method, and Mclust to call breakpoint ages. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-14396-9
skills.summary: A moving-window breakpoint analysis that tests whether age-related changes in temporal omics series (e.g., PBMC ATAC-seq/RNA-seq aging trajectories) accumulate gradually or spike abruptly at specific ages, using MANOVA on PCA-reduced windows, LOESS-smoothed p-values combined by Fisher's method, and Mclust to call breakpoint ages.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are cross-sectional samples without an ordered age axis, so no before/after age windows can be compared The goal is cell-type-resolved or single-cell sex-difference testing — the source study notes its bulk PBMC annotation approach 'is prone to biases in references' and that sex differences have not yet been described at single-cell resolution You expect strictly gradual change and only need a regression/trajectory fit; the moving-window MANOVA is designed to flag abrupt spikes, not model smooth trends

skills.description: Use when donor-level PCA coordinates (e.g., PC1 scores) from ATAC-seq or RNA-seq are available together with donor age and sex metadata, and the goal is to confirm that the top PC axis tracks aging and sex-dimorphism.
skills.name: age-correlation-analysis-of-pc1-scores
skills.search_text: age-correlation-analysis-of-pc1-scores Use when donor-level PCA coordinates (e.g., PC1 scores) from ATAC-seq or RNA-seq are available together with donor age and sex metadata, and the goal is to confirm that the top PC axis tracks aging and sex-dimorphism. Input data lacks donor age or sex metadata, so the age correlation and older-cohort sex contrast cannot be computed The analysis targets single-cell resolution or sorted-cell data, which the paper explicitly defers to future studies Only flow cytometry cell-frequency data are available without genome-wide ATAC-seq/RNA-seq PCA coordinates http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Verifies that PC1 from PCA of PBMC ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data captures age-driven variation by correlating per-donor PC1 scores with age, checking variance explained (~15% ATAC-seq, ~18.6% RNA-seq), and testing whether older men show higher PC1 than older women via a Wilcoxon rank-sum test. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-14396-9
skills.summary: Verifies that PC1 from PCA of PBMC ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data captures age-driven variation by correlating per-donor PC1 scores with age, checking variance explained (~15% ATAC-seq, ~18.6% RNA-seq), and testing whether older men show higher PC1 than older women via a Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data lacks donor age or sex metadata, so the age correlation and older-cohort sex contrast cannot be computed The analysis targets single-cell resolution or sorted-cell data, which the paper explicitly defers to future studies Only flow cytometry cell-frequency data are available without genome-wide ATAC-seq/RNA-seq PCA coordinates

skills.description: Use when you need to group peak regions from one or more ChIP-seq marks by signal-shape similarity without anchors such as TSSs or gene annotation, using DTW distances between binned coverage profiles.
skills.name: agglomerative-hierarchical-clustering-of-genomic-peaks
skills.search_text: agglomerative-hierarchical-clustering-of-genomic-peaks Use when you need to group peak regions from one or more ChIP-seq marks by signal-shape similarity without anchors such as TSSs or gene annotation, using DTW distances between binned coverage profiles. You have gene/TSS annotations available and prefer annotation-anchored alignment rather than unsupervised shape-based clustering Peaks are shorter than 5 bins or longer than 1000 bins (50 bp bins) or lack any bin with more than 10 reads — these are excluded by the DGW filters Standard Euclidean-profile hierarchical clustering suffices: the article shows standard hierarchical clustering only succeeds when added noise and modifications are small (v<0.15, p<0.15), so evaluate whether DTW is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3307 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Clusters epigenomic ChIP-seq peak regions by shape using agglomerative hierarchical clustering with complete linkage over strand-aware Dynamic Time Warping distances, as implemented in the DGW package for ENCODE K562 histone mark data (H3K4me3, H3K9ac). epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-016-1306-0
skills.summary: Clusters epigenomic ChIP-seq peak regions by shape using agglomerative hierarchical clustering with complete linkage over strand-aware Dynamic Time Warping distances, as implemented in the DGW package for ENCODE K562 histone mark data (H3K4me3, H3K9ac).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have gene/TSS annotations available and prefer annotation-anchored alignment rather than unsupervised shape-based clustering Peaks are shorter than 5 bins or longer than 1000 bins (50 bp bins) or lack any bin with more than 10 reads — these are excluded by the DGW filters Standard Euclidean-profile hierarchical clustering suffices: the article shows standard hierarchical clustering only succeeds when added noise and modifications are small (v<0.15, p<0.15), so evaluate whether DTW is needed

skills.description: Use when comparing CTCF-mediated loop callers (e.g., GILoop vs. Peakachu) on Hi-C contact maps and you need a threshold-independent visual/quantitative check that predicted loops are enriched in real contact signal, via APA z-scores computed around each caller's predicted loops.
skills.name: aggregate-peak-analysis-zscore
skills.search_text: aggregate-peak-analysis-zscore Use when comparing CTCF-mediated loop callers (e.g., GILoop vs. Peakachu) on Hi-C contact maps and you need a threshold-independent visual/quantitative check that predicted loops are enriched in real contact signal, via APA z-scores computed around each caller's predicted loops. Input is extremely sparse single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) data — the article states GILoop 'only focuses on bulk Hi-C' and is not capable of dealing with scHi-C You need absolute loop calls rather than a comparative quality assessment of existing caller predictions (APA here is a benchmarking readout, not a caller) The targeted cell line's sequencing depth differs from all pre-trained models in the repository, where the article warns of 'weak usability' http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Aggregate peak analysis (APA) with z-score enrichment to quantify whether a chromatin loop caller's predicted loops concentrate Hi-C contact signal at the loop center, used alongside PR curves and well-supported-loop recovery to benchmark GILoop against Peakachu (full and non-clustering) on the 520 million-read GM12878 Hi-C dataset. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2022.105535
skills.summary: Aggregate peak analysis (APA) with z-score enrichment to quantify whether a chromatin loop caller's predicted loops concentrate Hi-C contact signal at the loop center, used alongside PR curves and well-supported-loop recovery to benchmark GILoop against Peakachu (full and non-clustering) on the 520 million-read GM12878 Hi-C dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is extremely sparse single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) data — the article states GILoop 'only focuses on bulk Hi-C' and is not capable of dealing with scHi-C You need absolute loop calls rather than a comparative quality assessment of existing caller predictions (APA here is a benchmarking readout, not a caller) The targeted cell line's sequencing depth differs from all pre-trained models in the repository, where the article warns of 'weak usability'

skills.description: Decision support for choosing the number of sub-compartments (N_subcompartment) when running CscoreTool-M on Hi-C data, where no prior annotation fixes the compartment count.
skills.name: aic-likelihood-based-model-selection
skills.search_text: aic-likelihood-based-model-selection Decision support for choosing the number of sub-compartments (N_subcompartment) when running CscoreTool-M on Hi-C data, where no prior annotation fixes the compartment count. The compartment count is already fixed by prior biological annotation or a published sub-compartment assignment — no model selection sweep is needed Input Hi-C data is single-compartment analysis only (A/B compartments via PCA, e.g. HOMER runHiCpca.pl), since AIC selection applies to the multi-sub-compartment model The tool being tuned is not a likelihood-based probabilistic model, because AIC = 2k − 2lnL requires a maximized log-likelihood from each candidate fit Selects the statistically optimal number of sub-compartments for CscoreTool-M by sweeping the N_subcompartment argument, extracting the maximum log-likelihood from each run, and choosing the model with minimum AIC = 2k − 2lnL on down-sampled GM12878 Hi-C data. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad314
skills.summary: Selects the statistically optimal number of sub-compartments for CscoreTool-M by sweeping the N_subcompartment argument, extracting the maximum log-likelihood from each run, and choosing the model with minimum AIC = 2k − 2lnL on down-sampled GM12878 Hi-C data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The compartment count is already fixed by prior biological annotation or a published sub-compartment assignment — no model selection sweep is needed Input Hi-C data is single-compartment analysis only (A/B compartments via PCA, e.g. HOMER runHiCpca.pl), since AIC selection applies to the multi-sub-compartment model The tool being tuned is not a likelihood-based probabilistic model, because AIC = 2k − 2lnL requires a maximized log-likelihood from each candidate fit

skills.description: Use when you have a feature-by-donor abundance matrix (peaks or genes) from chronological samples and need to distinguish true age-driven longitudinal trends from noise before clustering trajectories.
skills.name: aic-model-order-selection
skills.search_text: aic-model-order-selection Use when you have a feature-by-donor abundance matrix (peaks or genes) from chronological samples and need to distinguish true age-driven longitudinal trends from noise before clustering trajectories. Data are cross-sectional with no donor age ordering, so no chronological series can be fit per feature Goal is differential abundance between conditions rather than identifying age-ordered temporal trends Features have already been clustered into age trajectories and only downstream functional enrichment or breakpoint analysis is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Identifies longitudinal age-trends in PBMC ATAC-seq/RNA-seq features by fitting auto.arima models per feature across an age-ordered donor series, selecting the minimum-AIC model, and retaining features whose selected ARIMA order (differencing plus AR/MA terms) indicates a genuine temporal trend rather than random fluctuation. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-14396-9
skills.summary: Identifies longitudinal age-trends in PBMC ATAC-seq/RNA-seq features by fitting auto.arima models per feature across an age-ordered donor series, selecting the minimum-AIC model, and retaining features whose selected ARIMA order (differencing plus AR/MA terms) indicates a genuine temporal trend rather than random fluctuation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are cross-sectional with no donor age ordering, so no chronological series can be fit per feature Goal is differential abundance between conditions rather than identifying age-ordered temporal trends Features have already been clustered into age trajectories and only downstream functional enrichment or breakpoint analysis is needed

skills.description: Use when binary RRBS read matrices Y (reads x CpGs) at a locus must be partitioned into an unknown number of epialleles and Q must be chosen without manual specification or overfitting.
skills.name: aic-model-selection
skills.search_text: aic-model-selection Use when binary RRBS read matrices Y (reads x CpGs) at a locus must be partitioned into an unknown number of epialleles and Q must be chosen without manual specification or overfitting. Loci with fewer than six CpGs, median read depth below 100, more than 25% missing data, or on chromosomes X and Y Loci observed in fewer than two samples, since pooling reads across tissue samples is required to determine the number of distinct epialleles Analyses requiring phasing of reads between disjoint loci, which the approach cannot do http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Selects the optimal number of Bayesian epialleles (Q) present at an RRBS locus by fitting the BED model across candidate Q values and minimising AIC(Q) = -2 log p(Y|X_hat, w_hat, epsilon_hat, Q) + 2*Q*d, where the Q*d epiallele matrix entries are counted as free parameters. This avoids overfitting while allowing the likelihood gain to justify extra epialleles. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-017-1753-2
skills.summary: Selects the optimal number of Bayesian epialleles (Q) present at an RRBS locus by fitting the BED model across candidate Q values and minimising AIC(Q) = -2 log p(Y|X_hat, w_hat, epsilon_hat, Q) + 2*Q*d, where the Q*d epiallele matrix entries are counted as free parameters. This avoids overfitting while allowing the likelihood gain to justify extra epialleles.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Loci with fewer than six CpGs, median read depth below 100, more than 25% missing data, or on chromosomes X and Y Loci observed in fewer than two samples, since pooling reads across tissue samples is required to determine the number of distinct epialleles Analyses requiring phasing of reads between disjoint loci, which the approach cannot do

skills.description: Use when an NGS workflow's alignment step dominates compute time (e.g. a 6-8 h baseline on 100 mammalian FASTQ files) and a decision is needed on whether swapping to HISAT2 or Rsubread within systemPipeR reduces it below ~3 h.
skills.name: aligner-runtime-benchmarking
skills.search_text: aligner-runtime-benchmarking Use when an NGS workflow's alignment step dominates compute time (e.g. a 6-8 h baseline on 100 mammalian FASTQ files) and a decision is needed on whether swapping to HISAT2 or Rsubread within systemPipeR reduces it below ~3 h. The input is already aligned (e.g. BAM or a feature/counts table) — no alignment step exists to benchmark or swap. When the input is raw multi-track epigenomic signal matrices rather than single-track state sequences produced by an annotation method such as ChromHMM. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 EpiAlign's local-alignment scores are driven by weight-scaled penalties — mismatch/N-gap NF = -epsilon_N*(W(k,S1)+W(l,S2)) and deletion DF(k,S) = -epsilon_D*W(k,S), with defaults epsilon_N=1.5 and epsilon_D=1 — combined with a chromatin state-weight scheme (equal W=1 vs frequency-based weights favoring rarer states). epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz287

skills.search_text: allele-stratification-by-detection-efficiency Use when evaluating how per-allele data quality (fraction of detected targeted segments in chromatin tracing/FISH data) affects chromatin loop caller sensitivity or false-positive discovery, or when deciding a detection-efficiency cutoff before loop calling. Input is bulk Hi-C / proximity-ligation data with count-based contacts — SnapFISH's Euclidean-distance local background T-test framework is designed for imaging-based tracing data, not count matrices. The goal is to detect a novel loop de novo in a full dataset, not to benchmark caller sensitivity — stratifying by detection efficiency reduces sample size and is a quality-control/benchmarking manipulation. skills.search_text: analytic-vs-empirical-power-comparison Use when validating or trusting scPower power estimates for low-mean eQTL genes, i.e. when pseudobulk mean expression falls below the regime where the analytic linear-model approximation holds and simulation is needed as a cross-check. The goal is to power large eQTL cohorts with hundreds of samples — simulation-based validation scales poorly, since larger data sets required for eQTL studies are very difficult to simulate Genes have sufficient pseudobulk mean expression (mean >= 5), where the analytic linear-model approximation is already accurate and simulation adds little The task is DEG power analysis or experimental-parameter optimization, where the analytic method should be used directly instead of simulations http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmark scPower's analytic eQTL power formula against an empirical simulation for genes whose pseudobulk mean expression is too small (mean < 5) for the analytic linear-model approximation to be accurate, using scPower's expression probability model to assign gene means. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-26779-7
skills.summary: Benchmark scPower's analytic eQTL power formula against an empirical simulation for genes whose pseudobulk mean expression is too small (mean < 5) for the analytic linear-model approximation to be accurate, using scPower's expression probability model to assign gene means.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to power large eQTL cohorts with hundreds of samples — simulation-based validation scales poorly, since larger data sets required for eQTL studies are very difficult to simulate Genes have sufficient pseudobulk mean expression (mean >= 5), where the analytic linear-model approximation is already accurate and simulation adds little The task is DEG power analysis or experimental-parameter optimization, where the analytic method should be used directly instead of simulations

skills.search_text: ari-clustering-agreement-evaluation Use when a clustering method's output assignments must be compared against known cell-type labels on single-cell data (e.g., scATAC-seq Forebrain, k=8), or when ARI degradation under graded input corruption must be tabulated across tools. When no ground-truth cell labels exist for the dataset — ARI cannot be computed against unknown clusters When the goal is batch-effect removal or data integration rather than clustering accuracy assessment — SCALE is 'not specifically designed to identify and remove batch effects' and ARI alone does not measure integration quality Compute the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between algorithm cluster assignments (e.g., Leiden clusters stored in SCALE's adata.h5ad output) and known cell labels to quantify clustering accuracy, optionally across graded corruption levels to measure robustness to data sparsity. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-12630-7

skills.description: Use when you have a normalized, filtered binned scATAC-seq accessibility matrix and need per-cell chromosome arm-level gains/losses (e.g., to separate malignant from nonmalignant cells or define genetic subclones).
skills.name: arm-level-copy-number-calling
skills.search_text: arm-level-copy-number-calling Use when you have a normalized, filtered binned scATAC-seq accessibility matrix and need per-cell chromosome arm-level gains/losses (e.g., to separate malignant from nonmalignant cells or define genetic subclones). Tumors driven primarily by single nucleotide variants with no or rare CNVs — the article notes Copy-scAT cannot be used in this setting since arm-level calling depends on CNV signals Task requires focal amplification calling rather than arm-level gains and losses — a separate focal-level workflow is used for focal amplifications Input is a raw fragment file rather than a filtered, normalized binned accessibility matrix — run process_fragment_file.py and filterCells/normalizeMatrixN first http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Calls chromosome arm-level copy number alterations per cell from binned scATAC-seq accessibility data using Copy-scAT: bins are collapsed to chromosome arms (CpG-island-length weighted, trimmed-mean summarized, log transformed), a modeled pseudodiploid control is generated, and Gaussian mixture models (Mclust) fit per cell are compared to that control to assign arm-level CNV states. epigenomics/v2 10.1126/sciadv.abg6045
skills.summary: Calls chromosome arm-level copy number alterations per cell from binned scATAC-seq accessibility data using Copy-scAT: bins are collapsed to chromosome arms (CpG-island-length weighted, trimmed-mean summarized, log transformed), a modeled pseudodiploid control is generated, and Gaussian mixture models (Mclust) fit per cell are compared to that control to assign arm-level CNV states.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Tumors driven primarily by single nucleotide variants with no or rare CNVs — the article notes Copy-scAT cannot be used in this setting since arm-level calling depends on CNV signals Task requires focal amplification calling rather than arm-level gains and losses — a separate focal-level workflow is used for focal amplifications Input is a raw fragment file rather than a filtered, normalized binned accessibility matrix — run process_fragment_file.py and filterCells/normalizeMatrixN first

skills.description: Use when you have per-sample ChIP-seq/DNase-seq QC metrics (FRiP, PBC, fragment size, mapping rate) and need to test whether metric correlations differ across assay categories before pooling them.
skills.name: assay-category-stratified-statistics
skills.search_text: assay-category-stratified-statistics Use when you have per-sample ChIP-seq/DNase-seq QC metrics (FRiP, PBC, fragment size, mapping rate) and need to test whether metric correlations differ across assay categories before pooling them. The analysis goal is overall sample QC rather than inter-metric correlation structure — use the per-sample ChiLin QC report instead. Samples cannot be reliably assigned to a literature-based assay category, since stratification is the core of the method and pooled correlations will be misleading. Fewer samples per category than needed to support a stable 13x13 pairwise correlation matrix. http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Compile per-sample QC metrics from ChiLin JSON outputs into a flat table, stratify samples into literature-based assay categories (accessibility, TF, chromatin regulator, histone modification, DNase), and compute within-category pairwise correlations (e.g., FRiP vs peak number, DNase FRiP vs fragment size) to expose relationships that differ by assay type. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-016-1274-4
skills.summary: Compile per-sample QC metrics from ChiLin JSON outputs into a flat table, stratify samples into literature-based assay categories (accessibility, TF, chromatin regulator, histone modification, DNase), and compute within-category pairwise correlations (e.g., FRiP vs peak number, DNase FRiP vs fragment size) to expose relationships that differ by assay type.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is overall sample QC rather than inter-metric correlation structure — use the per-sample ChiLin QC report instead. skills.search_text: assembly-quality-assessment-with-quast Use when two shotgun read sets (e.g. a chemically treated library such as RIMS-seq and its untreated control) have each been assembled de novo and you must quantify whether treatment altered assembly quality via N50 and mismatch rate. skills.summary: Evaluates de novo bacterial genome assemblies produced from paired-end reads (e.g. RIMS-seq alkaline-treated vs DNA-seq(+3H) control) by running Quast on each SPAdes contigs FASTA and comparing key metrics — specifically N50 and mismatch rate — to establish that a modified library protocol did not degrade assembly quality.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sequencing library was prepared by tagmentation or other non-adapter-ligation protocols — RIMS-seq data themselves are not valid inputs in that case An exactly matching reference genome is available and the analysis will be mapping-based rather than de novo assembly (the RIMS-seq pipeline's option 2 path, where SPAdes assembly is not needed) The question concerns methylase specificity discovery (motif calling) rather than assembly-quality metrics

skills.description: Use when you have ATAC-seq (or similar accessibility) data for two cell types and want sequences ±100 bp around an anchor motif scored by a log2 fold-change so downstream motif analysis can test whether motif spacing correlates with cell-type-specific accessibility.
skills.name: atac-seq-differential-accessibility-scoring
skills.search_text: atac-seq-differential-accessibility-scoring Use when you have ATAC-seq (or similar accessibility) data for two cell types and want sequences ±100 bp around an anchor motif scored by a log2 fold-change so downstream motif analysis can test whether motif spacing correlates with cell-type-specific accessibility. skills.summary: Compute a continuous differential chromatin accessibility score (e.g. log2 fold change of HCT116-vs-K562 ATAC-seq signal) for short genomic windows anchored on transcription factor motifs (GATA1), so that position-aware motif enrichment methods like MEPP can correlate motif position with cell-type-specific accessibility.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need motif presence/absence enrichment without positional information — bin- or quartile-based MEA tools (CentriMo, TFEA) or a ZOOPs-model tool like HOMER suffice You need de novo motif discovery: MEPP currently only functions with a fixed motif library and de novo motif recognition/assembly is left to future work Your sequences are not anchored on a defined feature (TSS or known motif) — the positional profile requires a biologically meaningful anchor point for the correlation to be interpretable

skills.description: Use when you need to derive a TF-target gene prior from open-chromatin ATAC-seq peaks (e.g. the TCGA Genomic Data Commons ATACseq-AWG atlas) to constrain a neural decoder's TF-to-gene layer, as in CITRUS.
skills.name: atacseq-peak-gene-annotation
skills.search_text: atacseq-peak-gene-annotation Use when you need to derive a TF-target gene prior from open-chromatin ATAC-seq peaks (e.g. the TCGA Genomic Data Commons ATACseq-AWG atlas) to constrain a neural decoder's TF-to-gene layer, as in CITRUS. You already have a curated TF-target gene matrix (e.g. packaged in dataset_CITRUS.pkl) — regenerating the prior from peaks is redundant Your analysis requires TF-target directionality (activation vs. repression) or co-binding TF complexes (e.g. AP-1–IRF) — this binary prior intentionally omits both You need to disambiguate TFs of the same family sharing near-identical motifs — the Jaccard > 0.5 deduplication collapses them http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 Constructs a binary TF-target gene prior matrix by scanning pan-cancer ATAC-seq open-chromatin peaks for TF motifs (FIMO vs. MEME-curated cis-BP at P < 1e-5), then assigning each motif-bearing peak to its nearest gene and binarizing into a {0,1} matrix (320 TF motifs x 5541 genes) that constrains CITRUS's decoder TF-to-gene connections. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkac881
skills.summary: Constructs a binary TF-target gene prior matrix by scanning pan-cancer ATAC-seq open-chromatin peaks for TF motifs (FIMO vs. MEME-curated cis-BP at P < 1e-5), then assigning each motif-bearing peak to its nearest gene and binarizing into a {0,1} matrix (320 TF motifs x 5541 genes) that constrains CITRUS's decoder TF-to-gene connections.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have a curated TF-target gene matrix (e.g. packaged in dataset_CITRUS.pkl) — regenerating the prior from peaks is redundant Your analysis requires TF-target directionality (activation vs. repression) or co-binding TF complexes (e.g. AP-1–IRF) — this binary prior intentionally omits both You need to disambiguate TFs of the same family sharing near-identical motifs — the Jaccard > 0.5 deduplication collapses them

skills.description: Use when a high-dimensional matrix (e.g., gene expression or CpG methylation) needs a feature-selection score for subgroup/consensus partitioning, especially when features should be ranked by their global correlation to other rows rather than by variance.
skills.name: atc-score-reconstruction
skills.search_text: atc-score-reconstruction Use when a high-dimensional matrix (e.g., gene expression or CpG methylation) needs a feature-selection score for subgroup/consensus partitioning, especially when features should be ranked by their global correlation to other rows rather than by variance. The matrix is already a small, curated feature table where no further feature ranking is needed before clustering The goal is a per-row dispersion-based ranking (SD, MAD, CV) and the global correlation structure is irrelevant to the analysis The dataset is single-cell RNA-Seq with several thousands of cells, where cola's runtime and memory usage may be unacceptable http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Reconstruct the ATC (ability to correlate to other rows) top-value scoring method from the cola R/Bioconductor framework, which assigns each matrix row a score in [0,1] based on the global correlation structure of that row to all other rows, so that the highest-scored rows can be selected for consensus partitioning. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa1146
skills.summary: Reconstruct the ATC (ability to correlate to other rows) top-value scoring method from the cola R/Bioconductor framework, which assigns each matrix row a score in [0,1] based on the global correlation structure of that row to all other rows, so that the highest-scored rows can be selected for consensus partitioning.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The matrix is already a small, curated feature table where no further feature ranking is needed before clustering The goal is a per-row dispersion-based ranking (SD, MAD, CV) and the global correlation structure is irrelevant to the analysis The dataset is single-cell RNA-Seq with several thousands of cells, where cola's runtime and memory usage may be unacceptable

skills.name: auc-metric-computation
skills.search_text: auc-metric-computation Use when a ranked, score-filtered list of candidate target regions (e.g. from adaptive_liftover plus gr_candidate_filter) must be evaluated against matched orthologous ground-truth regions, or when tuning a window-size parameter via AUROC/AUPR in leave-one-out cross-validation. There is no matched orthologous ground truth (e.g. no corresponding human epigenome peaks for the held-out dataset), so positives/negatives cannot be defined and AUROC/AUPR are meaningless. Candidate regions are unscored peak intervals that have not yet gone through adaptive_liftover, similarity computation, and gr_candidate_filter — ranking-based AUC evaluation would be premature. The task is parameter learning rather than evaluation: use training_module() to estimate logistic regression parameters and suggest an optimal score threshold instead. Computes area under the ROC (AUROC) and area under the PR (AUPR) curves to evaluate how well AdaLiftOver's scored candidate target regions rank true orthologous regions, sweeping the query-extension window size over a LOOCV grid to select the optimal local window. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad149
skills.summary: Computes area under the ROC (AUROC) and area under the PR (AUPR) curves to evaluate how well AdaLiftOver's scored candidate target regions rank true orthologous regions, sweeping the query-extension window size over a LOOCV grid to select the optimal local window.
skills.when_to_use_negative: There is no matched orthologous ground truth (e.g. no corresponding human epigenome peaks for the held-out dataset), so positives/negatives cannot be defined and AUROC/AUPR are meaningless. Candidate regions are unscored peak intervals that have not yet gone through adaptive_liftover, similarity computation, and gr_candidate_filter — ranking-based AUC evaluation would be premature. The task is parameter learning rather than evaluation: use training_module() to estimate logistic regression parameters and suggest an optimal score threshold instead.

skills.search_text: auc-prc-performance-computation Use when a set of ranked predicted regulatory interactions (e.g., gene–peak pairs) needs to be evaluated against a trusted positive set such as cis-eQTLs to quantify prediction performance. skills.name: bam-downsampling-normalization
skills.search_text: bam-downsampling-normalization Use when comparing two spike-in ChIP-seq conditions (e.g. H3K79me2 25:75 vs 75:25 mixed Jurkat cells) with unequal fly spike-in read totals, and you need to equalize spike-in depth by downsampling the human BAM, or you need a baseline uniform-scaling normalization to benchmark against spikChIP. When the goal is to minimize overcorrection of non-occupied/background regions — Tag removal applies the spike-in correction uniformly and overcorrects background bins; spikChIP's local regression, which applies the correction gradually from background to enriched regions, is the article's remedy. When spike-in sequencing depth is below the recommended ~1 million reads (2%–5% of the experimental genome) — the article recommends the -d option only for processing BAMs < 1 Million reads and warns shallow spike-in undermines normalization. It is one of the normalization approaches (RAW, TRADITIONAL, CHIPRX, TAG REMOVAL) computed by spikChIP, and is used here to quantify how a uniform global correction affects background genomic regions. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nargab/lqab064

It is one of the normalization approaches (RAW, TRADITIONAL, CHIPRX, TAG REMOVAL) computed by spikChIP, and is used here to quantify how a uniform global correction affects background genomic regions.

Input is raw FASTQ that has not yet been aligned — mapping must precede filtering and subsampling Single-sample analysis with no replicate comparison or cross-sample QC normalization, where fixed-depth subsampling discards data without benefit Long-read or non-ChIP/DNase assays where MAPQ > 1 unique-read filtering and 4M-read depth assumptions from ChiLin do not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Normalizes ChIP-seq BAM files by retaining uniquely mapped reads (mapping quality above 1) with samtools and subsampling each replicate to a fixed depth (4,000,000 reads) so downstream QC metrics such as MACS2 fragment-size estimation, PBC, FRiP, and wigCorrelate replicate correlation are computed on comparable input. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-016-1274-4
skills.summary: Normalizes ChIP-seq BAM files by retaining uniquely mapped reads (mapping quality above 1) with samtools and subsampling each replicate to a fixed depth (4,000,000 reads) so downstream QC metrics such as MACS2 fragment-size estimation, PBC, FRiP, and wigCorrelate replicate correlation are computed on comparable input.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTQ that has not yet been aligned — mapping must precede filtering and subsampling Single-sample analysis with no replicate comparison or cross-sample QC normalization, where fixed-depth subsampling discards data without benefit Long-read or non-ChIP/DNase assays where MAPQ > 1 unique-read filtering and 4M-read depth assumptions from ChiLin do not apply

skills.description: Use when running spike-in ChIP-seq normalization (e.g. ChIP-Rx in spikChIP) where each human bin count must be divided by total fly (dm3) spike-in reads, or when BAM totals must be reported or used for downsampling.
skills.name: bam-read-total-quantification
skills.search_text: bam-read-total-quantification Use when running spike-in ChIP-seq normalization (e.g. ChIP-Rx in spikChIP) where each human bin count must be divided by total fly (dm3) spike-in reads, or when BAM totals must be reported or used for downsampling. When the goal is the spikChIP local-regression normalization itself, which deliberately minimizes the influence of background-region reads rather than relying on a raw total-read division When a BAM file contains fewer than 1 million reads — spikChIP excludes these by default unless the -d option is explicitly set When the experiment has no exogenous spike-in genome; ChIP-Rx requires a second genome's read total as denominator http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Quantifies the total number of mapped reads in sample and spike-in BAM files using Samtools, providing the denominators required by spike-in normalization approaches (notably ChIP-Rx) computed within the spikChIP pipeline. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nargab/lqab064
skills.summary: Quantifies the total number of mapped reads in sample and spike-in BAM files using Samtools, providing the denominators required by spike-in normalization approaches (notably ChIP-Rx) computed within the spikChIP pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is the spikChIP local-regression normalization itself, which deliberately minimizes the influence of background-region reads rather than relying on a raw total-read division When a BAM file contains fewer than 1 million reads — spikChIP excludes these by default unless the -d option is explicitly set When the experiment has no exogenous spike-in genome; ChIP-Rx requires a second genome's read total as denominator

skills.search_text: barcode-span-annotation-processing Use when phasing with 10× linked-reads and fragments must be filtered against barcode-sharing artifacts — e.g. requiring end-read MAPQ >= 30, capping barcode span at 60 kb, and bounding haplotype blocks over filtered variants. Input is Hi-C, PacBio SMRT or Oxford Nanopore data without 10× barcodes — the barcode-span annotation and 60 kb span cap are 10× linked-read specific Phasing organisms with ploidy higher than diploid — the graph bisection model does not fit increased ploidy Assembling haplotype-resolved structural variation — SpecHap supports only SNPs, short insertions and deletions http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 A filtering and annotation skill for SpecHap 10× linked-reads phasing that counters reads sharing the same barcode but originating from different DNA molecules, by annotating each barcode's spanning range (BarcodeExtract / barcode_spanning.bed) and retaining only fragments passing mapping quality, span, and haplotype-block constraints. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab709

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is Hi-C, PacBio SMRT or Oxford Nanopore data without 10× barcodes — the barcode-span annotation and 60 kb span cap are 10× linked-read specific Phasing organisms with ploidy higher than diploid — the graph bisection model does not fit increased ploidy Assembling haplotype-resolved structural variation — SpecHap supports only SNPs, short insertions and deletions

skills.description: Use when preprocessing DNA sequences (uPBM, HT-SELEX, or gcPBM) into per-sequence feature matrices for DNAffinity affinity prediction, requiring tetramer counts and base-pair-step structural/electrostatic encoding.
skills.name: base-pair-step-stiffness-parameter-mapping
skills.search_text: base-pair-step-stiffness-parameter-mapping Use when preprocessing DNA sequences (uPBM, HT-SELEX, or gcPBM) into per-sequence feature matrices for DNAffinity affinity prediction, requiring tetramer counts and base-pair-step structural/electrostatic encoding. The sequences are already encoded as a feature matrix and only the regressor needs to be run (e.g. an existing Gata4_training.txt-processed pipeline). The analysis targets regression performance or competitor comparison (DeepBind, DNAShapeR, BEESEM, BindSpace) rather than feature construction. http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Encodes DNA sequences for DNAffinity by counting overlapping tetramers and mapping each base-pair step to indirect-readout structural parameters (AVG equilibrium geometry and DIAG stiffness from BigNASim MD tables) plus direct-readout electrostatic features. This converts raw sequences into the physical-property feature matrix consumed by the random forest regressor. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkac708
skills.summary: Encodes DNA sequences for DNAffinity by counting overlapping tetramers and mapping each base-pair step to indirect-readout structural parameters (AVG equilibrium geometry and DIAG stiffness from BigNASim MD tables) plus direct-readout electrostatic features. This converts raw sequences into the physical-property feature matrix consumed by the random forest regressor.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sequences are already encoded as a feature matrix and only the regressor needs to be run (e.g. an existing Gata4_training.txt-processed pipeline). The analysis targets regression performance or competitor comparison (DeepBind, DNAShapeR, BEESEM, BindSpace) rather than feature construction.

skills.search_text: baseline-classifier-benchmarking Use when a new sgRNA-activity prediction model must be shown competitive with established methods: you have binarized sgRNA labels and need a like-for-like ROC-AUC comparison table against Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, DeepHF, and C-RNNcrispr. skills.summary: Benchmark a deep learning sgRNA-activity classifier (EpiCas-DL) against shallow and published deep-learning baselines (Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, DeepHF, C-RNNcrispr) using ROC-AUC under 10-fold cross-validation on an identical sequence-plus-epigenetic input matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is regression/efficiency prediction of continuous sgRNA activity scores rather than binary classification (highly active vs. not) evaluated by ROC-AUC The target epigenetic features (nucleosome positioning, ATAC-seq accessibility, DNA methylation, RNA expression) are unavailable for the cell line of interest, making the sequence-plus-epigenetic input matrix unbuildable for a like-for-like comparison The dataset is not an sgRNA screening dataset with phenotype scores to binarize at the −0.1 cutoff (e.g., already aggregated per-gene summaries)

skills.description: Use when a new Hi-C or capture Hi-C normalization method must be evaluated against established baselines (ICE, SCN, KR, raw) using replicate contact map reproducibility rather than a single qualitative comparison.
skills.name: baseline-matrix-normalization-benchmarking
skills.search_text: baseline-matrix-normalization-benchmarking Use when a new Hi-C or capture Hi-C normalization method must be evaluated against established baselines (ICE, SCN, KR, raw) using replicate contact map reproducibility rather than a single qualitative comparison. When only a single Hi-C sample/replicate is available — the reproducibility benchmark requires a biological replicate pair (e.g., GM19204 vs GM19240). When the goal is compartment A/B calling or significant interaction detection rather than normalization-method benchmarking — those need different evaluation metrics. When contact maps are already normalized or produced by matrix balancing; re-running this benchmark on balanced maps would not evaluate the normalization step. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Benchmark a candidate Hi-C contact map normalization method (e.g., covNorm) against baseline matrix-balancing methods (ICE, SCN, KR) and raw data by scoring replicate reproducibility with the HiC-spector reproducibility metric, and report per-method median scores with paired t-tests. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.05.041
skills.summary: Benchmark a candidate Hi-C contact map normalization method (e.g., covNorm) against baseline matrix-balancing methods (ICE, SCN, KR) and raw data by scoring replicate reproducibility with the HiC-spector reproducibility metric, and report per-method median scores with paired t-tests.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only a single Hi-C sample/replicate is available — the reproducibility benchmark requires a biological replicate pair (e.g., GM19204 vs GM19240). When the goal is compartment A/B calling or significant interaction detection rather than normalization-method benchmarking — those need different evaluation metrics. When contact maps are already normalized or produced by matrix balancing; re-running this benchmark on balanced maps would not evaluate the normalization step.

skills.description: Use when a paper claims a new model outperforms methods on shared benchmarks and the reproduction requires merging locally reproduced metrics with reported baseline values into one comparison table.
skills.name: baseline-method-result-compilation
skills.search_text: baseline-method-result-compilation Use when a paper claims a new model outperforms methods on shared benchmarks and the reproduction requires merging locally reproduced metrics with reported baseline values into one comparison table. The task requires newly re-running baseline methods rather than comparing reproduced results against the paper's reported baseline values Input is raw DNA FASTA sequence that has not yet been encoded into dna2vec feature vectors by get_datavec.py The goal is SE/TE prediction itself (use DeepSE prediction skills) rather than compiling a benchmark comparison of results http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_3534 Reproduce a proposed model's performance (here DeepSE, a two-layer Keras CNN distinguishing super-enhancers from typical enhancers from dna2vec sequence embeddings) and compile it side-by-side with reported state-of-the-art baseline metrics into a single benchmark comparison table, validating the paper's claim that DeepSE outperforms all baselines. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.ygeno.2021.10.007
skills.summary: Reproduce a proposed model's performance (here DeepSE, a two-layer Keras CNN distinguishing super-enhancers from typical enhancers from dna2vec sequence embeddings) and compile it side-by-side with reported state-of-the-art baseline metrics into a single benchmark comparison table, validating the paper's claim that DeepSE outperforms all baselines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires newly re-running baseline methods rather than comparing reproduced results against the paper's reported baseline values Input is raw DNA FASTA sequence that has not yet been encoded into dna2vec feature vectors by get_datavec.py The goal is SE/TE prediction itself (use DeepSE prediction skills) rather than compiling a benchmark comparison of results

skills.search_text: baseline-model-benchmark-comparison Use when a trained predictor (e.g. a CNN regressor for sgRNA activity) must be benchmarked head-to-head against comparator algorithms on identical train/test splits, with significance testing on correlation, MSE, or cosine similarity metrics. The task is a classification benchmark (AUC/ROC comparison) rather than sgRNA activity regression — the article uses Spearman correlation, MSE, and cosine similarity for the regression setting The proposed model and baselines were trained on different training splits or different feature encodings — comparisons on non-identical inputs are invalid There is insufficient test-set size or fold count to support a Student's t-test across folds http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Reproduce and evaluate a proposed deep learning model (EpiCas-DL CNN regressor) against competing state-of-the-art baselines (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, DeepHF, C-RNNcrispr) on the same held-out data, using Spearman correlation, MSE, and cosine similarity with a Student's t-test to establish statistically significant superiority. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.11.034
skills.summary: Reproduce and evaluate a proposed deep learning model (EpiCas-DL CNN regressor) against competing state-of-the-art baselines (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, DeepHF, C-RNNcrispr) on the same held-out data, using Spearman correlation, MSE, and cosine similarity with a Student's t-test to establish statistically significant superiority.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is a classification benchmark (AUC/ROC comparison) rather than sgRNA activity regression — the article uses Spearman correlation, MSE, and cosine similarity for the regression setting The proposed model and baselines were trained on different training splits or different feature encodings — comparisons on non-identical inputs are invalid There is insufficient test-set size or fold count to support a Student's t-test across folds

skills.description: Use when fitting a hidden Markov model of DNA-binding factor occupancy to paired-end MNase-seq and/or ATAC-seq fragment data plus nucleotide sequence, requiring EM learning of transition probabilities with constrained TF transitions.
skills.name: baum-welch-em-parameter-estimation
skills.search_text: baum-welch-em-parameter-estimation Use when fitting a hidden Markov model of DNA-binding factor occupancy to paired-end MNase-seq and/or ATAC-seq fragment data plus nucleotide sequence, requiring EM learning of transition probabilities with constrained TF transitions. When the goal is peak calling or footprint identification rather than a joint probabilistic occupancy landscape — the article contrasts RoboCOP with MACS2 peak/footprint identification followed by FIMO TF-labeling When a quick TF-labeling scan of motifs is sufficient and no chromatin accessibility data (MNase-seq or ATAC-seq) are available to inform emission probabilities http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 Trains RoboCOP's multivariate hidden Markov model by Baum-Welch EM, initializing transition probabilities from a Boltzmann distribution and capping TF transition probabilities at two standard deviations above the mean of their initial values, so that sequence (PWM/dinucleotide) and accessibility (negative-binomial) emissions jointly yield genome-wide nucleosome and TF occupancy probabilities. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab553
skills.summary: Trains RoboCOP's multivariate hidden Markov model by Baum-Welch EM, initializing transition probabilities from a Boltzmann distribution and capping TF transition probabilities at two standard deviations above the mean of their initial values, so that sequence (PWM/dinucleotide) and accessibility (negative-binomial) emissions jointly yield genome-wide nucleosome and TF occupancy probabilities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is peak calling or footprint identification rather than a joint probabilistic occupancy landscape — the article contrasts RoboCOP with MACS2 peak/footprint identification followed by FIMO TF-labeling When a quick TF-labeling scan of motifs is sufficient and no chromatin accessibility data (MNase-seq or ATAC-seq) are available to inform emission probabilities

skills.description: Use when a time-series expression matrix must be segmented into bifurcating submatrices and an input-output HMM tree-structure model needs parameter initialization and Baum–Welch training, e.g. to assign TFs to the time points at which they act.
skills.name: baum-welch-hidden-markov-model-training
skills.search_text: baum-welch-hidden-markov-model-training Use when a time-series expression matrix must be segmented into bifurcating submatrices and an input-output HMM tree-structure model needs parameter initialization and Baum–Welch training, e.g. to assign TFs to the time points at which they act. The data are not time-series expression profiles and no candidate bifurcation (split) time points can be defined from fold changes between consecutive time points You only need static clustering of expression profiles without temporal dynamics of regulators — the article notes clustering methods cannot evaluate the temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways, but conversely this skill is not a substitute for simple module clustering You cannot supply a TF-gene interaction file, since the input-output HMM of the tree-structure model is trained jointly on the expression matrix and TF–TG interaction information http://edamontology.org/topic_0204 Trains the input-output hidden Markov model of a tree-structure model on a time-series expression matrix by initializing Baum–Welch with bifurcation-pattern-derived parameters and iterating until the likelihood score converges, as implemented in TSMiner (Java) for time-specific gene regulatory network construction. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: Trains the input-output hidden Markov model of a tree-structure model on a time-series expression matrix by initializing Baum–Welch with bifurcation-pattern-derived parameters and iterating until the likelihood score converges, as implemented in TSMiner (Java) for time-specific gene regulatory network construction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are not time-series expression profiles and no candidate bifurcation (split) time points can be defined from fold changes between consecutive time points You only need static clustering of expression profiles without temporal dynamics of regulators — the article notes clustering methods cannot evaluate the temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways, but conversely this skill is not a substitute for simple module clustering You cannot supply a TF-gene interaction file, since the input-output HMM of the tree-structure model is trained jointly on the expression matrix and TF–TG interaction information

skills.description: Use when you have an N-reads × d-CpGs binary methylation read matrix Y (0/1, RRBS-derived) for one locus and need to infer how many distinct epialleles are present, their methylation patterns, the noise level ε, and which epiallele each read originated from.
skills.name: bayesian-epiallele-model-fitting
skills.search_text: bayesian-epiallele-model-fitting Use when you have an N-reads × d-CpGs binary methylation read matrix Y (0/1, RRBS-derived) for one locus and need to infer how many distinct epialleles are present, their methylation patterns, the noise level ε, and which epiallele each read originated from. skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads cannot be phased between disjoint loci — do not apply per-locus epiallele calls expecting linkage information across distant CpG sites Loci falling below the study filters (median read depth < 100, fewer than 6 CpGs, more than 25% missing data, or chromosomes X/Y) were excluded in the paper's workflow You need a single global methylation summary (e.g. mean methylation level) rather than resolving distinct epiallele species per locus

skills.description: Use when the input is a processed peak/region set (BED from MACS2, DiffBind, or ArchR DARs) and the goal is an in-silico ranked list of TRs with credible intervals rather than motif-based or frequentist enrichment.
skills.name: bayesian-hierarchical-model-mcmc-inference
skills.search_text: bayesian-hierarchical-model-mcmc-inference Use when the input is a processed peak/region set (BED from MACS2, DiffBind, or ArchR DARs) and the goal is an in-silico ranked list of TRs with credible intervals rather than motif-based or frequentist enrichment. When the question is motif enrichment rather than context-specific binding — BIT deliberately bypasses computationally predicted motifs (as used by WhichTF/HOMER), so motif-only tools may be preferable for de novo motif discovery. skills.summary: Run BIT, an R package implementing a Bayesian hierarchical model with Gibbs-sampler MCMC, to convert a user-provided epigenomic region set (e.g., ATAC-seq DAR peaks such as mm10_RUNX1.bed) into a ranked table of transcriptional regulators with posterior uncertainty quantification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the question is motif enrichment rather than context-specific binding — BIT deliberately bypasses computationally predicted motifs (as used by WhichTF/HOMER), so motif-only tools may be preferable for de novo motif discovery. When the input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ/BAM) — BIT only requires processed peak coordinates; upstream peak calling (MACS2 q 0.01) and DAR calling (DiffBind, FDR <= 0.05 & abs(Log2FC) >= 2) must be done first. When a very large collection of epigenomic profiling datasets must be analyzed and runtime is critical — the Gibbs sampler can become increasingly time-consuming as the number of ChIP-seq experiments grows.

skills.search_text: bayesian-inla-model-fitting-in-r Use when bisulfite amplicon sequencing standard-control data (known methylation percentages per AMP) must be modelled jointly across CpGs with Bayesian inference in R, e.g. deriving PCR-bias calibration curves or correcting case/control methylation levels. The analysis goal is one-at-a-time per-CpG calibration or calibration of the average methylation level across CpGs — MethylCal's value is joint modelling of all CpGs within a CGI/DMR No INLA installation is possible: R-INLA is a mandatory dependency that must be downloaded and installed manually and is not auto-installed like lattice/latticeExtra The task only requires Moskalev's CPR or Warnecke's hyperbolic baseline curves, which are provided as separate package functions and do not involve INLA http://edamontology.org/topic_3674 http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 Fit Bayesian latent Gaussian models in R via the INLA engine, as implemented in the MethylCal package, to jointly calibrate methylation levels across all CpGs in a CpG island or DMR and select among candidate random-effects specifications using DIC. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz325
skills.summary: Fit Bayesian latent Gaussian models in R via the INLA engine, as implemented in the MethylCal package, to jointly calibrate methylation levels across all CpGs in a CpG island or DMR and select among candidate random-effects specifications using DIC.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is one-at-a-time per-CpG calibration or calibration of the average methylation level across CpGs — MethylCal's value is joint modelling of all CpGs within a CGI/DMR No INLA installation is possible: R-INLA is a mandatory dependency that must be downloaded and installed manually and is not auto-installed like lattice/latticeExtra The task only requires Moskalev's CPR or Warnecke's hyperbolic baseline curves, which are provided as separate package functions and do not involve INLA
