skills.search_text: cpg-oe-ratio-calculation Use when you have FASTA sequences of candidate regulatory regions (e.g., HOT vs COLD) and need CpG O/E and GC-related features to test whether CpG/GC-rich sequence characteristics discriminate between region classes. Input is already a computed feature table (e.g., k-mer frequencies or CpG O/E values) rather than raw region sequences The goal is TF motif enrichment analysis — the article notes HOT regions lack canonical motifs for transcription factors thought to be bound there, so motif-based features will not discriminate HOT from COLD Comparing ChIP-seq signal intensity rather than intrinsic sequence properties of regions http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Calculates the CpG observed/expected (O/E) ratio, alongside GC content, GC skew, and k-mer (k=2,3,4) frequencies, for HOT and COLD genomic regions to build sequence-feature matrices that discriminate HOT from non-HOT regions in elastic net classifiers. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz460
skills.summary: Calculates the CpG observed/expected (O/E) ratio, alongside GC content, GC skew, and k-mer (k=2,3,4) frequencies, for HOT and COLD genomic regions to build sequence-feature matrices that discriminate HOT from non-HOT regions in elastic net classifiers.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a computed feature table (e.g., k-mer frequencies or CpG O/E values) rather than raw region sequences The goal is TF motif enrichment analysis — the article notes HOT regions lack canonical motifs for transcription factors thought to be bound there, so motif-based features will not discriminate HOT from COLD Comparing ChIP-seq signal intensity rather than intrinsic sequence properties of regions

skills.description: Use when preprocessing an Illumina 450K methylation matrix for subgroup classification and deciding which top-value method (SD vs ATC) should drive CpG probe selection before consensus partitioning.
skills.name: cpg-probe-feature-selection-sd-atc
skills.search_text: cpg-probe-feature-selection-sd-atc Use when preprocessing an Illumina 450K methylation matrix for subgroup classification and deciding which top-value method (SD vs ATC) should drive CpG probe selection before consensus partitioning. When the goal is gene-expression subgrouping (e.g. RNA-Seq or microarray expression data), where the article's benchmarks favor ATC features and skmeans rather than the methylation-specific SD behavior When input probes have not yet been cleaned of sex-chromosome and SNP-overlapping probes — running SD/ATC selection on the raw matrix mixes global methylation artifacts into the feature scores When samples are ambiguous (silhouette score < 0.5) — cola excludes these from signature analysis, so downstream probe-set interpretation is unreliable http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Feature selection of Illumina 450K CpG probes for cola consensus partitioning, comparing the variance-based top-value method SD against the correlation-structure-based ATC method on the GBM 450K methylation dataset (GSE36278). In this dataset SD-selected probes recover DKFZ GBM subgroups while ATC-selected probes track global methylation levels. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa1146
skills.summary: Feature selection of Illumina 450K CpG probes for cola consensus partitioning, comparing the variance-based top-value method SD against the correlation-structure-based ATC method on the GBM 450K methylation dataset (GSE36278). In this dataset SD-selected probes recover DKFZ GBM subgroups while ATC-selected probes track global methylation levels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is gene-expression subgrouping (e.g. RNA-Seq or microarray expression data), where the article's benchmarks favor ATC features and skmeans rather than the methylation-specific SD behavior When input probes have not yet been cleaned of sex-chromosome and SNP-overlapping probes — running SD/ATC selection on the raw matrix mixes global methylation artifacts into the feature scores When samples are ambiguous (silhouette score < 0.5) — cola excludes these from signature analysis, so downstream probe-set interpretation is unreliable

skills.description: Use when Bismark alignment outputs (SAM/BAM or *.cov count tables) from one or more MethylC-seq samples must be aggregated from individual CpG sites into candidate regions prior to DMR testing with findDMRs.r or equivalent beta-binomial approaches.
skills.name: cpg-site-region-clustering
skills.search_text: cpg-site-region-clustering Use when Bismark alignment outputs (SAM/BAM or *.cov count tables) from one or more MethylC-seq samples must be aggregated from individual CpG sites into candidate regions prior to DMR testing with findDMRs.r or equivalent beta-binomial approaches. The sequencing reads have not yet been aligned and methylation counts extracted (run Bismark/Bowtie2 and extract_CpG_data.py first; clustering needs per-CpG count tables) The analysis requires modeling sets of regions, quantitative traits, or batch effects, which DMRfinder does not support Deduplicated or strand-aware site-level calls are needed without region aggregation (use Bismark's methylation extractor directly instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Clusters per-CpG methylation counts from Bismark-aligned MethylC-seq data into genomic regions using DMRfinder's combine_CpG_sites.py, a modified single-linkage clustering that is methylation-blind and therefore unbiased toward finding DMRs before differential testing. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-017-1909-0
skills.summary: Clusters per-CpG methylation counts from Bismark-aligned MethylC-seq data into genomic regions using DMRfinder's combine_CpG_sites.py, a modified single-linkage clustering that is methylation-blind and therefore unbiased toward finding DMRs before differential testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sequencing reads have not yet been aligned and methylation counts extracted (run Bismark/Bowtie2 and extract_CpG_data.py first; clustering needs per-CpG count tables) The analysis requires modeling sets of regions, quantitative traits, or batch effects, which DMRfinder does not support Deduplicated or strand-aware site-level calls are needed without region aggregation (use Bismark's methylation extractor directly instead)

skills.description: Use when you have chromosome start/end coordinates of REMs (e.g. the 2,404,861 REMs from Zenodo record 3758494) and need to merge them into CREMs and recompute the paper's clustering statistics.
skills.name: crem-cluster-statistics-reproduction
skills.search_text: crem-cluster-statistics-reproduction Use when you have chromosome start/end coordinates of REMs (e.g. the 2,404,861 REMs from Zenodo record 3758494) and need to merge them into CREMs and recompute the paper's clustering statistics. The input is not interval data with chr/start/end REM coordinates (e.g. it is already an aggregated feature or statistics table). The goal is motif enrichment or target-gene identification for a set of REMs (use the PASTAA/Gene Query workflow instead of CREM clustering). You need individual REM-gene associations rather than merged clusters of overlapping/adjacent REMs. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Reproduces EpiRegio's definition and quantitative characterization of Clusters of Regulatory EleMents (CREMs), i.e. groups of overlapping or directly adjacent REMs, and validates the aggregate statistics (total CREM count, average REMs per CREM, mean span, fully-overlapping clusters) against the published REM/CREM characteristics. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa382
skills.summary: Reproduces EpiRegio's definition and quantitative characterization of Clusters of Regulatory EleMents (CREMs), i.e. groups of overlapping or directly adjacent REMs, and validates the aggregate statistics (total CREM count, average REMs per CREM, mean span, fully-overlapping clusters) against the published REM/CREM characteristics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not interval data with chr/start/end REM coordinates (e.g. it is already an aggregated feature or statistics table). The goal is motif enrichment or target-gene identification for a set of REMs (use the PASTAA/Gene Query workflow instead of CREM clustering). You need individual REM-gene associations rather than merged clusters of overlapping/adjacent REMs.

skills.description: Use when a trained CRISPRoff sgRNA-activity model (or comparable tree-based efficiency model) must be interpreted to identify which epigenetic features (nucleosome positioning, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, RNA expression) most favor editing efficiency.
skills.name: crispr-off-sgrna-activity-feature-ranking
skills.search_text: crispr-off-sgrna-activity-feature-ranking Use when a trained CRISPRoff sgRNA-activity model (or comparable tree-based efficiency model) must be interpreted to identify which epigenetic features (nucleosome positioning, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, RNA expression) most favor editing efficiency. The goal is sgRNA activity prediction itself rather than model interpretation — use the EpiCas-DL prediction models (CRISPRoff_seq/CRISPRoff_epi) instead. Only sequence information is available with no epigenetic annotations (methylation, expression, accessibility, TSS distance), since the feature ranking is meant to expose epigenetic contributions. The dataset is CRISPRa activation screening where feature-favorability directions may differ from the CRISPRoff repression findings being reproduced. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Ranks epigenetic and sequence features that drive sgRNA activity in CRISPRoff gene silencing by computing mean |SHAP| values with Tree SHAP on an XGBoost model, exposing features such as nucleosome positioning (distance to TSS), RNA expression, and chromatin accessibility as top favorable predictors. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.11.034
skills.summary: Ranks epigenetic and sequence features that drive sgRNA activity in CRISPRoff gene silencing by computing mean |SHAP| values with Tree SHAP on an XGBoost model, exposing features such as nucleosome positioning (distance to TSS), RNA expression, and chromatin accessibility as top favorable predictors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is sgRNA activity prediction itself rather than model interpretation — use the EpiCas-DL prediction models (CRISPRoff_seq/CRISPRoff_epi) instead. Only sequence information is available with no epigenetic annotations (methylation, expression, accessibility, TSS distance), since the feature ranking is meant to expose epigenetic contributions. The dataset is CRISPRa activation screening where feature-favorability directions may differ from the CRISPRoff repression findings being reproduced.

skills.description: Use when sgRNA screening datasets provide continuous phenotype scores or activity scores that must be converted to binary high-activity labels for classification model training or independent validation.
skills.name: crispr-screen-label-thresholding
skills.search_text: crispr-screen-label-thresholding Use when sgRNA screening datasets provide continuous phenotype scores or activity scores that must be converted to binary high-activity labels for classification model training or independent validation. The downstream task is regression of sgRNA activity (use Spearman correlation on continuous scores instead of binarizing). The screening table already contains binary activity calls or the analysis goal does not require a classification label schema. The dataset is not a CRISPRi/CRISPRoff/CRISPRa gene silencing or activation screen, so the -0.1 phenotype / 0.75 activity-score cutoffs are not applicable. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Binarizes continuous sgRNA screening measurements (phenotype scores or activity scores) into high-activity ('1') versus low-activity labels so CRISPRi/CRISPRoff/CRISPRa datasets can be used for classification-style sgRNA efficacy prediction (e.g., EpiCas-DL ROC-AUC evaluation). epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.11.034
skills.summary: Binarizes continuous sgRNA screening measurements (phenotype scores or activity scores) into high-activity ('1') versus low-activity labels so CRISPRi/CRISPRoff/CRISPRa datasets can be used for classification-style sgRNA efficacy prediction (e.g., EpiCas-DL ROC-AUC evaluation).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The downstream task is regression of sgRNA activity (use Spearman correlation on continuous scores instead of binarizing). The screening table already contains binary activity calls or the analysis goal does not require a classification label schema. The dataset is not a CRISPRi/CRISPRoff/CRISPRa gene silencing or activation screen, so the -0.1 phenotype / 0.75 activity-score cutoffs are not applicable.

skills.description: Use when you have a trained sequence-based CNN for sgRNA activity (e.g., EpiCas-DL CRISPRoff/CRISPRa models) and need per-base, per-position feature attributions to explain sequence determinants of efficiency.
skills.name: crisproff-crispra-model-attribution-averaging
skills.search_text: crisproff-crispra-model-attribution-averaging Use when you have a trained sequence-based CNN for sgRNA activity (e.g., EpiCas-DL CRISPRoff/CRISPRa models) and need per-base, per-position feature attributions to explain sequence determinants of efficiency. You want feature attributions for tabular epigenetic features (nucleosome occupancy, methylation, accessibility) — the paper uses Tree SHAP with XGBoost for those, not DeepExplainer on sequence matrices You only need sgRNA efficiency predictions (use example.py prediction mode) rather than model interpretation Your model input is not one-hot encoded sequence with the 9/23/8 bp layout — attribution positions will not align to PAM-proximal coordinates http://edamontology.org/topic_3473 Applies DeepSHAP's DeepExplainer to the trained EpiCas-DL CNN models (CRISPRoff and CRISPRa, TensorFlow 2.4.1 backend) over one-hot encoded 40-bp sgRNA matrices, averaging per-base SHAP attributions across 1000 sgRNAs to expose position-specific nucleotide preferences such as the PAM-proximal guanine bias. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.11.034
skills.summary: Applies DeepSHAP's DeepExplainer to the trained EpiCas-DL CNN models (CRISPRoff and CRISPRa, TensorFlow 2.4.1 backend) over one-hot encoded 40-bp sgRNA matrices, averaging per-base SHAP attributions across 1000 sgRNAs to expose position-specific nucleotide preferences such as the PAM-proximal guanine bias.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You want feature attributions for tabular epigenetic features (nucleosome occupancy, methylation, accessibility) — the paper uses Tree SHAP with XGBoost for those, not DeepExplainer on sequence matrices You only need sgRNA efficiency predictions (use example.py prediction mode) rather than model interpretation Your model input is not one-hot encoded sequence with the 9/23/8 bp layout — attribution positions will not align to PAM-proximal coordinates

skills.description: Use when two alignment sets (e.g., a Msuite.final.bam and published reference BAMs) exist for the same murine ESC TAPS/WGBS samples and you need region-level (CpG island) read-coverage comparison rather than overall mapping-efficiency metrics.
skills.name: cross-aligner-coverage-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-aligner-coverage-comparison Use when two alignment sets (e.g., a Msuite.final.bam and published reference BAMs) exist for the same murine ESC TAPS/WGBS samples and you need region-level (CpG island) read-coverage comparison rather than overall mapping-efficiency metrics. Input is BS-seq (bisulfite) data processed with Msuite's 4-letter mode — per the README, BS-protocol data MUST use 3-letter mode with -m BS, so coverage gains inferred this way would not reflect the intended 4-letter/TAPS configuration The goal is whole-genome mapping-efficiency, speed, or memory benchmarking against Bismark/BWA-meth rather than region-resolved (CpG island) coverage comparison The two alignment sets derive from different samples or different reference assemblies — per-island coverage ratios would confound biological and aligner differences Quantifies how mapped-read coverage over CpG islands differs between Msuite alignments and a published alignment strategy (Liu et al.) for the same TAPS/WGBS samples on the mm10/GRCm38 reference, isolating the gain on highly methylated islands. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2020.100127
skills.summary: Quantifies how mapped-read coverage over CpG islands differs between Msuite alignments and a published alignment strategy (Liu et al.) for the same TAPS/WGBS samples on the mm10/GRCm38 reference, isolating the gain on highly methylated islands.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is BS-seq (bisulfite) data processed with Msuite's 4-letter mode — per the README, BS-protocol data MUST use 3-letter mode with -m BS, so coverage gains inferred this way would not reflect the intended 4-letter/TAPS configuration The goal is whole-genome mapping-efficiency, speed, or memory benchmarking against Bismark/BWA-meth rather than region-resolved (CpG island) coverage comparison The two alignment sets derive from different samples or different reference assemblies — per-island coverage ratios would confound biological and aligner differences

skills.description: Use when two or more open-chromatin peak files (BED-derived GRanges from ATAC-seq, DNase-seq, or similar) must be benchmarked against a gold-standard reference peak set to quantify assay-level differences in peak overlap.
skills.name: cross-assay-chromatin-accessibility-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-assay-chromatin-accessibility-comparison Use when two or more open-chromatin peak files (BED-derived GRanges from ATAC-seq, DNase-seq, or similar) must be benchmarked against a gold-standard reference peak set to quantify assay-level differences in peak overlap. Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ) rather than processed peak interval files — EpiCompare works on peak files, not alignment or peak calling There is no reference/gold-standard peak set to benchmark against, since precision and recall are defined relative to the reference The goal is general QC of a single sample (blacklist fraction, duplication rate) rather than cross-assay comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Benchmarks chromatin accessibility peak sets from different assays (e.g., ATAC-seq vs DNase-seq in K562) against a reference peak set by sweeping overlap thresholds and computing precision, recall, and F1, exposing assay-specific differences such as those seen in ChromHMM annotations and precision-recall plots (Fig. 1d–e). epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad049
skills.summary: Benchmarks chromatin accessibility peak sets from different assays (e.g., ATAC-seq vs DNase-seq in K562) against a reference peak set by sweeping overlap thresholds and computing precision, recall, and F1, exposing assay-specific differences such as those seen in ChromHMM annotations and precision-recall plots (Fig. 1d–e).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ) rather than processed peak interval files — EpiCompare works on peak files, not alignment or peak calling There is no reference/gold-standard peak set to benchmark against, since precision and recall are defined relative to the reference The goal is general QC of a single sample (blacklist fraction, duplication rate) rather than cross-assay comparison

skills.description: Use when you have FASTQ data from related 3D genome mapping assays (ChIA-PET, HiChIP, PLAC-seq) and need to check whether their interaction calls agree with each other and with Hi-C.
skills.name: cross-assay-chromatin-interaction-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-assay-chromatin-interaction-comparison Use when you have FASTQ data from related 3D genome mapping assays (ChIA-PET, HiChIP, PLAC-seq) and need to check whether their interaction calls agree with each other and with Hi-C. Data are already processed interaction call sets or .hic/.cool files rather than raw FASTQ reads The assay is none of ChIA-PET, HiChIP, or PLAC-seq and requires a different linker-filtering strategy not supported by the pseudolinker handling A quantitative numeric agreement threshold between assays is required, since the article validates comparability only qualitatively http://edamontology.org/topic_0607 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Process ChIA-PET, HiChIP, and PLAC-seq data with a single ChIA-PIPE run (handling their different junction sequences via pseudolinker handling) and compare the resulting chromatin interactions—2D contact maps and loop/domain calls—across assays and against Hi-C. epigenomics/v2 10.1126/sciadv.aay2078
skills.summary: Process ChIA-PET, HiChIP, and PLAC-seq data with a single ChIA-PIPE run (handling their different junction sequences via pseudolinker handling) and compare the resulting chromatin interactions—2D contact maps and loop/domain calls—across assays and against Hi-C.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are already processed interaction call sets or .hic/.cool files rather than raw FASTQ reads The assay is none of ChIA-PET, HiChIP, or PLAC-seq and requires a different linker-filtering strategy not supported by the pseudolinker handling A quantitative numeric agreement threshold between assays is required, since the article validates comparability only qualitatively

skills.description: Use when comparing peak files from different chromatin accessibility assays (e.g. ATAC-seq vs DNase-seq narrowPeak from ENCODE) to quantify assay-specific differences and benchmark against a ChIP-seq gold standard.
skills.name: cross-assay-open-chromatin-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-assay-open-chromatin-benchmarking Use when comparing peak files from different chromatin accessibility assays (e.g. ATAC-seq vs DNase-seq narrowPeak from ENCODE) to quantify assay-specific differences and benchmark against a ChIP-seq gold standard. Input data are not peak files (e.g. raw reads, BAM files, or feature tables) — EpiCompare operates on peak files such as narrowPeak/BED Goal is within-technology comparison of experimental conditions without a reference assay to benchmark against a gold standard like ChIP-seq Peaks are not on hg19/hg38 human genome builds or no blacklist file is available, since blacklist and non-standard chromosome filtering is central to the QC metrics http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_3179 http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 Benchmark ATAC-seq versus DNase-seq open-chromatin peak profiles from ENCODE K562 cells using EpiCompare's single-call QC report, with a ChIP-seq H3K27ac peak file as reference and ENCODE hg38 blacklist filtering. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad049
skills.summary: Benchmark ATAC-seq versus DNase-seq open-chromatin peak profiles from ENCODE K562 cells using EpiCompare's single-call QC report, with a ChIP-seq H3K27ac peak file as reference and ENCODE hg38 blacklist filtering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data are not peak files (e.g. raw reads, BAM files, or feature tables) — EpiCompare operates on peak files such as narrowPeak/BED Goal is within-technology comparison of experimental conditions without a reference assay to benchmark against a gold standard like ChIP-seq Peaks are not on hg19/hg38 human genome builds or no blacklist file is available, since blacklist and non-standard chromosome filtering is central to the QC metrics

skills.description: Use when two or more peak files from different epigenomic assays or technologies (narrowPeak/BED, e.g. ENCODE ATAC-seq and DNase-seq) must be compared at the chromatin-state annotation level, as in EpiCompare's ChromHMM functional-annotation report section.
skills.name: cross-assay-peak-overlap-tabulation
skills.search_text: cross-assay-peak-overlap-tabulation Use when two or more peak files from different epigenomic assays or technologies (narrowPeak/BED, e.g. ENCODE ATAC-seq and DNase-seq) must be compared at the chromatin-state annotation level, as in EpiCompare's ChromHMM functional-annotation report section. Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ) or un-called alignments — EpiCompare operates on already-called peak files Only a single peak file with no second assay/condition to contrast — there is no cross-assay comparison to tabulate Non-human genomes (hg19/hg38) — the packaged ENCODE blacklists and ChromHMM annotations cover human builds only http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Quantify how peak sets from different chromatin-profiling assays (e.g. K562 ATAC-seq vs DNase-seq narrowPeak files) are distributed across ChromHMM chromatin states using EpiCompare, then contrast per-state overlap percentages between the assays. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad049
skills.summary: Quantify how peak sets from different chromatin-profiling assays (e.g. K562 ATAC-seq vs DNase-seq narrowPeak files) are distributed across ChromHMM chromatin states using EpiCompare, then contrast per-state overlap percentages between the assays.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ) or un-called alignments — EpiCompare operates on already-called peak files Only a single peak file with no second assay/condition to contrast — there is no cross-assay comparison to tabulate Non-human genomes (hg19/hg38) — the packaged ENCODE blacklists and ChromHMM annotations cover human builds only

skills.description: Use when input peak files (e.g. BED files from CUT&Run, CUT&Tag or ChIP-sek studies) carry coordinates from mixed genome builds (hg19 vs hg38) and must be harmonized to one build before overlap/QC analysis.
skills.name: cross-build-chain-file-application
skills.search_text: cross-build-chain-file-application Use when input peak files (e.g. BED files from CUT&Run, CUT&Tag or ChIP-sek studies) carry coordinates from mixed genome builds (hg19 vs hg38) and must be harmonized to one build before overlap/QC analysis. All peak files are already annotated with the same genome build as genome_build_output, so no liftOver is invoked Input is not genomic interval data (e.g. Picard summary txt files imported as data frames), which contain no coordinates to translate The target build has no UCSC chain available for the source build (e.g. unchained non-model assemblies) Harmonizes epigenomic peak files generated against different genome reference builds by applying a UCSC chain file via rtracklayer::liftOver (wrapped by EpiCompare's liftover_grlist), so that hg19- and hg38-derived peak intervals can be compared in a single EpiCompare QC report. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad049
skills.summary: Harmonizes epigenomic peak files generated against different genome reference builds by applying a UCSC chain file via rtracklayer::liftOver (wrapped by EpiCompare's liftover_grlist), so that hg19- and hg38-derived peak intervals can be compared in a single EpiCompare QC report.
skills.when_to_use_negative: All peak files are already annotated with the same genome build as genome_build_output, so no liftOver is invoked Input is not genomic interval data (e.g. Picard summary txt files imported as data frames), which contain no coordinates to translate The target build has no UCSC chain available for the source build (e.g. unchained non-model assemblies)

skills.description: Use when benchmarking ChIP-seq/DNase-seq QC: you need cumulative distributions and cutoffs for read-layer metrics (FastQC score, uniquely mapped ratio, PBC) across many public samples, or to place a new sample against the historical quality atlas.
skills.name: cross-category-qc-distribution-aggregation
skills.search_text: cross-category-qc-distribution-aggregation Use when benchmarking ChIP-seq/DNase-seq QC: you need cumulative distributions and cutoffs for read-layer metrics (FastQC score, uniquely mapped ratio, PBC) across many public samples, or to place a new sample against the historical quality atlas. The question concerns signal-layer QC (replicate peak overlap/correlation, FRiP scores, PhastCons conservation, motif analysis — ChiLin steps 5–12) rather than read-layer metrics. Input is a single small dataset where a per-sample ChiLin QC report suffices; category-level aggregation over 23,677 historical samples adds no value. The assay falls outside ChIP-seq/DNase-seq — the cutoffs were derived from, and are suggested as usable for, ChIP-seq data. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Aggregates per-sample read-layer QC metrics — FastQC sequence quality score, uniquely mapped read ratio, and PBC — from 23,677 public ChIP-seq/DNase-seq samples (11,265 datasets) across eight literature-based classified categories into cumulative distributions. It supports assay-insensitive quality cutoffs (>85% of samples pass quality score >25, uniquely mapped ratio >0.5, PBC >0.8) and median depths (25M ChIP-seq, 40M DNase-seq). epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-016-1274-4
skills.summary: Aggregates per-sample read-layer QC metrics — FastQC sequence quality score, uniquely mapped read ratio, and PBC — from 23,677 public ChIP-seq/DNase-seq samples (11,265 datasets) across eight literature-based classified categories into cumulative distributions. It supports assay-insensitive quality cutoffs (>85% of samples pass quality score >25, uniquely mapped ratio >0.5, PBC >0.8) and median depths (25M ChIP-seq, 40M DNase-seq).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The question concerns signal-layer QC (replicate peak overlap/correlation, FRiP scores, PhastCons conservation, motif analysis — ChiLin steps 5–12) rather than read-layer metrics. Input is a single small dataset where a per-sample ChiLin QC report suffices; category-level aggregation over 23,677 historical samples adds no value. The assay falls outside ChIP-seq/DNase-seq — the cutoffs were derived from, and are suggested as usable for, ChIP-seq data.

skills.description: Use when FASTA enhancer sequences with binary labels for specific human cell lines (e.g. NHLF, HEK293, HUVEC, K562, NHEK, HMEC) must be classified, or when models trained on one cell line must be evaluated on or transferred to other cell lines' test sets.
skills.name: cross-cell-line-enhancer-prediction
skills.search_text: cross-cell-line-enhancer-prediction Use when FASTA enhancer sequences with binary labels for specific human cell lines (e.g. NHLF, HEK293, HUVEC, K562, NHEK, HMEC) must be classified, or when models trained on one cell line must be evaluated on or transferred to other cell lines' test sets. Input is already an extracted feature table rather than raw enhancer FASTA sequences — dna2vec/motif extraction is unnecessary. The task is generic (non-cell-specific) enhancer classification on the Liu et al. iEnhancer-2L dataset or enhancer-promoter data (EPdata folder), which are separate experiment tracks rather than the eight cell-line-specific datasets. The goal is interpretation of which TFBS motifs matter — SHAP.py / 'force-plot' outputs are the appropriate skill, not cross-cell-line prediction. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Predict cell-specific enhancers across multiple human cell lines using Enhancer-MDLF, a TensorFlow multi-input deep network combining dna2vec word-vector features and HOCOMOCO v11 motif features, and evaluate/transfer these models across cell lines (including transfer_1/2/3 strategies). epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbae083
skills.summary: Predict cell-specific enhancers across multiple human cell lines using Enhancer-MDLF, a TensorFlow multi-input deep network combining dna2vec word-vector features and HOCOMOCO v11 motif features, and evaluate/transfer these models across cell lines (including transfer_1/2/3 strategies).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an extracted feature table rather than raw enhancer FASTA sequences — dna2vec/motif extraction is unnecessary. The task is generic (non-cell-specific) enhancer classification on the Liu et al. iEnhancer-2L dataset or enhancer-promoter data (EPdata folder), which are separate experiment tracks rather than the eight cell-line-specific datasets. The goal is interpretation of which TFBS motifs matter — SHAP.py / 'force-plot' outputs are the appropriate skill, not cross-cell-line prediction.

skills.description: Use when a trained promoter-prediction model on one human cell line must be evaluated on independent test sets of the other cell lines, and results compared to Z-curve and same-cell line baselines.
skills.name: cross-cell-line-generalization-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-cell-line-generalization-evaluation Use when a trained promoter-prediction model on one human cell line must be evaluated on independent test sets of the other cell lines, and results compared to Z-curve and same-cell line baselines. The goal is within-species or cross-species promoter prediction on the 12 benchmark datasets of seven species rather than human cross-cell line generalization The input is already a computed feature matrix — this skill starts from raw promoter sequences and requires the feature_code.py + iLearnPlus extraction steps Evaluating enhancer-promoter discrimination from 'EPdata' rather than cross-cell line promoter prediction http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Protocol for testing whether the iPro-WAEL promoter predictor (weighted-average ensemble of an RF model and a CNN model) trained on one human cell line retains performance on independent test sets from other cell lines, benchmarked against the previous best method (Z-curve) and against same-cell line performance. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkac824
skills.summary: Protocol for testing whether the iPro-WAEL promoter predictor (weighted-average ensemble of an RF model and a CNN model) trained on one human cell line retains performance on independent test sets from other cell lines, benchmarked against the previous best method (Z-curve) and against same-cell line performance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is within-species or cross-species promoter prediction on the 12 benchmark datasets of seven species rather than human cross-cell line generalization The input is already a computed feature matrix — this skill starts from raw promoter sequences and requires the feature_code.py + iLearnPlus extraction steps Evaluating enhancer-promoter discrimination from 'EPdata' rather than cross-cell line promoter prediction

skills.description: Use when a Hi-C loop-calling model trained on one cell line must be applied to Hi-C data from a different cell line, and transferability must be quantified via precision-recall curve comparison against the source-cell-line baseline.
skills.name: cross-cell-line-loop-transfer-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-cell-line-loop-transfer-evaluation Use when a Hi-C loop-calling model trained on one cell line must be applied to Hi-C data from a different cell line, and transferability must be quantified via precision-recall curve comparison against the source-cell-line baseline. Input is single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) data — the paper states GILoop 'only focuses on bulk Hi-C' and is not capable of handling extremely sparse scHi-C data The target cell line has a sequencing depth that differs from any pre-trained model provided in the GILoop repository — the discussion flags this as weak usability The goal is de novo loop calling on the training cell line rather than cross-cell-line transfer evaluation — use standard GILoop training/inference instead Evaluates whether a GILoop model trained on one cell line's Hi-C data (e.g., GM12878) can predict CTCF-mediated loops in another cell line (e.g., K562, HeLa-S3) with minimal performance decay, by running inference with pre-trained checkpoints and comparing precision-recall curves across source and target cell lines. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2022.105535
skills.summary: Evaluates whether a GILoop model trained on one cell line's Hi-C data (e.g., GM12878) can predict CTCF-mediated loops in another cell line (e.g., K562, HeLa-S3) with minimal performance decay, by running inference with pre-trained checkpoints and comparing precision-recall curves across source and target cell lines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) data — the paper states GILoop 'only focuses on bulk Hi-C' and is not capable of handling extremely sparse scHi-C data The target cell line has a sequencing depth that differs from any pre-trained model provided in the GILoop repository — the discussion flags this as weak usability The goal is de novo loop calling on the training cell line rather than cross-cell-line transfer evaluation — use standard GILoop training/inference instead

skills.description: Use when you have encoded SE/TE sequence datasets for multiple cell lines and need to evaluate whether a sequence-only classifier trained on some cell lines predicts super-enhancers in a novel, held-out cell line.
skills.name: cross-cell-line-model-generalization
skills.search_text: cross-cell-line-model-generalization Use when you have encoded SE/TE sequence datasets for multiple cell lines and need to evaluate whether a sequence-only classifier trained on some cell lines predicts super-enhancers in a novel, held-out cell line. Input already consists of numeric feature tables (e.g. pre-encoded matrices) — re-running get_datavec.py is unnecessary; proceed directly to training The goal is ChIP-seq-based or epigenomic-feature-based SE/TE classification — DeepSE is designed to identify super-enhancers without ChIP-seq data using DNA sequence only You need a cell-line specific predictor rather than a generalization test — use train_specific.py instead of the integrative scripts http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Trains DeepSE, a two-layer CNN on dna2vec k-mer feature embeddings, on pooled cell line datasets (e.g. mESC, myotube, H2171) and tests whether the pooled or integrative model generalizes to held-out cell lines, testing whether cell-type specific super-enhancers share hidden sequence patterns. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.ygeno.2021.10.007
skills.summary: Trains DeepSE, a two-layer CNN on dna2vec k-mer feature embeddings, on pooled cell line datasets (e.g. mESC, myotube, H2171) and tests whether the pooled or integrative model generalizes to held-out cell lines, testing whether cell-type specific super-enhancers share hidden sequence patterns.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input already consists of numeric feature tables (e.g. pre-encoded matrices) — re-running get_datavec.py is unnecessary; proceed directly to training The goal is ChIP-seq-based or epigenomic-feature-based SE/TE classification — DeepSE is designed to identify super-enhancers without ChIP-seq data using DNA sequence only You need a cell-line specific predictor rather than a generalization test — use train_specific.py instead of the integrative scripts

skills.description: Use when a DNA-sequence-only super-enhancer vs typical-enhancer classifier must be evaluated per cell line and compared against reported baseline methods on shared test benchmarks.
skills.name: cross-cell-line-performance-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-cell-line-performance-comparison Use when a DNA-sequence-only super-enhancer vs typical-enhancer classifier must be evaluated per cell line and compared against reported baseline methods on shared test benchmarks. The task involves predicting super-enhancers with ChIP-seq-derived features rather than DNA sequence only — DeepSE is explicitly designed to avoid ChIP-seq data The input is a single pooled dataset with no cell-line stratification, since this skill depends on per-cell-line shared test benchmarks Only one method or one cell line is in scope, so no cross-method/cross-cell-line comparison table can be constructed http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark the DeepSE two-layer CNN (trained on dna2vec sequence embeddings) against state-of-the-art SE/TE discrimination methods across the paper's nine encoded cell-line datasets, merging reproduced and reported metrics into one side-by-side comparison table. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.ygeno.2021.10.007
skills.summary: Benchmark the DeepSE two-layer CNN (trained on dna2vec sequence embeddings) against state-of-the-art SE/TE discrimination methods across the paper's nine encoded cell-line datasets, merging reproduced and reported metrics into one side-by-side comparison table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task involves predicting super-enhancers with ChIP-seq-derived features rather than DNA sequence only — DeepSE is explicitly designed to avoid ChIP-seq data The input is a single pooled dataset with no cell-line stratification, since this skill depends on per-cell-line shared test benchmarks Only one method or one cell line is in scope, so no cross-method/cross-cell-line comparison table can be constructed

skills.description: Use when a choice among feature-selection (top-value) or partitioning methods for consensus clustering must be justified by large-scale empirical comparison across many datasets rather than a single example.
skills.name: cross-dataset-method-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-method-comparison Use when a choice among feature-selection (top-value) or partitioning methods for consensus clustering must be justified by large-scale empirical comparison across many datasets rather than a single example. You need to partition a single dataset and just pick a method, with no cross-dataset benchmarking required — use cola's per-dataset comparison of method results instead The data are scRNA-Seq with several thousands of cells — the article notes cola's runtime and memory usage 'might not be acceptable' at that scale The input is already a partition or a feature table rather than a raw gene expression matrix — the preprocessing and partitioning steps here assume row-level expression matrices Benchmarks all 24 combinations of top-value methods (SD, MAD, CV, ATC) and partitioning methods across 435 public gene expression datasets (206 GDS microarray + 223 recount2 RNA-Seq), scoring each combination by the mean 1-PAC score at the best k to identify which method combinations (notably ATC and skmeans) yield the most stable partitions. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa1146
skills.summary: Benchmarks all 24 combinations of top-value methods (SD, MAD, CV, ATC) and partitioning methods across 435 public gene expression datasets (206 GDS microarray + 223 recount2 RNA-Seq), scoring each combination by the mean 1-PAC score at the best k to identify which method combinations (notably ATC and skmeans) yield the most stable partitions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to partition a single dataset and just pick a method, with no cross-dataset benchmarking required — use cola's per-dataset comparison of method results instead The data are scRNA-Seq with several thousands of cells — the article notes cola's runtime and memory usage 'might not be acceptable' at that scale The input is already a partition or a feature table rather than a raw gene expression matrix — the preprocessing and partitioning steps here assume row-level expression matrices

skills.description: Use when multiple peak files from different epigenomic assays (e.g. CUT&Tag, CUT&Run, ChIP-seq BED/narrowPeak) must be benchmarked against a reference for QC, overlap statistics, and functional annotation.
skills.name: cross-dataset-peak-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-peak-overlap-analysis Use when multiple peak files from different epigenomic assays (e.g. CUT&Tag, CUT&Run, ChIP-seq BED/narrowPeak) must be benchmarked against a reference for QC, overlap statistics, and functional annotation. Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ/BAM) rather than already-called peak files — EpiCompare starts from peak files, not alignments Only a single peak file with no reference or comparison dataset exists — the overlap/benchmarking sections need multiple query files or a reference Peaks are on a genome build with no ENCODE blacklist available (e.g. non-human hg19/hg38 genomes) http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Run EpiCompare to compare epigenomic peak files across datasets and technologies (e.g. CUT&Tag and CUT&Run H3K27ac against an ENCODE ChIP-seq reference), producing a single interactive HTML report with General Metrics, Peak Overlap, and Functional Annotation sections. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad049
skills.summary: Run EpiCompare to compare epigenomic peak files across datasets and technologies (e.g. CUT&Tag and CUT&Run H3K27ac against an ENCODE ChIP-seq reference), producing a single interactive HTML report with General Metrics, Peak Overlap, and Functional Annotation sections.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ/BAM) rather than already-called peak files — EpiCompare starts from peak files, not alignments Only a single peak file with no reference or comparison dataset exists — the overlap/benchmarking sections need multiple query files or a reference Peaks are on a genome build with no ENCODE blacklist available (e.g. non-human hg19/hg38 genomes)

skills.description: Use when cell type-specific genomic features (loops, peaks, enhancers) from one dataset must be validated against independent cell type-matched epigenomic or transcriptomic reference datasets.
skills.name: cross-dataset-reference-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-reference-enrichment-analysis Use when cell type-specific genomic features (loops, peaks, enhancers) from one dataset must be validated against independent cell type-matched epigenomic or transcriptomic reference datasets. When the input features are not cell type-resolved (e.g., bulk loops or peaks from mixed populations) — matched-vs-unmatched enrichment is undefined without cell type labels. When no independent cell type-matched reference dataset exists for the tissue of interest; the skill's core comparison cannot be performed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Validates cell type-specific features (e.g., SnapHiC loop anchors and linked promoters) by quantifying CPM-normalized ATAC-seq/H3K27ac signal and FPKM expression and testing whether they are highest in the matched cell type of external reference datasets (Nott et al. epigenomics, Zhang et al. expression). epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41592-021-01231-2
skills.summary: Validates cell type-specific features (e.g., SnapHiC loop anchors and linked promoters) by quantifying CPM-normalized ATAC-seq/H3K27ac signal and FPKM expression and testing whether they are highest in the matched cell type of external reference datasets (Nott et al. epigenomics, Zhang et al. expression).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input features are not cell type-resolved (e.g., bulk loops or peaks from mixed populations) — matched-vs-unmatched enrichment is undefined without cell type labels. When no independent cell type-matched reference dataset exists for the tissue of interest; the skill's core comparison cannot be performed.

skills.description: Use when evaluating cross-platform transfer of a TF binding affinity model — train on HT-SELEX per-cycle enrichment data, test on uPBM affinities, and benchmark Pearson correlation against DeepBind, BEESEM, and BindSpace.
skills.name: cross-dataset-tf-binding-transfer-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-tf-binding-transfer-evaluation Use when evaluating cross-platform transfer of a TF binding affinity model — train on HT-SELEX per-cycle enrichment data, test on uPBM affinities, and benchmark Pearson correlation against DeepBind, BEESEM, and BindSpace. Training and test data come from the same platform (e.g. an 80/20 uPBM or gcPBM split) — use the paper's within-dataset R2 evaluation instead (gcPBM 0.93 ± 0.02, uPBM 0.69 ± 0.17) The goal is in vivo binding site prediction — combine in vitro predictions with yeast G1-phase nucleosome positioning maps rather than running cross-dataset transfer Input files do not follow the required layouts (proteins/{protein}/{cycle}.txt for selex_regressor.py, proteins/{protein}/{protein}_training.txt for upbm_regressor.py) — the regressors expect these exact templates http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmarking skill that measures how well a transcription factor binding affinity model trained on HT-SELEX per-cycle enrichments transfers to uPBM data, using DNAffinity's random forest (average Pearson 0.47) against DeepBind, BEESEM, BindSpace, and DeepSELEX baselines. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkac708
skills.summary: Benchmarking skill that measures how well a transcription factor binding affinity model trained on HT-SELEX per-cycle enrichments transfers to uPBM data, using DNAffinity's random forest (average Pearson 0.47) against DeepBind, BEESEM, BindSpace, and DeepSELEX baselines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Training and test data come from the same platform (e.g. an 80/20 uPBM or gcPBM split) — use the paper's within-dataset R2 evaluation instead (gcPBM 0.93 ± 0.02, uPBM 0.69 ± 0.17) The goal is in vivo binding site prediction — combine in vitro predictions with yeast G1-phase nucleosome positioning maps rather than running cross-dataset transfer Input files do not follow the required layouts (proteins/{protein}/{cycle}.txt for selex_regressor.py, proteins/{protein}/{protein}_training.txt for upbm_regressor.py) — the regressors expect these exact templates

skills.description: Use when a ranked TR list (e.g., BIT scores/ranks from TCGA cancer-type accessible regions) must be independently validated by asking whether top-ranked TRs are essential upon CRISPR/Cas9 knockout in the same cancer lineages (DepMap Chronos).
skills.name: cross-dataset-validation-of-tr-identification
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-validation-of-tr-identification Use when a ranked TR list (e.g., BIT scores/ranks from TCGA cancer-type accessible regions) must be independently validated by asking whether top-ranked TRs are essential upon CRISPR/Cas9 knockout in the same cancer lineages (DepMap Chronos). The TR list is unranked or has no BIT scores/ranks — the validation depends on intersecting top-ranked TRs with the essential set The goal is de novo TR identification from motifs or ChIP-seq alone (e.g., WhichTF/HOMER, BART) rather than post hoc functional validation of an existing ranked list The knockout data perturb only coding-gene viability but the query regions target non-coding regulatory elements without a corresponding gene-level essentiality readout http://edamontology.org/topic_0204 Validates computationally ranked transcriptional regulators (e.g., BIT-ranked TRs from cancer-type-specific accessible regions) against an independent functional dataset — DepMap CRISPR/Cas9 Chronos gene-effect scores — to determine what fraction of top-ranked TRs are functionally essential genes. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-60269-4
skills.summary: Validates computationally ranked transcriptional regulators (e.g., BIT-ranked TRs from cancer-type-specific accessible regions) against an independent functional dataset — DepMap CRISPR/Cas9 Chronos gene-effect scores — to determine what fraction of top-ranked TRs are functionally essential genes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The TR list is unranked or has no BIT scores/ranks — the validation depends on intersecting top-ranked TRs with the essential set The goal is de novo TR identification from motifs or ChIP-seq alone (e.g., WhichTF/HOMER, BART) rather than post hoc functional validation of an existing ranked list The knockout data perturb only coding-gene viability but the query regions target non-coding regulatory elements without a corresponding gene-level essentiality readout

skills.description: Use when two trained promoter classifiers (RF probability outputs and CNN/Keras outputs) must be fused via a weighted average whose weights are tuned by minimizing cross-entropy on a labeled weighted set.
skills.name: cross-entropy-weight-optimization
skills.search_text: cross-entropy-weight-optimization Use when two trained promoter classifiers (RF probability outputs and CNN/Keras outputs) must be fused via a weighted average whose weights are tuned by minimizing cross-entropy on a labeled weighted set. Only a single trained classifier is available (no RF + CNN pair to combine into a weighted average). The task is feature extraction rather than ensemble combination — use feature_code.py or iLearnPlus instead. Input is a different model family whose outputs were not produced by RF.py and CNN.py with the iPro-WAEL feature encodings. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Optimizes the weighted-average combination of a random forest (RF) and a CNN promoter-prediction model in iPro-WAEL by minimizing cross-entropy loss between predicted values and true labels on a dedicated weighted set, implemented in Weighted_average.py using SLSQP. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkac824
skills.summary: Optimizes the weighted-average combination of a random forest (RF) and a CNN promoter-prediction model in iPro-WAEL by minimizing cross-entropy loss between predicted values and true labels on a dedicated weighted set, implemented in Weighted_average.py using SLSQP.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single trained classifier is available (no RF + CNN pair to combine into a weighted average). The task is feature extraction rather than ensemble combination — use feature_code.py or iLearnPlus instead. Input is a different model family whose outputs were not produced by RF.py and CNN.py with the iPro-WAEL feature encodings.

skills.description: Use when multiple sequencing lanes exist within the same sample group (e.g., stimulated or unstimulated STAT1 ChIP-Seq lanes) and you must quantify whether their genome-wide read distributions are consistent before downstream peak calling.
skills.name: cross-lane-reproducibility-assessment
skills.search_text: cross-lane-reproducibility-assessment Use when multiple sequencing lanes exist within the same sample group (e.g., stimulated or unstimulated STAT1 ChIP-Seq lanes) and you must quantify whether their genome-wide read distributions are consistent before downstream peak calling. Only one lane is available per condition, so no within-group lane pair exists to compare Input consists of already-called peak sets rather than raw genome-wide read-count distributions — peak-level overlap analysis answers a different question than distribution-level reproducibility The goal is cross-condition differential binding (stimulated vs unstimulated) rather than within-group assay reproducibility; cross-group K-S results (36-42/48 significant) reflect biological difference, not noise http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Quantitatively assesses reproducibility of a ChIP-Seq assay by applying two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) tests to genome-wide read-count distributions between lane pairs, partitioned across 24 chromosomes x 2 strands = 48 chromosome/strand combinations, with Bonferroni correction at threshold 0.001. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/1471-2105-11-369
skills.summary: Quantitatively assesses reproducibility of a ChIP-Seq assay by applying two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) tests to genome-wide read-count distributions between lane pairs, partitioned across 24 chromosomes x 2 strands = 48 chromosome/strand combinations, with Bonferroni correction at threshold 0.001.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one lane is available per condition, so no within-group lane pair exists to compare Input consists of already-called peak sets rather than raw genome-wide read-count distributions — peak-level overlap analysis answers a different question than distribution-level reproducibility The goal is cross-condition differential binding (stimulated vs unstimulated) rather than within-group assay reproducibility; cross-group K-S results (36-42/48 significant) reflect biological difference, not noise

skills.description: Use when a new cell type annotation method must be quantitatively compared to established baselines on shared scRNA-seq datasets, with accuracy expressed as consistent rates against curated reference cell types.
skills.name: cross-method-accuracy-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-accuracy-comparison Use when a new cell type annotation method must be quantitatively compared to established baselines on shared scRNA-seq datasets, with accuracy expressed as consistent rates against curated reference cell types. The goal is per-cell rather than per-cluster annotation accuracy, since scCATCH and this comparison operate at the cluster level No manually curated reference cell types are available, so consistent rates cannot be computed against a ground truth The tissue/species of the dataset is not covered by the CellMatch reference database, which can itself cause incorrect annotation http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Benchmark a cluster-based cell type annotation method (scCATCH) against cell-based annotators (CellAssign, Garnett, SingleR, scMap, CHETAH) by computing per-cluster and overall consistent rates against manually curated reference cell types on benchmark datasets (Chen, 203 cells; Xin, 1,600 cells; Gierahn, 3,694 cells). epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2020.100882
skills.summary: Benchmark a cluster-based cell type annotation method (scCATCH) against cell-based annotators (CellAssign, Garnett, SingleR, scMap, CHETAH) by computing per-cluster and overall consistent rates against manually curated reference cell types on benchmark datasets (Chen, 203 cells; Xin, 1,600 cells; Gierahn, 3,694 cells).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is per-cell rather than per-cluster annotation accuracy, since scCATCH and this comparison operate at the cluster level No manually curated reference cell types are available, so consistent rates cannot be computed against a ground truth The tissue/species of the dataset is not covered by the CellMatch reference database, which can itself cause incorrect annotation

skills.description: Use when you have ranked TR lists from multiple TR-identification methods applied to the same query region sets (e.g., TR perturbation-derived DARs or cancer-type-specific accessible regions) and need to quantify inter-method agreement or rank-based accuracy.
skills.name: cross-method-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-benchmark-comparison Use when you have ranked TR lists from multiple TR-identification methods applied to the same query region sets (e.g., TR perturbation-derived DARs or cancer-type-specific accessible regions) and need to quantify inter-method agreement or rank-based accuracy. Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ/BAM) rather than already-generated ranked TR lists — peak calling and TR identification must happen first Only one method's ranked TR list is available, so no pairwise or MRR comparison can be made The goal is de novo TR identification from a query region set rather than benchmarking agreement among existing method outputs http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Reproduces the paper's cross-method benchmarking by computing all pairwise Jaccard indices of top-10/50/100 ranked TR lists from six methods (BIT, BART, ChIP-Atlas, i-cisTarget, HOMER, WhichTF) and benchmarking ranking quality with mean reciprocal rank (MRR). epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-60269-4
skills.summary: Reproduces the paper's cross-method benchmarking by computing all pairwise Jaccard indices of top-10/50/100 ranked TR lists from six methods (BIT, BART, ChIP-Atlas, i-cisTarget, HOMER, WhichTF) and benchmarking ranking quality with mean reciprocal rank (MRR).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ/BAM) rather than already-generated ranked TR lists — peak calling and TR identification must happen first Only one method's ranked TR list is available, so no pairwise or MRR comparison can be made The goal is de novo TR identification from a query region set rather than benchmarking agreement among existing method outputs

skills.description: Use when a scATAC-seq (or scRNA-seq) dataset with reference cell-type labels is available and you must quantify how accurately competing clustering tools recover those labels, including under graded data corruption.
skills.name: cross-method-clustering-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-clustering-comparison Use when a scATAC-seq (or scRNA-seq) dataset with reference cell-type labels is available and you must quantify how accurately competing clustering tools recover those labels, including under graded data corruption. The dataset has no reference cell-type labels, so ARI/NMI/micro-F1 against a ground truth cannot be computed You only need to run and tune a single clustering method rather than compare several tools head-to-head on identical input SCALE is being used for batch-effect removal — the article notes it 'is not specifically designed to identify and remove these artifacts from the input data', so it is the wrong tool for that goal rather than for clustering comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark a candidate single-cell clustering method (e.g. SCALE's VAE+GMM latent features clustered with K-means/Leiden) against baselines such as scABC, scVI, cisTopic, and SC3 by computing ARI, NMI, and micro-F1 against reference cell-type labels on the same input count matrix. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-12630-7
skills.summary: Benchmark a candidate single-cell clustering method (e.g. SCALE's VAE+GMM latent features clustered with K-means/Leiden) against baselines such as scABC, scVI, cisTopic, and SC3 by computing ARI, NMI, and micro-F1 against reference cell-type labels on the same input count matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has no reference cell-type labels, so ARI/NMI/micro-F1 against a ground truth cannot be computed You only need to run and tune a single clustering method rather than compare several tools head-to-head on identical input SCALE is being used for batch-effect removal — the article notes it 'is not specifically designed to identify and remove these artifacts from the input data', so it is the wrong tool for that goal rather than for clustering comparison

skills.description: Use when you have compartment-score tracks from dcHiC, HOMER, and/or CscoreTool over identical genomic bins of the same Hi-C map (e.g., mouse ESC at 100 kb) and need to quantify cross-method concordance and lamin-association agreement.
skills.name: cross-method-compartment-score-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-compartment-score-comparison Use when you have compartment-score tracks from dcHiC, HOMER, and/or CscoreTool over identical genomic bins of the same Hi-C map (e.g., mouse ESC at 100 kb) and need to quantify cross-method concordance and lamin-association agreement. When the goal is detecting statistically significant differential compartments across two or more contact maps rather than benchmarking concordance of compartment scores from a single map — dcHiC's Mahalanobis-distance/chi-square significance testing is the appropriate mode there When single-cell Hi-C maps are too sparse for reliable compartment identification even at coarse resolution — single-cell sparsity is a known major limitation for compartment calling When contact maps are at resolutions finer than dcHiC's supported range or come from organisms outside the human/mouse data scope validated in this work http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmarks compartment-score tracks from dcHiC against established compartment callers (HOMER and CscoreTool) on the same Hi-C contact map, quantifying genome-wide concordance by Pearson correlation and orthogonal validation against Lamin B1 data. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-34626-6
skills.summary: Benchmarks compartment-score tracks from dcHiC against established compartment callers (HOMER and CscoreTool) on the same Hi-C contact map, quantifying genome-wide concordance by Pearson correlation and orthogonal validation against Lamin B1 data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is detecting statistically significant differential compartments across two or more contact maps rather than benchmarking concordance of compartment scores from a single map — dcHiC's Mahalanobis-distance/chi-square significance testing is the appropriate mode there When single-cell Hi-C maps are too sparse for reliable compartment identification even at coarse resolution — single-cell sparsity is a known major limitation for compartment calling When contact maps are at resolutions finer than dcHiC's supported range or come from organisms outside the human/mouse data scope validated in this work

skills.description: Use when comparing loop sets from a supervised predictor (Peakachu) with enrichment-based callers (HiCCUPS, Fit-Hi-C) on the same Hi-C matrix, to quantify overlap and orthogonal validation.
skills.name: cross-method-loop-set-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-method-loop-set-overlap-analysis Use when comparing loop sets from a supervised predictor (Peakachu) with enrichment-based callers (HiCCUPS, Fit-Hi-C) on the same Hi-C matrix, to quantify overlap and orthogonal validation. The input matrix is low depth (e.g., 1.5% down-sample) such that Fit-Hi-C retains no interactions at q < 1e-5 and HiCCUPS with default parameters yields less than 1/3 of Peakachu loops — cutoffs must be retuned rather than compared as-is The goal is de novo loop detection rather than method benchmarking — use peakachu train/score_genome directly Data are from a platform without a dedicated enrichment-based loop caller (e.g., DNA SPRITE), making the three-way comparison impossible http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Benchmarks Peakachu's Random Forest-predicted chromatin loops against enrichment-based loop callers (HiCCUPS, Fit-Hi-C) by intersecting the three loop sets and computing method-specific validation ratios against orthogonal data in GM12878 Hi-C. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-17239-9
skills.summary: Benchmarks Peakachu's Random Forest-predicted chromatin loops against enrichment-based loop callers (HiCCUPS, Fit-Hi-C) by intersecting the three loop sets and computing method-specific validation ratios against orthogonal data in GM12878 Hi-C.

skills.description: Use when two genome-wide protein-DNA binding assays (e.g., ChIP-Seq and ChIP-chip) must be compared on biological signal quality rather than peak overlap, using motif enrichment of the expected TF-binding motif as the figure of merit.

Input is a single-platform peak set with no comparable alternative-assay region set — use standard peak-calling QC instead No expected motif or motif-family database is available for the assayed transcription factor, since the comparison relies on enriching the known TF motif family The goal is peak-coordinate overlap (Jaccard/intersection) rather than biological signal-quality comparison — a direct interval-overlap tool is more appropriate http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Compares ChIP-Seq peaks (called by HPeak) against ChIP-chip enriched regions (e.g., 3,701 STAT1 regions at FDR 0.05 from Euskirchen et al.) by quantifying transcription-factor motif enrichment in test vs. matched control sequences, demonstrating ChIP-Seq's advantage in motif recovery and rank-dependence. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/1471-2105-11-369
