skills.search_text: genomic-region-bed-interval-handling Use when you need read-level methylation linkage (phase) information within defined genomic intervals from MethylC-seq/Bismark alignments, e.g. to test whether methylation differences occur in a nonrandom pattern. You only need aggregate per-CpG or per-region methylation counts for DMR calling — use extract_CpG_data.py -i plus combine_CpG_sites.py and findDMRs.r instead of the -n linked-data mode The input alignment lacks a header, XM methylation strings, or XG genome designations (e.g. a non-Bismark SAM) — extract_CpG_data.py will not parse it You need to model sets of regions, quantitative traits, or batch effects — the article notes DMRfinder does not support these http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Prepare tab-delimited BED files of genomic regions of interest and use DMRfinder's extract_CpG_data.py -n option to collect read-level, spatially-linked methylation patterns within each region from Bismark SAM alignments. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-017-1909-0
skills.summary: Prepare tab-delimited BED files of genomic regions of interest and use DMRfinder's extract_CpG_data.py -n option to collect read-level, spatially-linked methylation patterns within each region from Bismark SAM alignments.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need aggregate per-CpG or per-region methylation counts for DMR calling — use extract_CpG_data.py -i plus combine_CpG_sites.py and findDMRs.r instead of the -n linked-data mode The input alignment lacks a header, XM methylation strings, or XG genome designations (e.g. a non-Bismark SAM) — extract_CpG_data.py will not parse it You need to model sets of regions, quantitative traits, or batch effects — the article notes DMRfinder does not support these

skills.description: Reference for removing non-informative or artifact-prone regions (sex chromosomes, chrM, ENCODE blacklist) from bin-sample methylation quantification matrices before downstream group/batch comparisons.
skills.name: genomic-region-blacklist-filtering
skills.search_text: genomic-region-blacklist-filtering Reference for removing non-informative or artifact-prone regions (sex chromosomes, chrM, ENCODE blacklist) from bin-sample methylation quantification matrices before downstream group/batch comparisons. Input is a per-sample (not aggregated) methylation quantification file where filtering should be handled by the upstream quantification tool The analysis intentionally requires sex chromosome or mitochondrial methylation signal (e.g. studying sex-chromosome methylation), since this filter uniformly removes those bins Quantification matrices are already filtered or the downstream method expects blacklist regions to be handled with its own annotation scheme http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Uniformly filters aggregated bin-sample methylation matrices produced by cfMeDIP-seq pipelines (MEDIPIPE-style) by removing genomic bins on sex chromosomes, the mitochondrial chromosome, and ENCODE blacklist regions (Amemiya et al. 2019), producing both original and filtered TAB-delimited outputs that are bgzip-compressed and Tabix-indexed. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad423
skills.summary: Uniformly filters aggregated bin-sample methylation matrices produced by cfMeDIP-seq pipelines (MEDIPIPE-style) by removing genomic bins on sex chromosomes, the mitochondrial chromosome, and ENCODE blacklist regions (Amemiya et al. 2019), producing both original and filtered TAB-delimited outputs that are bgzip-compressed and Tabix-indexed.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a per-sample (not aggregated) methylation quantification file where filtering should be handled by the upstream quantification tool The analysis intentionally requires sex chromosome or mitochondrial methylation signal (e.g. studying sex-chromosome methylation), since this filter uniformly removes those bins Quantification matrices are already filtered or the downstream method expects blacklist regions to be handled with its own annotation scheme

skills.description: Use when individual-CpG methylation count tables (e.g. Bismark-derived .cov files with methylated/unmethylated counts per site) must be collapsed into genomic regions before differential methylation testing.
skills.name: genomic-region-coordinate-aggregation
skills.search_text: genomic-region-coordinate-aggregation Use when individual-CpG methylation count tables (e.g. Bismark-derived .cov files with methylated/unmethylated counts per site) must be collapsed into genomic regions before differential methylation testing. Input is already a region-level methylation table rather than per-CpG-site counts The analysis goal requires modeling sets of regions or quantitative traits, or accounting for batch effects — DMRfinder explicitly does not support these Methylation-level-guided region definition is desired; this clustering deliberately ignores methylation levels http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Aggregates per-CpG-site methylation counts into genomic regions using a modified single-linkage clustering that chains sites within a maximum inter-site distance, then splits oversized regions, so downstream DMR testing operates on multi-CpG regions rather than individual sites. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-017-1909-0
skills.summary: Aggregates per-CpG-site methylation counts into genomic regions using a modified single-linkage clustering that chains sites within a maximum inter-site distance, then splits oversized regions, so downstream DMR testing operates on multi-CpG regions rather than individual sites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a region-level methylation table rather than per-CpG-site counts The analysis goal requires modeling sets of regions or quantitative traits, or accounting for batch effects — DMRfinder explicitly does not support these Methylation-level-guided region definition is desired; this clustering deliberately ignores methylation levels

skills.description: Use when you have TF binding locations (e.g. an ENCODE ChIP-seq peak BED file) and need to find which EpiRegio REMs overlap them and which target genes those REMs are associated with.
skills.name: genomic-region-overlap-querying
skills.search_text: genomic-region-overlap-querying Use when you have TF binding locations (e.g. an ENCODE ChIP-seq peak BED file) and need to find which EpiRegio REMs overlap them and which target genes those REMs are associated with. You already have REM identifiers or genes of interest and should use EpiRegio's Gene Query instead of mapping regions You need REMs covering less than half of each peak's length (a lower overlap threshold is required than the 50% default used here) You want de novo identification of regulatory elements rather than mapping known binding regions onto EpiRegio's REM collection http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 Maps TF ChIP-seq peak regions (BED) onto EpiRegio's regulatory elements (REMs) using the Region Query with a minimum overlap percentage, to retrieve REM–gene associations for downstream target-gene analyses. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa382
skills.summary: Maps TF ChIP-seq peak regions (BED) onto EpiRegio's regulatory elements (REMs) using the Region Query with a minimum overlap percentage, to retrieve REM–gene associations for downstream target-gene analyses.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have REM identifiers or genes of interest and should use EpiRegio's Gene Query instead of mapping regions You need REMs covering less than half of each peak's length (a lower overlap threshold is required than the 50% default used here) You want de novo identification of regulatory elements rather than mapping known binding regions onto EpiRegio's REM collection

skills.description: Use when BED peak lists (e.g. MACS-called H3K4me3, H3K27me3, or bivalent peaks) must be classified into promoter, intergenic, or intragenic features using a RefSeq refGene annotation for a genome assembly such as mouse mm9.
skills.name: genomic-region-promoter-intergenic-intragenic-assignment
skills.search_text: genomic-region-promoter-intergenic-intragenic-assignment Use when BED peak lists (e.g. MACS-called H3K4me3, H3K27me3, or bivalent peaks) must be classified into promoter, intergenic, or intragenic features using a RefSeq refGene annotation for a genome assembly such as mouse mm9. The goal is peak-level signal quantification or read counting over regions rather than feature-category annotation (use SeqCode recoverChIPlevels/counting instead). Only a genome browser-style track profile (e.g. bigwig) is needed — SeqCode defers bigwig generation to future versions. The peak coordinates and the refGene annotation correspond to different assemblies (e.g. mm9 peaks vs mm10 refGene), which would corrupt promoter assignments. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Assigns every interval in a BED-formatted peak list (e.g. MACS-called ChIP-seq peaks) to a genomic feature category — promoter, intergenic, or intragenic — using the SeqCode genomeDistribution command against a RefSeq refGene annotation and a chromosome-size file for a specific genome assembly, enabling feature-composition charts such as the promoter enrichment of bivalent H3K4me3+H3K27me3 peaks. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-98889-7
skills.summary: Assigns every interval in a BED-formatted peak list (e.g. MACS-called ChIP-seq peaks) to a genomic feature category — promoter, intergenic, or intragenic — using the SeqCode genomeDistribution command against a RefSeq refGene annotation and a chromosome-size file for a specific genome assembly, enabling feature-composition charts such as the promoter enrichment of bivalent H3K4me3+H3K27me3 peaks.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is peak-level signal quantification or read counting over regions rather than feature-category annotation (use SeqCode recoverChIPlevels/counting instead). Only a genome browser-style track profile (e.g. bigwig) is needed — SeqCode defers bigwig generation to future versions. The peak coordinates and the refGene annotation correspond to different assemblies (e.g. mm9 peaks vs mm10 refGene), which would corrupt promoter assignments.

skills.description: Use when testing whether a genomic feature (R-loops, G-quadruplexes, GC/CpG content) is enriched on HOT region coordinates relative to control regions binned by TF occupancy percentiles.
skills.name: genomic-region-set-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: genomic-region-set-enrichment-analysis Use when testing whether a genomic feature (R-loops, G-quadruplexes, GC/CpG content) is enriched on HOT region coordinates relative to control regions binned by TF occupancy percentiles. The question is about TF binding specificity or motif presence rather than enrichment of a physical genomic feature over region sets No matched control library (mock or RNaseH-treated) exists for the signal dataset, making log2(IP/control) enrichment ill-defined http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Computes log2(IP/control) enrichment of genomic signals (e.g. DRIP-seq R-loop data) over defined region sets (HOT regions vs. occupancy-binned controls) to test whether a discriminatory feature is enriched on HOT regions across cell lines and species. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz460
skills.summary: Computes log2(IP/control) enrichment of genomic signals (e.g. DRIP-seq R-loop data) over defined region sets (HOT regions vs. occupancy-binned controls) to test whether a discriminatory feature is enriched on HOT regions across cell lines and species.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The question is about TF binding specificity or motif presence rather than enrichment of a physical genomic feature over region sets No matched control library (mock or RNaseH-treated) exists for the signal dataset, making log2(IP/control) enrichment ill-defined

skills.description: Use when you hold a set of chromosome coordinates from epigenomic profiling (e.g., ATAC-seq DAR peaks called by MACS2 or DiffBind) and need to identify transcriptional regulators for that region set via BIT.
skills.name: genomic-region-set-processing
skills.search_text: genomic-region-set-processing Use when you hold a set of chromosome coordinates from epigenomic profiling (e.g., ATAC-seq DAR peaks called by MACS2 or DiffBind) and need to identify transcriptional regulators for that region set via BIT. Your input is already a ranked gene set or scored list rather than a genomic region set — BART's geneset mode (bart2 geneset -i genelist.txt) is designed for gene-set queries instead You need motif-based TR identification from sequences rather than overlap against real ChIP-seq binding profiles — BIT's reference-library approach explicitly bypasses computationally predicted motifs Your regions are on a genome build not covered by BIT's reference libraries (hg38 or mm10) http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 Converts a processed genomic region set (e.g., a BED file of differentially accessible peaks) into the fixed-length binary overlap vectors that BIT's Bayesian hierarchical model requires, then samples the joint posterior via a Gibbs-sampler MCMC to produce a per-TR ranked table (rank_table.csv) with Theta_i estimates, 95% credible intervals, and BIT scores. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-60269-4
skills.summary: Converts a processed genomic region set (e.g., a BED file of differentially accessible peaks) into the fixed-length binary overlap vectors that BIT's Bayesian hierarchical model requires, then samples the joint posterior via a Gibbs-sampler MCMC to produce a per-TR ranked table (rank_table.csv) with Theta_i estimates, 95% credible intervals, and BIT scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your input is already a ranked gene set or scored list rather than a genomic region set — BART's geneset mode (bart2 geneset -i genelist.txt) is designed for gene-set queries instead You need motif-based TR identification from sequences rather than overlap against real ChIP-seq binding profiles — BIT's reference-library approach explicitly bypasses computationally predicted motifs Your regions are on a genome build not covered by BIT's reference libraries (hg38 or mm10)

skills.description: Use when benchmarking TPX-prediction software (3plex, Triplexator, TriplexAligner, fasim-LongTarget) and a matched randomised genomic negative set is needed to compute ROC AUCs against experimentally derived positive peaks.
skills.name: genomic-region-shuffling-negative-control
skills.search_text: genomic-region-shuffling-negative-control Use when benchmarking TPX-prediction software (3plex, Triplexator, TriplexAligner, fasim-LongTarget) and a matched randomised genomic negative set is needed to compute ROC AUCs against experimentally derived positive peaks. The analysis goal is to test sequence-level rather than region-level discrimination — use the shuffled-transcript strategy (fasta-shuffle-letters, -kmer 1) on the positive regions instead. No experimentally supported positive peak set exists; AUC benchmarking against randomised negatives is not meaningful without true positives. Only a small positive set is available (e.g. fewer than the Top1000 peaks), making 1000 resampled AUC estimates unstable. http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Generates matched negative-control genomic regions with bedtools shuffle to benchmark RNA:DNA triplex (TPX) prediction tools, resampling the negatives 1000 times to estimate AUC standard deviation when comparing 3plex against Triplexator, TriplexAligner and fasim-LongTarget. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.05.016
skills.summary: Generates matched negative-control genomic regions with bedtools shuffle to benchmark RNA:DNA triplex (TPX) prediction tools, resampling the negatives 1000 times to estimate AUC standard deviation when comparing 3plex against Triplexator, TriplexAligner and fasim-LongTarget.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is to test sequence-level rather than region-level discrimination — use the shuffled-transcript strategy (fasta-shuffle-letters, -kmer 1) on the positive regions instead. No experimentally supported positive peak set exists; AUC benchmarking against randomised negatives is not meaningful without true positives. Only a small positive set is available (e.g. fewer than the Top1000 peaks), making 1000 resampled AUC estimates unstable.

skills.description: Use when a published pipeline reports a total differential-region span (e.g. Mb or % of genome) and you must reproduce the pipeline and confirm your summed call-set span matches that value.
skills.name: genomic-region-span-verification
skills.search_text: genomic-region-span-verification Use when a published pipeline reports a total differential-region span (e.g. Mb or % of genome) and you must reproduce the pipeline and confirm your summed call-set span matches that value. The modification has peak-like (narrow) footprints rather than broad marks like H3K27me3/H3K9me3 — histoneHMM was designed for broad diffuse modifications Input is already a processed peak/differential-region BED file rather than aligned BAM reads, so the binning-and-HMM pipeline cannot be rerun to recompute the span No published numeric span or percentage exists to verify against, making the comparison step meaningless http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Verifies a ChIP-seq differential calling result by summing the genomic span of called differentially modified regions and comparing it against a reported total, e.g. histoneHMM's 24.96 Mb (0.9% of rat rn4) for SHR vs BN heart H3K27me3. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-015-0491-6
skills.summary: Verifies a ChIP-seq differential calling result by summing the genomic span of called differentially modified regions and comparing it against a reported total, e.g. histoneHMM's 24.96 Mb (0.9% of rat rn4) for SHR vs BN heart H3K27me3.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The modification has peak-like (narrow) footprints rather than broad marks like H3K27me3/H3K9me3 — histoneHMM was designed for broad diffuse modifications Input is already a processed peak/differential-region BED file rather than aligned BAM reads, so the binning-and-HMM pipeline cannot be rerun to recompute the span No published numeric span or percentage exists to verify against, making the comparison step meaningless

skills.description: Use when Microcket-generated .hic contact-matrix files (e.g., QSC and FISC Hi-C replicates) must be visualized as contact maps for specific regions, resolutions, and downstream comparative analyses.
skills.name: genomic-region-subsetting-of-hic-data
skills.search_text: genomic-region-subsetting-of-hic-data Use when Microcket-generated .hic contact-matrix files (e.g., QSC and FISC Hi-C replicates) must be visualized as contact maps for specific regions, resolutions, and downstream comparative analyses. The raw data are still FASTQ reads and have not yet been processed by Microcket into .hic files — run the upstream Microcket pipeline first The analysis goal is genome-wide quantification (e.g., compartment or TAD calling) rather than subsetting and visualizing specific genomic regions The .hic files were not balanced/normalized (KR normalization unavailable), making cross-condition comparison of contact intensities unreliable http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Extract KR-normalized Hi-C contact matrices for defined chromosomal regions and bin sizes from .hic files using JuicerTools (straw/dump), merge per-replicate matrices per condition, and render square contact-map heatmaps (e.g., chr16 views of QSC vs FISC) for direct visual comparison of chromatin architecture. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.xpro.2025.103962
skills.summary: Extract KR-normalized Hi-C contact matrices for defined chromosomal regions and bin sizes from .hic files using JuicerTools (straw/dump), merge per-replicate matrices per condition, and render square contact-map heatmaps (e.g., chr16 views of QSC vs FISC) for direct visual comparison of chromatin architecture.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The raw data are still FASTQ reads and have not yet been processed by Microcket into .hic files — run the upstream Microcket pipeline first The analysis goal is genome-wide quantification (e.g., compartment or TAD calling) rather than subsetting and visualizing specific genomic regions The .hic files were not balanced/normalized (KR normalization unavailable), making cross-condition comparison of contact intensities unreliable

skills.description: Use when binarized topic or cluster region sets from single-cell ATAC-seq (e.g. cisTopic topics) must be converted to the region identifiers of a cistarget/RcisTarget database (e.g. hg19-regions-9species) before running motif enrichment.
skills.name: genomic-region-to-ctx-region-mapping
skills.search_text: genomic-region-to-ctx-region-mapping Use when binarized topic or cluster region sets from single-cell ATAC-seq (e.g. cisTopic topics) must be converted to the region identifiers of a cistarget/RcisTarget database (e.g. hg19-regions-9species) before running motif enrichment. The dataset regions were already defined directly in the cistarget database region space, so no coordinate conversion is needed You only need topic region scores/rankings within cells (use getRegionsScores or signatureCellEnrichment) rather than motif enrichment The database is for a different genome assembly than the binarized topics (e.g. mm10 or hg38 topics against an hg19 database) http://edamontology.org/topic_3175 http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 Maps binarized cisTopic topic regions onto the region coordinate space of an RcisTarget feather database so that motif enrichment can be computed against database rankings. A single dataset region may map to multiple ctx regions. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41592-019-0367-1
skills.summary: Maps binarized cisTopic topic regions onto the region coordinate space of an RcisTarget feather database so that motif enrichment can be computed against database rankings. A single dataset region may map to multiple ctx regions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset regions were already defined directly in the cistarget database region space, so no coordinate conversion is needed You only need topic region scores/rankings within cells (use getRegionsScores or signatureCellEnrichment) rather than motif enrichment The database is for a different genome assembly than the binarized topics (e.g. mm10 or hg38 topics against an hg19 database)

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a tiled/smoothed genome-wide model implementation's runtime and memory footprint scale linearly with parameters per tile, or when reproducing version-to-version speedup benchmarks (e.g. 2-3 orders of magnitude).
skills.name: genomic-scaling-benchmark-profiling
skills.search_text: genomic-scaling-benchmark-profiling Use when evaluating whether a tiled/smoothed genome-wide model implementation's runtime and memory footprint scale linearly with parameters per tile, or when reproducing version-to-version speedup benchmarks (e.g. 2-3 orders of magnitude). The goal is statistical validation of fits (p-values, differential occupancy) rather than runtime/memory scaling — use computeSignificance()/plotGenoGAM workflows instead The analysis requires parallel, genome-wide production fitting (e.g. ~300 million human parameters on 60 cores) — this skill measures single-core scaling only Smoothing parameter estimation by cross-validation must be performed — fix lambda and theta instead, as parameter estimation would confound the timing http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0769 A benchmarking skill for measuring how single-core coefficient-estimation runtime and peak memory scale with the number of model parameters, as done for GenoGAM 2.0 (Newton-Raphson + SuperLU, HDF5 out-of-core) versus GenoGAM 1.0 (Fig. 2). epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2238-7
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill for measuring how single-core coefficient-estimation runtime and peak memory scale with the number of model parameters, as done for GenoGAM 2.0 (Newton-Raphson + SuperLU, HDF5 out-of-core) versus GenoGAM 1.0 (Fig. 2).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is statistical validation of fits (p-values, differential occupancy) rather than runtime/memory scaling — use computeSignificance()/plotGenoGAM workflows instead The analysis requires parallel, genome-wide production fitting (e.g. ~300 million human parameters on 60 cores) — this skill measures single-core scaling only Smoothing parameter estimation by cross-validation must be performed — fix lambda and theta instead, as parameter estimation would confound the timing

skills.description: Use when sequences are centered on an anchor point (e.g. TSS) with a continuous per-sequence score, and the goal is to find motif positions whose occurrence correlates with that score.
skills.name: genomic-sequence-anchor-alignment
skills.search_text: genomic-sequence-anchor-alignment Use when sequences are centered on an anchor point (e.g. TSS) with a continuous per-sequence score, and the goal is to find motif positions whose occurrence correlates with that score. The question is motif presence/absence across uncentered sequences without regard to motif position — standard MEA tools like HOMER under a ZOOPs model are more appropriate You need de novo motif discovery: MEPP currently only functions with a fixed motif library; de novo recognition/assembly is left to future work Sequences lack a continuous per-sequence score or a meaningful shared anchor point, so positional correlations relative to the anchor cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_3179 Positional motif enrichment profiling with MEPP: compute position-dependent enrichment profiles for a fixed motif library across scored DNA sequences centered on biologically meaningful anchor points (e.g. TSSs), revealing where motif presence correlates with a score continuum. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nargab/lqac075
skills.summary: Positional motif enrichment profiling with MEPP: compute position-dependent enrichment profiles for a fixed motif library across scored DNA sequences centered on biologically meaningful anchor points (e.g. TSSs), revealing where motif presence correlates with a score continuum.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The question is motif presence/absence across uncentered sequences without regard to motif position — standard MEA tools like HOMER under a ZOOPs model are more appropriate You need de novo motif discovery: MEPP currently only functions with a fixed motif library; de novo recognition/assembly is left to future work Sequences lack a continuous per-sequence score or a meaningful shared anchor point, so positional correlations relative to the anchor cannot be computed

skills.description: Use when a training run for deepC (or a similar sequence-based chromatin interaction model) needs genome sequence windows plus 5 kb Hi-C skeleton targets assembled from raw genome assemblies, BED intervals, and Hi-C contact data.
skills.name: genomic-sequence-data-preparation
skills.search_text: genomic-sequence-data-preparation Use when a training run for deepC (or a similar sequence-based chromatin interaction model) needs genome sequence windows plus 5 kb Hi-C skeleton targets assembled from raw genome assemblies, BED intervals, and Hi-C contact data. A trained deepC checkpoint already exists and the goal is running predictions — deepC predictions are feasible without GPU and do not require re-preparing training data The model of interest is Akita or another non-deepC architecture whose input and target formats differ from deepC's 5 kb skeleton scheme Hi-C data comes from a tissue/cell type for which no matching chromatin feature compendium or reference genome preparation is available http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3292 Prepare megabase-scale DNA sequence inputs and Hi-C-derived training targets for deepC's transfer learning models: install pysam and pybedtools alongside TensorFlow, clone the deepC repository, and derive 5 kb skeleton target tracks from Hi-C data such as Rao et al. (GSE63525) for GM12878 and K562. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41592-020-0960-3
skills.summary: Prepare megabase-scale DNA sequence inputs and Hi-C-derived training targets for deepC's transfer learning models: install pysam and pybedtools alongside TensorFlow, clone the deepC repository, and derive 5 kb skeleton target tracks from Hi-C data such as Rao et al. (GSE63525) for GM12878 and K562.
skills.when_to_use_negative: A trained deepC checkpoint already exists and the goal is running predictions — deepC predictions are feasible without GPU and do not require re-preparing training data The model of interest is Akita or another non-deepC architecture whose input and target formats differ from deepC's 5 kb skeleton scheme Hi-C data comes from a tissue/cell type for which no matching chromatin feature compendium or reference genome preparation is available

skills.description: Use when a positional motif enrichment analysis (e.g. MEPP) requires centered sequences around anchors such as deduplicated, RepeatMasker-filtered motif sites, TSSs, or cleavage sites, with a score attached per sequence.
skills.name: genomic-sequence-extraction-around-anchor-motifs
skills.search_text: genomic-sequence-extraction-around-anchor-motifs Use when a positional motif enrichment analysis (e.g. MEPP) requires centered sequences around anchors such as deduplicated, RepeatMasker-filtered motif sites, TSSs, or cleavage sites, with a score attached per sequence. Sequences are already centered and scored for MEPP — re-extraction would change positional offsets relative to the anchor The goal is de novo motif discovery rather than profiling known motifs relative to anchors — MEPP currently functions only with a fixed motif library Motif enrichment is needed independent of position within the sequence — standard MEA methods (e.g. HOMER, MEIRLOP under a ZOOPs model) suffice and do not require centered anchors http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 Extract fixed-width genomic sequences centered on biologically meaningful anchor points (transcription factor motif sites, transcription start sites, or Tn5/MNase cleavage sites) so that positional motif enrichment profiles can be computed relative to those anchors with tools like MEPP. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nargab/lqac075
skills.summary: Extract fixed-width genomic sequences centered on biologically meaningful anchor points (transcription factor motif sites, transcription start sites, or Tn5/MNase cleavage sites) so that positional motif enrichment profiles can be computed relative to those anchors with tools like MEPP.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Sequences are already centered and scored for MEPP — re-extraction would change positional offsets relative to the anchor The goal is de novo motif discovery rather than profiling known motifs relative to anchors — MEPP currently functions only with a fixed motif library Motif enrichment is needed independent of position within the sequence — standard MEA methods (e.g. HOMER, MEIRLOP under a ZOOPs model) suffice and do not require centered anchors

skills.description: Use when raw enhancer FASTA sequences (e.g. data/train/NHLF.fasta) must be converted into fixed-dimensional numeric vectors before training or predicting with a deep learning model such as Enhancer-MDLF.
skills.name: genomic-sequence-feature-encoding
skills.search_text: genomic-sequence-feature-encoding Use when raw enhancer FASTA sequences (e.g. data/train/NHLF.fasta) must be converted into fixed-dimensional numeric vectors before training or predicting with a deep learning model such as Enhancer-MDLF. Input is already a feature table or numeric matrix rather than raw FASTA sequences — encoding would be redundant The target model expects other encodings (e.g. one-hot sequence tensors) instead of dna2vec k-mer embeddings Sequences are not DNA enhancer/promoter sequences in the project's FASTA layout, so the k-mer lookup vocabulary from the pre-trained dna2vec vectors does not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 Encodes DNA enhancer sequences into fixed-length numeric feature vectors for the Enhancer-MDLF multi-input deep learning framework, using pre-trained dna2vec k-mer embeddings (k=3, 100-dim per k-mer) pooled to a 10,000-dimensional input, complemented by HOCOMOCO motif-frequency features. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbae083
skills.summary: Encodes DNA enhancer sequences into fixed-length numeric feature vectors for the Enhancer-MDLF multi-input deep learning framework, using pre-trained dna2vec k-mer embeddings (k=3, 100-dim per k-mer) pooled to a 10,000-dimensional input, complemented by HOCOMOCO motif-frequency features.

The input is already a processed gene-level count matrix or the authors' final DE gene list — retrieval of raw reads is unnecessary. The target dataset is ChIP-seq-only occupancy analysis (GSE136050) with no transcript-level differential expression goal. skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a processed gene-level count matrix or the authors' final DE gene list — retrieval of raw reads is unnecessary. skills.description: Use when a methylation-analysis reproduction task requires the raw sequencing reads of a published dataset identified by a GEO accession (e.g., GSE129673 for TAPS murine ESCs) before alignment or methylation calling can begin.

skills.search_text: geodata-fastq-retrieval Use when a methylation-analysis reproduction task requires the raw sequencing reads of a published dataset identified by a GEO accession (e.g., GSE129673 for TAPS murine ESCs) before alignment or methylation calling can begin. The dataset is already available locally as FASTQ/BAM and only re-analysis (alignment, methylation call) is needed — go straight to Msuite. The analysis target is a different tissue/sample type not covered by the cited accessions (e.g., GSM2191922 murine liver or GSM1545829 murine placenta) without confirming those accessions separately. http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_3674 Retrieves raw paired-end FASTQ sequencing files for DNA methylation assays (e.g., WGBS and TAPS datasets from murine ESCs, GEO accessions GSE112520 and GSE129673) from GEO so they can serve as real-data inputs to downstream methylation analysis pipelines such as Msuite. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2020.100127
skills.summary: Retrieves raw paired-end FASTQ sequencing files for DNA methylation assays (e.g., WGBS and TAPS datasets from murine ESCs, GEO accessions GSE112520 and GSE129673) from GEO so they can serve as real-data inputs to downstream methylation analysis pipelines such as Msuite.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is already available locally as FASTQ/BAM and only re-analysis (alignment, methylation call) is needed — go straight to Msuite. The target data are in silico simulated reads (e.g., generated with the SHERMAN script for benchmarking) rather than deposited GEO samples. The analysis target is a different tissue/sample type not covered by the cited accessions (e.g., GSM2191922 murine liver or GSM1545829 murine placenta) without confirming those accessions separately.

skills.description: Use when you need fixed genomic windows for CLIP-seq binding-site testing over annotated transcripts (e.g., GENCODE GFF3 for Skipper) instead of peak calling, ensuring no window spans intron/exon or gene boundaries.
skills.name: gff-transcript-partitioning
skills.search_text: gff-transcript-partitioning Use when you need fixed genomic windows for CLIP-seq binding-site testing over annotated transcripts (e.g., GENCODE GFF3 for Skipper) instead of peak calling, ensuring no window spans intron/exon or gene boundaries. The GFF has not been filtered/processed to select one best transcript per gene — raw multi-isoform GENCODE GFFs make window selection suboptimal and results uninterpretable You need peak calling on unannotated or poorly annotated transcriptomes where fixed windows over annotated transcripts would miss binding sites The analysis requires variable-width peaks or windows spanning exon-intron boundaries rather than Skipper's annotation-aware fixed tiling http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Partitions an annotated transcriptome (filtered GENCODE GFF3) into disjoint windows of at most 100 nt that never cross exon-intron junctions or gene boundaries, replacing peak calling in the Skipper eCLIP workflow with fixed candidate binding-site windows. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.xgen.2023.100317
skills.summary: Partitions an annotated transcriptome (filtered GENCODE GFF3) into disjoint windows of at most 100 nt that never cross exon-intron junctions or gene boundaries, replacing peak calling in the Skipper eCLIP workflow with fixed candidate binding-site windows.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The GFF has not been filtered/processed to select one best transcript per gene — raw multi-isoform GENCODE GFFs make window selection suboptimal and results uninterpretable You need peak calling on unannotated or poorly annotated transcriptomes where fixed windows over annotated transcripts would miss binding sites The analysis requires variable-width peaks or windows spanning exon-intron boundaries rather than Skipper's annotation-aware fixed tiling

skills.description: Use when runModels has built several LDA models (e.g. 2–40 topics) on single-cell ATAC-seq data and you must verify the log-likelihood stabilized after burnin and pick the model.

For the 5k PBMC 10X dataset, this criterion selects the 30-topic model. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41592-019-0367-1
skills.summary: Assess convergence of cisTopic's LDA (WarpLDA) Gibbs-sampler runs and select the optimal topic model by comparing final-iteration log likelihood P(D|T) across models fitted with different numbers of topics. For the 5k PBMC 10X dataset, this criterion selects the 30-topic model.

skills.description: Use when fitting DriverPower BMR background models and needing to decide between the GLM and GBM methods, or when reproducing the paper's finding that GBM outperforms GLM in low mutational burden tumour cohorts.
skills.name: glm-vs-gbm-predictive-metrics-comparison
skills.search_text: glm-vs-gbm-predictive-metrics-comparison Use when fitting DriverPower BMR background models and needing to decide between the GLM and GBM methods, or when reproducing the paper's finding that GBM outperforms GLM in low mutational burden tumour cohorts. The goal is calling driver candidates from test elements — use the 'driverpower infer' sub-command instead of comparing model-fit metrics Only one BMR algorithm will be used in the downstream analysis, so the head-to-head comparison adds no decision value http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Side-by-side comparison of DriverPower's two background mutation rate (BMR) modelling algorithms — generalized linear model with randomized lasso feature selection and 5-fold cross-validated XGBoost gradient boosting (GBM) — by tabulating their training metrics (r2, variance explained, Pearson correlation) stratified by cohort mutational burden. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-13929-1
skills.summary: Side-by-side comparison of DriverPower's two background mutation rate (BMR) modelling algorithms — generalized linear model with randomized lasso feature selection and 5-fold cross-validated XGBoost gradient boosting (GBM) — by tabulating their training metrics (r2, variance explained, Pearson correlation) stratified by cohort mutational burden.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is calling driver candidates from test elements — use the 'driverpower infer' sub-command instead of comparing model-fit metrics Only one BMR algorithm will be used in the downstream analysis, so the head-to-head comparison adds no decision value

skills.description: Use when you have a BED list of bivalent (H3K4me3+/H3K27me3+) peaks in mESCs and need to assign them to nearby genes and test whether the resulting gene list is enriched for development-related GO terms.
skills.name: go-term-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: go-term-enrichment-analysis Use when you have a BED list of bivalent (H3K4me3+/H3K27me3+) peaks in mESCs and need to assign them to nearby genes and test whether the resulting gene list is enriched for development-related GO terms. skills.summary: Links ChIP-seq-derived bivalent peak sets (overlapping H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 MACS peaks) to genes via SeqCode matchpeaksgenes and tests them for functional enrichment of developmental GO Biological Process terms in Enrichr, reproducing the Fig. 5c result of the mESC bivalency study.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a curated gene list from a different gene-assignment rule — the 2500 bp TSS-window definition would no longer be the origin of the list The peaks of interest are unimodal (single H3K4me3 or H3K27me3 marks) rather than overlapping bivalent peaks The genome annotation is not RefSeq-based (e.g. Gencode-only pipelines), since SeqCode relies on RefSeq reference annotations

skills.description: Use when you have a collection of region sets (e.g. binarized cisTopics from scATAC-seq) and need per-set GO functional annotation via rGREAT, or when you need to identify which topics lack cell-type-signature enrichment.
skills.name: go-term-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: go-term-enrichment-analysis Use when you have a collection of region sets (e.g. binarized cisTopics from scATAC-seq) and need per-set GO functional annotation via rGREAT, or when you need to identify which topics lack cell-type-signature enrichment. The input is already a gene list rather than a set of genomic regions — standard gene-set over-representation tools are more appropriate than GREAT's region-based test. The regions come from a genome assembly other than the one the GREAT query is configured for (the wrapper shown uses genome='hg19'), without adjusting the genome argument. The goal is topic model construction or cell-type assignment (runModels/selectModel/signatureCellEnrichment), not functional annotation of already-selected region sets. http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 Performs GREAT-based Gene Ontology enrichment on genomic region sets, as applied to cisTopic topics from single-cell ATAC-seq data: each binarized topic (a set of top co-accessible regions) is tested for over-represented GO terms against the hg19 background. In the cisTopic workflow this characterizes the function of each cis-regulatory topic, e.g. distinguishing promoter topics from cell-type-specific enhancer topics. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41592-019-0367-1
skills.summary: Performs GREAT-based Gene Ontology enrichment on genomic region sets, as applied to cisTopic topics from single-cell ATAC-seq data: each binarized topic (a set of top co-accessible regions) is tested for over-represented GO terms against the hg19 background. In the cisTopic workflow this characterizes the function of each cis-regulatory topic, e.g. distinguishing promoter topics from cell-type-specific enhancer topics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a gene list rather than a set of genomic regions — standard gene-set over-representation tools are more appropriate than GREAT's region-based test. The regions come from a genome assembly other than the one the GREAT query is configured for (the wrapper shown uses genome='hg19'), without adjusting the genome argument. The goal is topic model construction or cell-type assignment (runModels/selectModel/signatureCellEnrichment), not functional annotation of already-selected region sets.

skills.description: Use when you have a list of differentially modified genomic regions from a ChIP-seq differential caller and a list of differentially expressed genes, and you need to test overlap significance and GO term enrichment of the shared genes.
skills.name: go-term-enrichment-statistics
skills.search_text: go-term-enrichment-statistics Use when you have a list of differentially modified genomic regions from a ChIP-seq differential caller and a list of differentially expressed genes, and you need to test overlap significance and GO term enrichment of the shared genes. Input is peak-like ChIP-seq data (e.g. sharp transcription factor peaks) rather than broad diffuse marks like H3K27me3/H3K9me3 — the histoneHMM calls feeding this overlap test were designed for broad genomic footprints Gene sets cannot be mapped to a common identifier via the available GFF annotation, making the contingency table undefined You need pathway-level effect sizes or ranked-gene tests rather than a binary DE x differential-modification overlap test http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 A statistical skill for testing whether differentially modified histone regions (called by histoneHMM) overlap with differentially expressed genes more than expected, using Fisher's exact test on 2x2 contingency tables, followed by GO term enrichment (e.g. 'antigen processing and presentation', GO:0019882). epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-015-0491-6
skills.summary: A statistical skill for testing whether differentially modified histone regions (called by histoneHMM) overlap with differentially expressed genes more than expected, using Fisher's exact test on 2x2 contingency tables, followed by GO term enrichment (e.g. 'antigen processing and presentation', GO:0019882).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is peak-like ChIP-seq data (e.g. sharp transcription factor peaks) rather than broad diffuse marks like H3K27me3/H3K9me3 — the histoneHMM calls feeding this overlap test were designed for broad genomic footprints Gene sets cannot be mapped to a common identifier via the available GFF annotation, making the contingency table undefined You need pathway-level effect sizes or ranked-gene tests rather than a binary DE x differential-modification overlap test

skills.description: Use when comparing supervised scATAC-seq celltyping methods on tasks whose target dataset carries FACS-sorted gold-standard cell labels (human PBMCs), or when validating reported benchmark accuracies against the paper's Source Data.
skills.name: gold-standard-target-task-evaluation
skills.search_text: gold-standard-target-task-evaluation Use when comparing supervised scATAC-seq celltyping methods on tasks whose target dataset carries FACS-sorted gold-standard cell labels (human PBMCs), or when validating reported benchmark accuracies against the paper's Source Data. Target data lacks FACS-sorted gold-standard labels (e.g., unlabeled target cells or non-PBMC datasets) — this skill reproduces the specific gold-standard benchmark, not the full 50-task panel The goal is to run Cellcano celltyping prediction on new data (gene scores via ArchR, F-test feature selection, two-round MLP/KD model) rather than to evaluate or reproduce published benchmark accuracies Input is already an aggregated per-method summary rather than the per-task accuracy table from the Source Data sheet Benchmarks supervised scATAC-seq celltyping methods (Cellcano, scJoint, ACTINN) on the seven celltyping tasks that use FACS-sorted gold-standard human PBMCs as target data, reproducing the average-accuracy ranking reported for Fig. 3a of the Cellcano Nature Communications paper. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-37439-3
skills.summary: Benchmarks supervised scATAC-seq celltyping methods (Cellcano, scJoint, ACTINN) on the seven celltyping tasks that use FACS-sorted gold-standard human PBMCs as target data, reproducing the average-accuracy ranking reported for Fig. 3a of the Cellcano Nature Communications paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Target data lacks FACS-sorted gold-standard labels (e.g., unlabeled target cells or non-PBMC datasets) — this skill reproduces the specific gold-standard benchmark, not the full 50-task panel The goal is to run Cellcano celltyping prediction on new data (gene scores via ArchR, F-test feature selection, two-round MLP/KD model) rather than to evaluate or reproduce published benchmark accuracies Input is already an aggregated per-method summary rather than the per-task accuracy table from the Source Data sheet

skills.description: Use when benchmarking calibration models for methylation standard-control data (known AMP percentages such as 0/25/50/75/100%) and you need in-sample fit (RSS) plus leave-one-out predictive measures (MSEP, CV-index).
skills.name: goodness-of-fit-metrics-computation-rss-msep
skills.search_text: goodness-of-fit-metrics-computation-rss-msep Use when benchmarking calibration models for methylation standard-control data (known AMP percentages such as 0/25/50/75/100%) and you need in-sample fit (RSS) plus leave-one-out predictive measures (MSEP, CV-index). When only correcting methylation levels of case/control samples (use MoskalevCorrection / MethycalCorrection instead of computing calibration fit metrics) When the data are not standard controls with known methylation percentages — RSS/MSEP from calibration curves are meaningless for uncontrolled case samples When assessing outlier CpGs (use MethylCalCalibrationOutlierPlot with the Q1−1.5IQR / Q3+1.5IQR interval rather than fit-metric comparison) http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Computes and compares in-sample residual sum of squares (RSS) and out-of-sample predictive measures (MSEP, CV-index) for methylation calibration curves, as used to benchmark MethylCal against Moskalev's CPR across eight bisulfite-amplicon assays. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz325
skills.summary: Computes and compares in-sample residual sum of squares (RSS) and out-of-sample predictive measures (MSEP, CV-index) for methylation calibration curves, as used to benchmark MethylCal against Moskalev's CPR across eight bisulfite-amplicon assays.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only correcting methylation levels of case/control samples (use MoskalevCorrection / MethycalCorrection instead of computing calibration fit metrics) When the data are not standard controls with known methylation percentages — RSS/MSEP from calibration curves are meaningless for uncontrolled case samples When assessing outlier CpGs (use MethylCalCalibrationOutlierPlot with the Q1−1.5IQR / Q3+1.5IQR interval rather than fit-metric comparison)

skills.description: Use when ChIP-Seq HDF counts per 25 bp bin must be assigned a probability model, and competing discrete distributions need to be fitted and ranked (e.g. GP vs. Poisson vs. NB) via AIC/log-likelihood.
skills.name: goodness-of-fit-rank-comparison
skills.search_text: goodness-of-fit-rank-comparison Use when ChIP-Seq HDF counts per 25 bp bin must be assigned a probability model, and competing discrete distributions need to be fitted and ranked (e.g. GP vs. Poisson vs. NB) via AIC/log-likelihood. The count data are continuous or non-genomic-binned; the GP/ZIP/Poisson/NB comparison here is specific to discrete HDF bin counts. Bin-level enrichment classification is unavailable — the skill requires pre-partitioned ChIP-enriched vs. background bins from an HMM state assignment. The goal is peak boundary definition or motif discovery rather than distribution selection; use HPeak peak calling or downstream MatInspector-based motif analysis instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Fits candidate count distributions (GP, ZIP, Poisson, negative binomial) by maximum likelihood to HDF bin counts from HPeak ChIP-Seq analysis and ranks them by a goodness-of-fit criterion to select the best emission model for enriched vs. background genomic bins. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/1471-2105-11-369
skills.summary: Fits candidate count distributions (GP, ZIP, Poisson, negative binomial) by maximum likelihood to HDF bin counts from HPeak ChIP-Seq analysis and ranks them by a goodness-of-fit criterion to select the best emission model for enriched vs. background genomic bins.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The count data are continuous or non-genomic-binned; the GP/ZIP/Poisson/NB comparison here is specific to discrete HDF bin counts. Bin-level enrichment classification is unavailable — the skill requires pre-partitioned ChIP-enriched vs. background bins from an HMM state assignment. The goal is peak boundary definition or motif discovery rather than distribution selection; use HPeak peak calling or downstream MatInspector-based motif analysis instead.

skills.description: Use when a trained deep learning model must be applied to thousands of inputs (e.g. ~96,805 genomic elements in a deletion screen) and CPU inference would be prohibitively slow.
skills.name: gpu-accelerated-deep-learning-inference
skills.search_text: gpu-accelerated-deep-learning-inference Use when a trained deep learning model must be applied to thousands of inputs (e.g. ~96,805 genomic elements in a deletion screen) and CPU inference would be prohibitively slow. Only a handful of predictions are needed and no GPU environment is set up — the article states predictions are feasible without a GPU, just slower The task is model training rather than inference — training deepC models essentially requires GPU support for hours to days, so use the training-specific workflow instead The installed TensorFlow version is untested (the article lists only v1.8, 1.14 and 2.1 as supported; other versions have not been tested) http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Run deep learning model predictions (e.g. deepC chromatin interaction maps from megabase-scale DNA sequence) on GPU-enabled TensorFlow to make large-scale inference like genome-wide deletion screens tractable. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41592-020-0960-3
skills.summary: Run deep learning model predictions (e.g. deepC chromatin interaction maps from megabase-scale DNA sequence) on GPU-enabled TensorFlow to make large-scale inference like genome-wide deletion screens tractable.

skills.description: Use when you have a trained deepC checkpoint (e.g. GM12878) and hg19 sequence, and need a non-negative per-base track of sequence importance underlying predicted chromatin interactions.

skills.search_text: gradient-based-saliency-score-computation Use when you have a trained deepC checkpoint (e.g. GM12878) and hg19 sequence, and need a non-negative per-base track of sequence importance underlying predicted chromatin interactions. skills.description: Use when you have per-sequence motif count matrices (e.g., from FIMO scans against gimme.vertebrate.v5.0.meme) and labeled CRE sets (chromosome, start, stop, condition) and need to train binary or multiclass classifiers for context-specific regulatory elements.
skills.name: gradient-boosted-tree-classifier-training
skills.search_text: gradient-boosted-tree-classifier-training Use when you have per-sequence motif count matrices (e.g., from FIMO scans against gimme.vertebrate.v5.0.meme) and labeled CRE sets (chromosome, start, stop, condition) and need to train binary or multiclass classifiers for context-specific regulatory elements. The task is de novo phasing or pedigree/trio statistical phasing rather than single-individual haplotype assembly from read-backed fragments Haplotype-resolved structural variation or polyploid (non-diploid) phasing is required — the article states the graph bisection model does not fit increased ploidy and SVs are not supported Only variant calling or read alignment is needed without any fragment-to-haplotype assignment step http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Benchmark diploid haplotype-assembly (SIH) tools such as SpecHap against FastHare, HapCUT, HapCUT2, DCHap and ReFHap by running each on identical fragment files, recording CPU time and peak memory, and scoring phased VCFs against 1000 Genomes trio-phased ground truth (AN50, phased variant count, switch and mismatch error rates). epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab709

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is bulk proximity-ligation data (Hi-C contact counts) rather than continuous per-allele 3D Euclidean distances — count-based callers like HiCCUPS are designed for that data type, and existing loop callers are not directly applicable to imaging data You only need per-cell pairwise distances without loop calling — run 'SnapFISH step1' instead of the full call-loops workflow Data are not allele-resolved (no per-cell haplotype assignment), so a mixed call cannot yield haplotype-specific CAST vs 129 summits

skills.description: Use when a power or association analysis needs simulated genotype covariates for a reference sample set — e.g. scPower's simulation eQTL power for small-mean genes requires HWE-drawn SNP genotypes paired with negative binomial pseudobulk counts.
skills.name: hardy-weinberg-genotype-simulation
skills.search_text: hardy-weinberg-genotype-simulation Use when a power or association analysis needs simulated genotype covariates for a reference sample set — e.g. scPower's simulation eQTL power for small-mean genes requires HWE-drawn SNP genotypes paired with negative binomial pseudobulk counts. Analytic power estimation is sufficient — scPower's own analytic eQTL power is the default; simulation (and hence HWE genotype sampling) is reserved for genes with small pseudobulk mean expression where the analytic linear-model approximation is inaccurate The target cohort has known population stratification, relatedness, or non-random mating that violates Hardy-Weinberg assumptions Extremely large eQTL cohorts (hundreds of samples) are needed — the article notes such data sets 'will be very difficult to simulate' due to runtime and memory costs http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Generates synthetic SNP genotype data under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for reference samples, as used by scPower to supply genotypes for its simulation-based eQTL power estimation in genes whose pseudobulk mean expression is too small for the analytic linear-model approximation. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-26779-7
skills.summary: Generates synthetic SNP genotype data under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for reference samples, as used by scPower to supply genotypes for its simulation-based eQTL power estimation in genes whose pseudobulk mean expression is too small for the analytic linear-model approximation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Analytic power estimation is sufficient — scPower's own analytic eQTL power is the default; simulation (and hence HWE genotype sampling) is reserved for genes with small pseudobulk mean expression where the analytic linear-model approximation is inaccurate The target cohort has known population stratification, relatedness, or non-random mating that violates Hardy-Weinberg assumptions Extremely large eQTL cohorts (hundreds of samples) are needed — the article notes such data sets 'will be very difficult to simulate' due to runtime and memory costs

skills.description: Use when a scATAC-seq (or scRNA-seq) dataset combines cells from multiple samples/preparations and sample-to-sample technical variability could dominate the low-dimensional embedding, driving clustering to separate batches rather than cell types.
skills.name: harmony-batch-effect-correction
skills.search_text: harmony-batch-effect-correction Use when a scATAC-seq (or scRNA-seq) dataset combines cells from multiple samples/preparations and sample-to-sample technical variability could dominate the low-dimensional embedding, driving clustering to separate batches rather than cell types. The dataset comes from a single sample/library with no batch variable to correct — correction would remove genuine biological signal. Cells have not yet been embedded in low-dimensional space; Harmony should be applied to the embedding, not to the raw cell-by-bin accessibility matrix. Differences between sample groups are biological (e.g. distinct conditions you want to compare) rather than technical; correcting on that variable would erase the contrast of interest. http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Corrects batch effects between samples introduced by technical variability in the low-dimensional embedding prior to clustering, as used within the SnapATAC pipeline on the mouse secondary motor cortex snATAC-seq atlas (55,592 nuclei). epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-21583-9
skills.summary: Corrects batch effects between samples introduced by technical variability in the low-dimensional embedding prior to clustering, as used within the SnapATAC pipeline on the mouse secondary motor cortex snATAC-seq atlas (55,592 nuclei).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset comes from a single sample/library with no batch variable to correct — correction would remove genuine biological signal. Cells have not yet been embedded in low-dimensional space; Harmony should be applied to the embedding, not to the raw cell-by-bin accessibility matrix. Differences between sample groups are biological (e.g. distinct conditions you want to compare) rather than technical; correcting on that variable would erase the contrast of interest.

skills.search_text: hash-partitioning-load-balancing Decision support for choosing between BiSpark --testmode plain and balancing when scaling bisulfite read alignment across 10-, 20-, or 40-node Spark/HDFS clusters and throughput is limited by the slowest node. skills.summary: A BiSpark execution mode that applies Spark's portable_hash partitioning to redistribute key-value RDD tuples evenly across slave nodes during bisulfite 'three-letter' alignment, trading shuffling overhead for protection against straggler nodes that dominates as cluster size grows.

skills.search_text: healthy-cohort-sv-specificity-benchmarking Use when validating the specificity of an SV pathogenicity classifier: SV sets from healthy individuals (e.g. gnomAD) should yield predominantly non-pathogenic calls, so a low non-pathogenic rate flags poor Type-1 error control. SVs in coordinates other than hg19 — the required input format mandates hg19 genomic coordinates, so liftover is needed first or results are invalid. skills.summary: Benchmark a structural-variant pathogenicity predictor's Type-1 error control by running SVs from healthy individuals (gnomAD) through the tool and measuring the percentage of SV-phenotype associations called non-pathogenic under each running mode.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating sensitivity on known pathogenic patient SVs — this skill measures Type-1 error control on healthy-cohort SVs, not disease-causative SV recovery (e.g. the BOFS TFAP2A inversion case is assessed separately). SVs in coordinates other than hg19 — the required input format mandates hg19 genomic coordinates, so liftover is needed first or results are invalid. SVs implicating phenotypes outside POSTRE's supported categories (limb, craniofacial, cardiac, neurodevelopmental, vision_eye, liver_biliary_system, pituitary) — the tool cannot provide a meaningful cell type-specific prediction for other contexts.

skills.search_text: hi-c-compartment-dynamics-interpretation Use when you have compartment scores (e.g., 100 kb bin PCA scores) for three or more ordered Hi-C time points and need to cluster bins by their relative trajectory across the full time course instead of comparing single stage transitions. You only have two Hi-C conditions — use dcHiC's Mahalanobis-distance differential compartment test instead of time-series clustering. Compartment scores have not been quantile-normalized across all input Hi-C maps — raw per-map PCA scores are not comparable and clustering would reflect scale artifacts rather than dynamics. The goal is detecting statistically significant differential compartments rather than grouping trajectory patterns; use dcHiC's Mahalanobis distance with chi-square testing and IHW/FDR correction. http://edamontology.org/topic_3922 Groups dynamic compartmentalization score patterns across a multi-point Hi-C time course by z-transforming dcHiC's quantile-normalized PCA scores per genomic bin and applying TCseq time-series clustering, so all developmental transitions are compared simultaneously rather than pairwise. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-34626-6

skills.search_text: hi-c-coverage-bias-normalization Use when cis-interaction fragment-pair tables (frag1, frag2, cov_frag1, cov_frag2, freq, dist) at ~40 kb resolution show coverage-dependent ligation bias and you need coverage-normalized interaction frequencies or reproducible replicates. Input lacks per-fragment coverage values (cov_frag1/cov_frag2) — the negative binomial model is fit on coverage, so matrix balancing methods (ICE, KR, SCN) are the appropriate choice instead Data are inter-chromosomal interactions — the study filters these out and demonstrates covNorm on cis-interactions only Input fragment pairs include zero-valued frequencies or fragments below the coverage cut-off that have not been pre-filtered, since these must be removed before model fitting http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Coverage-based implicit normalization of Hi-C/capture Hi-C interaction tables using covNorm's negative binomial GLM (MASS::glm.nb), which removes coverage bias from raw ligated-fragment frequencies and can be followed by genomic distance-dependent background removal and significance calling. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.05.041
skills.summary: Coverage-based implicit normalization of Hi-C/capture Hi-C interaction tables using covNorm's negative binomial GLM (MASS::glm.nb), which removes coverage bias from raw ligated-fragment frequencies and can be followed by genomic distance-dependent background removal and significance calling.

skills.search_text: hi-c-enclave-hierarchy-annotation Use when a BHi-Cect output (nested tree list plus named per-cluster locus list) needs nestedness scoring and enrichment against epigenomic tracks to test whether nesting along the BPT relates to chromatin activity. When the goal is initial delineation of clusters from raw Hi-C contacts rather than annotating an existing BHi-Cect tree — use the BHi-Cect spectral clustering pipeline (Rao_matrix, pow_trans, spec_bipart) first When input Hi-C data lacks the resolution or enclave structure (no nested local-within-global clusters) needed to define top/bottom enclave anchors for NS scoring When no epigenomic annotation tracks for the matching cell type (e.g. IMR90) are available, since the enrichment contrast cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Annotates the BHi-Cect partition tree (BPT) of Hi-C-derived chromosome enclaves with a nestedness (NS) score (0/0.5/1 anchoring of top enclaves, intermediate nodes, and bottom/leaf enclaves) and intersects enclave loci with epigenomic tracks (DNase, LAD, ChromHMM, CAGE, RNA-seq, TF, RNAP2, CTCF/RAD21/CHD1) to test the top-vs-bottom enclave activity antagonism. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa004

skills.description: Use when raw Hi-C or pcHi-C feature tables (e.g. GM19204.chr17.cis.feature.gz with columns frag1, frag2, cov_frag1, cov_frag2, freq, dist) must be cleaned before normalization or reproducibility scoring.

skills.search_text: hi-c-input-table-preprocessing Use when raw Hi-C or pcHi-C feature tables (e.g. GM19204.chr17.cis.feature.gz with columns frag1, frag2, cov_frag1, cov_frag2, freq, dist) must be cleaned before normalization or reproducibility scoring. The input is already a filtered/normalized covNorm result table (e.g. output of normCoverage), not a raw feature table with freq and coverage columns The analysis targets inter-chromosomal (trans) interactions, which the pipeline explicitly filters out because it focuses on cis-interactions only The data are already at lower resolution or from a protocol where the 40 kb bin and 200 coverage cut-off do not apply and a different threshold is needed without adaptation http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Preprocess Hi-C/capture Hi-C input feature tables (frag1, frag2, cov_frag1, cov_frag2, freq, dist) by removing zero-valued DNA fragment pairs and filtering fragments below a coverage cut-off (default 200 at 40 kb resolution) so that covNorm normalization operates on a clean, comparable cis-interaction table. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.05.041
skills.summary: Preprocess Hi-C/capture Hi-C input feature tables (frag1, frag2, cov_frag1, cov_frag2, freq, dist) by removing zero-valued DNA fragment pairs and filtering fragments below a coverage cut-off (default 200 at 40 kb resolution) so that covNorm normalization operates on a clean, comparable cis-interaction table.

skills.description: Use when fitting a generative model of Hi-C interaction counts (e.g. CscoreTool-M) where expected counts Fij must incorporate Rabl-position effects, bias factors, and per-window sub-compartment probabilities, and the likelihood of observed trans reads is needed.
skills.name: hi-c-interaction-modeling
skills.search_text: hi-c-interaction-modeling Use when fitting a generative model of Hi-C interaction counts (e.g. CscoreTool-M) where expected counts Fij must incorporate Rabl-position effects, bias factors, and per-window sub-compartment probabilities, and the likelihood of observed trans reads is needed. The input interactions involve regions with known translocations but no ExcludedInteractions.txt is supplied — the README notes excluded expectations differ from simply deleting interactions, so omitting this file biases the model differently than intended Interactions within blacklisted regions (e.g. encode blacklist regions with copy number variations) that should be excluded via Blacklist.bed rather than modeled The goal is a visualization-only compartment track rather than probabilistic modeling — the bedgraph output (XXX_cscore.bedgraph) normalizes c-scores to add up to 1 per region and drops regions with no reads, which is not the Poisson model itself http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Model expected Hi-C trans-interaction counts between genomic windows with a Rabl-effect term Rij = 1 + alpha*ri*rj + beta*(ri+rj)*ri*rj combined with window biases Bi, Bj and sub-compartment probability products, then evaluate the Poisson log-likelihood of observed reads as in CscoreTool-M Section 2.1.1. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad314
skills.summary: Model expected Hi-C trans-interaction counts between genomic windows with a Rabl-effect term Rij = 1 + alpha*ri*rj + beta*(ri+rj)*ri*rj combined with window biases Bi, Bj and sub-compartment probability products, then evaluate the Poisson log-likelihood of observed reads as in CscoreTool-M Section 2.1.1.

skills.search_text: hi-c-loop-calling-benchmarking Use when comparing a Hi-C loop caller (e.g., GILoop) against machine-learning baselines like Peakachu on matched contact maps, requiring PR-AUC, APA enrichment, and loop-recovery evaluation against a ground-truth loop set. The contact maps are inter-chromosomal — the underlying study focuses on cis-interactions only and filters inter-chromosomal interactions You need detection of reproducible significant long-range contacts or compartment A/B profiles rather than the spectral eigenvector-based reproducibility score — those were measured with separate metrics in the paper Only one replicate is available — the HiC-spector score requires two contact maps to compare http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 Benchmark Hi-C contact map normalization methods by scoring replicate reproducibility (e.g., GM19204 vs GM19240 chr17 maps at 40 kb resolution) with the HiC-spector run_reproducibility_v2.py script, comparing covNorm against ICE, KR, SCN, and raw data. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.05.041

skills.description: Use when you have covNorm distance-normalized contact tables (frag1/frag2, cov, freq, dist) and need p-value/FDR-based significant long-range interaction calling.

skills.search_text: hi-c-significant-contact-calling Use when you have covNorm distance-normalized contact tables (frag1/frag2, cov, freq, dist) and need p-value/FDR-based significant long-range interaction calling. The input is raw ligation frequencies that have not been coverage-normalized (normCoverage) and distance-normalized (normDistance) by covNorm; p-values on raw counts reflect uncorrected coverage and distance biases The goal is differential or inter-chromosomal interaction analysis — the article focuses on cis-interactions and filters inter-chromosomal contacts, and pcHi-C P-P vs P-O interactions are processed separately (promoter side coverage threshold 200, other side 50) You need reproducibility scoring between biological replicates rather than per-contact significance — use HiC-spector's run_reproducibility script instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Calls statistically significant chromatin interactions from covNorm distance-normalized Hi-C/pcHi-C contacts by fitting a three-parameter Weibull background (via propagate::fitDistr) and computing per-contact p-values (FAdist::pweibull3) and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (p.adjust). epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.05.041
skills.summary: Calls statistically significant chromatin interactions from covNorm distance-normalized Hi-C/pcHi-C contacts by fitting a three-parameter Weibull background (via propagate::fitDistr) and computing per-contact p-values (FAdist::pweibull3) and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (p.adjust).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw ligation frequencies that have not been coverage-normalized (normCoverage) and distance-normalized (normDistance) by covNorm; p-values on raw counts reflect uncorrected coverage and distance biases The goal is differential or inter-chromosomal interaction analysis — the article focuses on cis-interactions and filters inter-chromosomal contacts, and pcHi-C P-P vs P-O interactions are processed separately (promoter side coverage threshold 200, other side 50) You need reproducibility scoring between biological replicates rather than per-contact significance — use HiC-spector's run_reproducibility script instead

skills.name: hi-c-trans-interaction-simulation-from-compartment-model
skills.search_text: hi-c-trans-interaction-simulation-from-compartment-model Use when validating that a sub-compartment inference method recovers known compartment scores from simulated Hi-C trans-interaction data, or when testing how low sequencing depth can go before inference degrades. The goal is real biological discovery in a primary Hi-C dataset rather than validating or benchmarking sub-compartment inference against a known reference model. The analysis targets intra-chromosomal contact maps or TAD/calling-loop tasks — CscoreTool-M here is applied to trans-interaction summary data with a Rabl-position window model. skills.summary: Simulates Hi-C trans-interaction summary files by downsampling reads from a GM12878-derived 5-compartment reference model (Rao et al. 2014) at multiple sequencing depths (1x, 0.1x, 0.01x), then re-infers sub-compartment scores with CscoreTool-M to benchmark depth robustness.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is real biological discovery in a primary Hi-C dataset rather than validating or benchmarking sub-compartment inference against a known reference model. skills.name: hic-cluster-loci-annotation
skills.search_text: hic-cluster-loci-annotation Use when BHi-Cect spectral clustering of IMR90 (or similar) Hi-C data has produced a tree of enclaves plus a named list of loci per cluster, and you need to relate enclave regulatory content to ChIP-seq data (e.g. ten TFs) via contingency-table analysis. skills.summary: Annotate BHi-Cect chromosome clusters (bottom/leaf enclaves) with epigenomic content by counting TF ChIP-seq binding per enclave and summarizing regulatory regimes via correspondence analysis on the TF-by-enclave contingency table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is TAD-style segmentation that assumes clusters of loci contiguous along the genome coordinate — BHi-Cect clustering and its enclave annotation explicitly avoid genomic-contiguity assumptions. skills.name: hic-compartment-calling
skills.search_text: hic-compartment-calling Use when you need genome-wide A/B compartment scores from one or more Hi-C contact maps (bulk, pseudo-replicate, or pseudo-bulk single-cell) at resolutions from 100 kb down to 5-10 kb, or comparable scores across replicates/conditions. You need statistically significant differential compartmentalization between conditions rather than per-map compartment scores — use dcHiC's Mahalanobis-distance differential testing instead Single-cell Hi-C maps are too sparse to call compartments per cell — aggregate to pseudo-bulk first; the article notes single-cell compartment identification is limited by sparsity even at coarse resolution You only need significant chromatin interactions/loops rather than compartments — Fit-Hi-C, not compartment calling, is the appropriate tool http://edamontology.org/topic_3940 Calls A/B compartments from Hi-C contact maps using distance normalization to a correlation matrix, partial SVD/PCA to extract PC1 compartment scores, and quantile normalization across maps — as implemented in dcHiC with a memory-efficient Filebacked Big Matrix and validated against HOMER and CscoreTool. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-34626-6
skills.summary: Calls A/B compartments from Hi-C contact maps using distance normalization to a correlation matrix, partial SVD/PCA to extract PC1 compartment scores, and quantile normalization across maps — as implemented in dcHiC with a memory-efficient Filebacked Big Matrix and validated against HOMER and CscoreTool.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need statistically significant differential compartmentalization between conditions rather than per-map compartment scores — use dcHiC's Mahalanobis-distance differential testing instead Single-cell Hi-C maps are too sparse to call compartments per cell — aggregate to pseudo-bulk first; the article notes single-cell compartment identification is limited by sparsity even at coarse resolution You only need significant chromatin interactions/loops rather than compartments — Fit-Hi-C, not compartment calling, is the appropriate tool
