skills.description: Use when you have per-cluster differentially enriched regions from single-cell ChIP/epigenomic data (e.g. H3K27me3 scChIP-seq) and need pathway-level interpretation by gene-set over-representation.
skills.name: hypergeometric-gene-set-overrepresentation-analysis
skills.search_text: hypergeometric-gene-set-overrepresentation-analysis Use when you have per-cluster differentially enriched regions from single-cell ChIP/epigenomic data (e.g. H3K27me3 scChIP-seq) and need pathway-level interpretation by gene-set over-representation. Input is single-cell transcriptomic data where standard GSEA-style ranking of expressed genes applies — this workflow is built for region-level chromatin data that must first be linked to genes via Gencode_hg38_v26. No cluster-level differential regions available (e.g. only a count matrix without cluster labels or differential test results) — there is no gene list to over-representation-test. Non-human epigenomic data — the region-to-gene linking in ChromSCape uses the human Gencode_hg38_v26 reference. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Links cluster-specific differentially enriched (or depleted) chromatin regions to genes and runs a hypergeometric over-representation test against MSigDB v5 gene sets, with multiple-testing correction, to interpret cluster epigenomes in ChromSCape. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-19542-x
skills.summary: Links cluster-specific differentially enriched (or depleted) chromatin regions to genes and runs a hypergeometric over-representation test against MSigDB v5 gene sets, with multiple-testing correction, to interpret cluster epigenomes in ChromSCape.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is single-cell transcriptomic data where standard GSEA-style ranking of expressed genes applies — this workflow is built for region-level chromatin data that must first be linked to genes via Gencode_hg38_v26. No cluster-level differential regions available (e.g. only a count matrix without cluster labels or differential test results) — there is no gene list to over-representation-test. Non-human epigenomic data — the region-to-gene linking in ChromSCape uses the human Gencode_hg38_v26 reference.

skills.description: Use when you have pruned lists of significant cis/trans gene sets from iEDGE differential expression and mediation analysis and need to identify recurrently enriched MSigDB pathways across multiple alterations (e.g., TCGA BRCA SCNAs).
skills.name: hypergeometric-pathway-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: hypergeometric-pathway-enrichment-analysis Use when you have pruned lists of significant cis/trans gene sets from iEDGE differential expression and mediation analysis and need to identify recurrently enriched MSigDB pathways across multiple alterations (e.g., TCGA BRCA SCNAs). When no significant cis/trans gene sets have been identified — pruning at FDR thresholds must precede enrichment, otherwise the drawn set is meaningless When input gene sets are already pathway-level annotations rather than gene lists drawn from the tested universe (ntotal) When the goal is ranking candidate cis drivers by mediation of trans effects (use calc_sobel mediation analysis instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Annotate iEDGE cis and trans gene expression signatures by hypergeometric over-representation testing of significant gene sets against MSigDB hallmark (h.all), curated (c2.cp), and transcription factor target (c3.tft) gene sets, revealing recurrent downstream regulatory effects of SCNAs. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-019-52886-z
skills.summary: Annotate iEDGE cis and trans gene expression signatures by hypergeometric over-representation testing of significant gene sets against MSigDB hallmark (h.all), curated (c2.cp), and transcription factor target (c3.tft) gene sets, revealing recurrent downstream regulatory effects of SCNAs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When no significant cis/trans gene sets have been identified — pruning at FDR thresholds must precede enrichment, otherwise the drawn set is meaningless When input gene sets are already pathway-level annotations rather than gene lists drawn from the tested universe (ntotal) When the goal is ranking candidate cis drivers by mediation of trans effects (use calc_sobel mediation analysis instead)

skills.description: Use when building a gold-standard set of experimentally determined lncRNA:DNA binding sites from raw fastq files with replicate structure (even/odd probe sets), where reproducible peaks are needed as positives for prediction benchmarks.
skills.name: idr-reproducibility-filtering
skills.search_text: idr-reproducibility-filtering Use when building a gold-standard set of experimentally determined lncRNA:DNA binding sites from raw fastq files with replicate structure (even/odd probe sets), where reproducible peaks are needed as positives for prediction benchmarks. The experiment lacks raw fastq data or has unclear replicate annotation — such datasets were explicitly excluded from the benchmark collection The data are Xist ChIRP-seq (X-chromosome-limited), which the authors excluded from the curated collection A published peak set is already available and accepted as-is — though the authors found IDR conservative filtering gave a +0.09 average AUC gain over published peaks, so re-filtering is preferred when raw data exist http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0160 A replicate-handling procedure that converts raw ChIP-seq-style lncRNA:DNA binding data (ChIRP-seq, ChOP-seq, CHART-seq, RAP-seq) into reproducibility-filtered peak sets using ENCODE IDR/Overlap peak filtering methods, providing the experimental benchmark used to evaluate 3plex TPX predictions. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.05.016
skills.summary: A replicate-handling procedure that converts raw ChIP-seq-style lncRNA:DNA binding data (ChIRP-seq, ChOP-seq, CHART-seq, RAP-seq) into reproducibility-filtered peak sets using ENCODE IDR/Overlap peak filtering methods, providing the experimental benchmark used to evaluate 3plex TPX predictions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The experiment lacks raw fastq data or has unclear replicate annotation — such datasets were explicitly excluded from the benchmark collection The data are Xist ChIRP-seq (X-chromosome-limited), which the authors excluded from the curated collection A published peak set is already available and accepted as-is — though the authors found IDR conservative filtering gave a +0.09 average AUC gain over published peaks, so re-filtering is preferred when raw data exist

skills.description: Use when you need to train or reproduce a loop-calling model on Hi-C cis-contact maps represented as image patches (KR-normalized O/E matrices or .cool input), including low-depth downsampled runs.
skills.name: image-based-loop-prediction-model-training
skills.search_text: image-based-loop-prediction-model-training Use when you need to train or reproduce a loop-calling model on Hi-C cis-contact maps represented as image patches (KR-normalized O/E matrices or .cool input), including low-depth downsampled runs. Input is extremely sparse single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) data — the article states GILoop 'is still not capable enough to deal with' scHi-C You only have raw FASTQ reads or unprocessed contact maps and cannot produce KR-normalized O/E matrices or .cool files The question concerns the graph view alone (GCN branch on the graph representation) rather than image-based prediction http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 Trains GILoop's U-Net image branch (or the fused dual-branch model) to predict CTCF-mediated loops from Hi-C contact maps treated as images, using matrix downsampling to control sequencing depth and PR-AUC as the evaluation metric. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2022.105535
skills.summary: Trains GILoop's U-Net image branch (or the fused dual-branch model) to predict CTCF-mediated loops from Hi-C contact maps treated as images, using matrix downsampling to control sequencing depth and PR-AUC as the evaluation metric.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is extremely sparse single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) data — the article states GILoop 'is still not capable enough to deal with' scHi-C You only have raw FASTQ reads or unprocessed contact maps and cannot produce KR-normalized O/E matrices or .cool files The question concerns the graph view alone (GCN branch on the graph representation) rather than image-based prediction

skills.description: Use when building a supervised classifier (e.g. a Keras/TensorFlow variant-scoring network) from a training set where positives are orders of magnitude rarer than negatives — in iMEGES, 574 dsQTL positives vs 27,735 negatives — so the sigmoid output is not dominated by the majority class.
skills.name: imbalanced-class-resampling
skills.search_text: imbalanced-class-resampling Use when building a supervised classifier (e.g. a Keras/TensorFlow variant-scoring network) from a training set where positives are orders of magnitude rarer than negatives — in iMEGES, 574 dsQTL positives vs 27,735 negatives — so the sigmoid output is not dominated by the majority class. The training classes are already balanced or nearly so — ROSE synthetic oversampling would add noise without benefit and distort the natural class prior. Resampling the held-out test/validation folds: evaluation AUCs must be computed on the original imbalanced distribution; ROSE is only for the training data feeding the Keras network. You need calibrated per-variant probabilities reflecting population frequencies — resampled training changes the effective prior, so sigmoid outputs must be interpreted as ranking scores (ncDeepBrain scores), not calibrated probabilities. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Balances severely skewed positive/negative class ratios in a training feature matrix using the ROSE R library before fitting a deep neural network — here applied to ncDeepBrain's 574 positive dsQTL SNPs vs 27,735 negative SNPs (MAF > 5%) used to train the iMEGES non-coding variant score. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2469-7
skills.summary: Balances severely skewed positive/negative class ratios in a training feature matrix using the ROSE R library before fitting a deep neural network — here applied to ncDeepBrain's 574 positive dsQTL SNPs vs 27,735 negative SNPs (MAF > 5%) used to train the iMEGES non-coding variant score.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The training classes are already balanced or nearly so — ROSE synthetic oversampling would add noise without benefit and distort the natural class prior. Resampling the held-out test/validation folds: evaluation AUCs must be computed on the original imbalanced distribution; ROSE is only for the training data feeding the Keras network. You need calibrated per-variant probabilities reflecting population frequencies — resampled training changes the effective prior, so sigmoid outputs must be interpreted as ranking scores (ncDeepBrain scores), not calibrated probabilities.

skills.description: Use when training or evaluating a variant/gene classifier on datasets with extreme positive-to-negative imbalance (e.g., PGC schizophrenia GWAS-derived sets with hundreds of positives and tens of thousands of negatives), prior to fitting the model and computing ROC/AUC.
skills.name: imbalanced-dataset-resampling-with-rose
skills.search_text: imbalanced-dataset-resampling-with-rose Use when training or evaluating a variant/gene classifier on datasets with extreme positive-to-negative imbalance (e.g., PGC schizophrenia GWAS-derived sets with hundreds of positives and tens of thousands of negatives), prior to fitting the model and computing ROC/AUC. When the positive/negative classes are already balanced — resampling would discard or duplicate variants needlessly When the goal is to report prevalence-realistic precision metrics on the untouched original testing distribution rather than cross-validated ROC/AUC When the task is feature imputation of missing scores (use bPCA via the -B/--bPCA option of ncDeepBrain.py instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Balance highly imbalanced positive/negative variant datasets using the ROSE R library before training and testing the ncDeepBrain deep neural network, so that class skew (e.g., 574 disease positives vs 27,735 negatives in training dataset 1) does not dominate the learned model or the resulting ROC/AUC evaluation. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2469-7
skills.summary: Balance highly imbalanced positive/negative variant datasets using the ROSE R library before training and testing the ncDeepBrain deep neural network, so that class skew (e.g., 574 disease positives vs 27,735 negatives in training dataset 1) does not dominate the learned model or the resulting ROC/AUC evaluation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the positive/negative classes are already balanced — resampling would discard or duplicate variants needlessly When the goal is to report prevalence-realistic precision metrics on the untouched original testing distribution rather than cross-validated ROC/AUC When the task is feature imputation of missing scores (use bPCA via the -B/--bPCA option of ncDeepBrain.py instead)

skills.description: Use when you have cluster assignments from scATAC-seq data (e.g. SCALE Leiden clusters on an h5ad like Breast_Tumor.h5ad) and need to assign biological identity to clusters via enriched TF binding motifs in type-specific peaks.
skills.name: immune-and-epithelial-motif-interpretation
skills.search_text: immune-and-epithelial-motif-interpretation Use when you have cluster assignments from scATAC-seq data (e.g. SCALE Leiden clusters on an h5ad like Breast_Tumor.h5ad) and need to assign biological identity to clusters via enriched TF binding motifs in type-specific peaks. Input is already a motif enrichment table or feature matrix rather than raw peak-by-cell scATAC-seq counts needing clustering The goal is single-batch scRNA-seq expression analysis, since SCALE/Homer motif interpretation requires open-chromatin peak data You need batch-effect removal as the primary objective — the article states SCALE 'is not specifically designed to identify and remove these artifacts from the input data' http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 Interprets cell-type identity from scATAC-seq clusters by running Homer known-motif enrichment on cluster-specific peaks, recovering immune-specific motifs (Maz, Pu.1-Irf, Irf8, Runx1, Elk4, Nfy, Elf3, SpiB) in CD45+ cells and tumor-related motifs (Klf14, Mitf, Ets1, Nrf2, Nrf1) in Epcam+ cells. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-12630-7
skills.summary: Interprets cell-type identity from scATAC-seq clusters by running Homer known-motif enrichment on cluster-specific peaks, recovering immune-specific motifs (Maz, Pu.1-Irf, Irf8, Runx1, Elk4, Nfy, Elf3, SpiB) in CD45+ cells and tumor-related motifs (Klf14, Mitf, Ets1, Nrf2, Nrf1) in Epcam+ cells.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a motif enrichment table or feature matrix rather than raw peak-by-cell scATAC-seq counts needing clustering The goal is single-batch scRNA-seq expression analysis, since SCALE/Homer motif interpretation requires open-chromatin peak data You need batch-effect removal as the primary objective — the article states SCALE 'is not specifically designed to identify and remove these artifacts from the input data'

skills.description: Use when you have per-donor cell population proportions (flow cytometry) plus donor metadata (continuous age, sex) and need to test which factor—age, sex, or their interaction—is most strongly associated with each cell subset.
skills.name: immune-cell-subset-statistical-testing
skills.search_text: immune-cell-subset-statistical-testing Use when you have per-donor cell population proportions (flow cytometry) plus donor metadata (continuous age, sex) and need to test which factor—age, sex, or their interaction—is most strongly associated with each cell subset. The input is already a fitted model object or a coefficient table rather than per-donor proportion data with donor metadata. The question is about bulk transcriptomic or ATAC-seq signal changes rather than cytometry-derived cell composition proportions. The cohort lacks both male and female donors across a sufficient age range, making the age-by-sex interaction term unestimable. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Fits per-population generalized linear models (GLMs) of flow-cytometry-derived PBMC cell proportions against age, sex, and an age-by-sex interaction term, then ranks coefficient magnitudes to identify which donor factor most strongly shapes each immune cell subset. It operationalizes the Márquez et al. (Nature Communications, 2020) finding that age dominates CD8+/naive T cell variation while sex dominates naive CD4+ T cell variation. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-14396-9
skills.summary: Fits per-population generalized linear models (GLMs) of flow-cytometry-derived PBMC cell proportions against age, sex, and an age-by-sex interaction term, then ranks coefficient magnitudes to identify which donor factor most strongly shapes each immune cell subset. It operationalizes the Márquez et al. (Nature Communications, 2020) finding that age dominates CD8+/naive T cell variation while sex dominates naive CD4+ T cell variation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a fitted model object or a coefficient table rather than per-donor proportion data with donor metadata. The question is about bulk transcriptomic or ATAC-seq signal changes rather than cytometry-derived cell composition proportions. The cohort lacks both male and female donors across a sufficient age range, making the age-by-sex interaction term unestimable.

skills.description: Use when time-series RNA-seq expression data plus TF–gene interactions and pathway gene sets are available and the goal is to identify TFs regulating pathway cascades at specific time points.
skills.name: immune-response-cascade-reconstruction
skills.search_text: immune-response-cascade-reconstruction Use when time-series RNA-seq expression data plus TF–gene interactions and pathway gene sets are available and the goal is to identify TFs regulating pathway cascades at specific time points. The expression data are not time-series (no time-course sampling); clustering methods cannot evaluate temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways, and TSMiner's time-specific construction is unnecessary. Only differentially expressed gene lists are available without TF–TG interaction data or pathway gene sets — TSMiner integrates all three input file types. The goal is static co-expression module detection rather than identifying which TFs interact with pathways at specific time points. http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0204 Reconstructs time-specific TF–pathway regulatory cascades across late-stage mouse liver regeneration (LR) using TSMiner, quantifying shared transcription factor regulators between consecutive immune-related KEGG pathway stages (e.g. 61 and 38 TFs with 33 overlapping for p53 signalling and apoptosis at 36 h). epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: Reconstructs time-specific TF–pathway regulatory cascades across late-stage mouse liver regeneration (LR) using TSMiner, quantifying shared transcription factor regulators between consecutive immune-related KEGG pathway stages (e.g. 61 and 38 TFs with 33 overlapping for p53 signalling and apoptosis at 36 h).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The expression data are not time-series (no time-course sampling); clustering methods cannot evaluate temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways, and TSMiner's time-specific construction is unnecessary. Only differentially expressed gene lists are available without TF–TG interaction data or pathway gene sets — TSMiner integrates all three input file types. The goal is static co-expression module detection rather than identifying which TFs interact with pathways at specific time points.

skills.description: Use when bisulfite sequencing data (bismark/bsmap/biscuit .cov output) must be tested for allele-specific methylation at imprinted DMRs or X-linked CGIs, e.g. detecting state-dependent imprinting loss in naive ES cells.
skills.name: imprinted-dmr-allele-specific-methylation-calling
skills.search_text: imprinted-dmr-allele-specific-methylation-calling Use when bisulfite sequencing data (bismark/bsmap/biscuit .cov output) must be tested for allele-specific methylation at imprinted DMRs or X-linked CGIs, e.g. detecting state-dependent imprinting loss in naive ES cells. Sample has high 5-hydroxymethylation (e.g. neuronal cell types) since DXM does not consider 5hmC Regions carry copy number variants or complex multi-allelic (more than two) subpopulations where a two-subpopulation allelic interpretation is invalid Single-CpG or very short regions: larger regions need more CpGs with methylation change to be solved as a distinct profile, and sparse regions will not deconvolve reliably http://edamontology.org/topic_3674 http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 Applies DXM deconvolution to bisulfite sequencing data restricted to known imprinted DMRs (and X-linked CpG islands) to detect allele-specific methylation as two subpopulation methylation profiles, distinguishing states such as primed vs naive ES cells where imprints are lost. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab516
skills.summary: Applies DXM deconvolution to bisulfite sequencing data restricted to known imprinted DMRs (and X-linked CpG islands) to detect allele-specific methylation as two subpopulation methylation profiles, distinguishing states such as primed vs naive ES cells where imprints are lost.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Sample has high 5-hydroxymethylation (e.g. neuronal cell types) since DXM does not consider 5hmC Regions carry copy number variants or complex multi-allelic (more than two) subpopulations where a two-subpopulation allelic interpretation is invalid Single-CpG or very short regions: larger regions need more CpGs with methylation change to be solved as a distinct profile, and sparse regions will not deconvolve reliably

skills.description: Use when a WGBS/bisulfite-seq dataset must be interpreted at a known imprinted or allele-specifically methylated locus, and per-read methylation phased by a heterozygous SNP genotype is needed.
skills.name: imprinted-locus-methylation-interpretation
skills.search_text: imprinted-locus-methylation-interpretation Use when a WGBS/bisulfite-seq dataset must be interpreted at a known imprinted or allele-specifically methylated locus, and per-read methylation phased by a heterozygous SNP genotype is needed. Data generated with TAPS or 5hmC-CATCH protocols — the README restricts 4-letter mode to those and mandates 3-letter mode with `-m BS` for BS-seq; mixing these invalidates the calls Analyses requiring only aggregated CpG methylation levels with no allele/resolution read-out — Mviewer's per-read, genotype-preserved view adds nothing Loci without a heterozygous SNP marker to phase reads by — allele-specific methylation cannot be interpreted at single-allele level from the track http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_0160 Interprets allele-specific DNA methylation at imprinted loci (e.g., MEST on chr7) by visualizing nucleotide-level, genotype-preserved per-read methylation states with Mviewer on Msuite bisulfite-mode outputs, annotating heterozygous SNPs such as rs2301335. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2020.100127
skills.summary: Interprets allele-specific DNA methylation at imprinted loci (e.g., MEST on chr7) by visualizing nucleotide-level, genotype-preserved per-read methylation states with Mviewer on Msuite bisulfite-mode outputs, annotating heterozygous SNPs such as rs2301335.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data generated with TAPS or 5hmC-CATCH protocols — the README restricts 4-letter mode to those and mandates 3-letter mode with `-m BS` for BS-seq; mixing these invalidates the calls Analyses requiring only aggregated CpG methylation levels with no allele/resolution read-out — Mviewer's per-read, genotype-preserved view adds nothing Loci without a heterozygous SNP marker to phase reads by — allele-specific methylation cannot be interpreted at single-allele level from the track

skills.description: Use when bisulfite amplicon/pyrosequencing methylation data for an imprinted DMR (e.g. KCNQ1OT1, H19/IGF2) include standard controls (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) plus case/control samples and you must correct PCR bias and call hyper/hypo-methylated cases.
skills.name: imprinting-dmr-methylation-analysis
skills.search_text: imprinting-dmr-methylation-analysis Use when bisulfite amplicon/pyrosequencing methylation data for an imprinted DMR (e.g. KCNQ1OT1, H19/IGF2) include standard controls (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) plus case/control samples and you must correct PCR bias and call hyper/hypo-methylated cases. The assay has no standard controls with known methylation percentages (0/25/50/75/100%), so no calibration curve can be derived for PCR-bias correction The data are genome-wide methylation profiles (e.g. arrays or WGBS) rather than targeted bisulfite amplicon/pyrosequencing of a CGI or imprinting DMR — MethylCal is designed for targeted assays analysed jointly across CpGs within a DMR Only CpG-level 'one-at-a-time' calibration or average-methylation calibration is acceptable for the analysis, since MethylCal's joint-DMR approach assumes CpG-level variability should be modelled http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Reproduce PCR-bias-corrected gain/loss-of-methylation classification of imprinted DMR assays (e.g. KCNQ1OT1 and H19/IGF2 in BWS patients) using the MethylCal R package's INLA-based Bayesian calibration, outlier detection, and 3SD confidence-interval differential methylation testing against healthy controls. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz325
skills.summary: Reproduce PCR-bias-corrected gain/loss-of-methylation classification of imprinted DMR assays (e.g. KCNQ1OT1 and H19/IGF2 in BWS patients) using the MethylCal R package's INLA-based Bayesian calibration, outlier detection, and 3SD confidence-interval differential methylation testing against healthy controls.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The assay has no standard controls with known methylation percentages (0/25/50/75/100%), so no calibration curve can be derived for PCR-bias correction The data are genome-wide methylation profiles (e.g. arrays or WGBS) rather than targeted bisulfite amplicon/pyrosequencing of a CGI or imprinting DMR — MethylCal is designed for targeted assays analysed jointly across CpGs within a DMR Only CpG-level 'one-at-a-time' calibration or average-methylation calibration is acceptable for the analysis, since MethylCal's joint-DMR approach assumes CpG-level variability should be modelled

skills.description: Use when a deduplicated ChIA-PET bedpe (e.g., GM12878 CTCF) is available together with phased heterozygous genotypes, and the goal is to determine which chromatin loops at an imprinted locus are maternal- versus paternal-specific.
skills.name: imprinting-locus-allele-specific-loop-interpretation
skills.search_text: imprinting-locus-allele-specific-loop-interpretation Use when a deduplicated ChIA-PET bedpe (e.g., GM12878 CTCF) is available together with phased heterozygous genotypes, and the goal is to determine which chromatin loops at an imprinted locus are maternal- versus paternal-specific. No phased heterozygous genotype data exist for the sample, so PETs cannot be assigned to a parental haplotype and the allele-specific step is meaningless. The goal is allele-aggregated loop calling from raw reads (linker trimming, alignment, duplicate removal, peak calling) — use the standard ChIA-PET2 pipeline workflow instead of the allele-specific interpretation step. The locus of interest has no heterozygous sites spanned by PETs, so no allele assignment can be made there. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Interprets allele-specific chromatin loops at imprinted loci (e.g., H19/IGF2 in GM12878) by combining ChIA-PET2's phased-genotype loop calling with bedtools-based filtering of both-mapped PETs against Illumina Platinum Genomes phased variants. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkw809
skills.summary: Interprets allele-specific chromatin loops at imprinted loci (e.g., H19/IGF2 in GM12878) by combining ChIA-PET2's phased-genotype loop calling with bedtools-based filtering of both-mapped PETs against Illumina Platinum Genomes phased variants.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No phased heterozygous genotype data exist for the sample, so PETs cannot be assigned to a parental haplotype and the allele-specific step is meaningless. The goal is allele-aggregated loop calling from raw reads (linker trimming, alignment, duplicate removal, peak calling) — use the standard ChIA-PET2 pipeline workflow instead of the allele-specific interpretation step. The locus of interest has no heterozygous sites spanned by PETs, so no allele assignment can be made there.

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether an imputation method recovers cell-type-specific signal in sparse scATAC-seq data, e.g. comparing SCALE's adata.obsm['imputed'] matrix against scImpute, SAVER, MAGIC or scVI via meta-cell correlation.
skills.name: imputation-method-benchmarking
skills.search_text: imputation-method-benchmarking Use when evaluating whether an imputation method recovers cell-type-specific signal in sparse scATAC-seq data, e.g. comparing SCALE's adata.obsm['imputed'] matrix against scImpute, SAVER, MAGIC or scVI via meta-cell correlation. The goal is explicit identification and removal of batch effects or other technical artifacts — the paper states SCALE 'is not specifically designed to identify and remove these artifacts from the input data' Input is scRNA-seq data without an scATAC-seq sparsity/binary structure concern; the benchmark rationale rests on scATAC-seq 'missingness' and close-to-binary data Only a small preview of denoised values is needed — use the storage-efficient --binary option instead of numerical --impute imputation http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmark denoising/imputation of sparse single-cell data by running SCALE's VAE-GMM imputation (--impute) on a scATAC-seq dataset such as Forebrain and evaluating cell-wise Pearson correlations against per-cell-type meta-cells, in comparison with scRNA-seq methods (scImpute, SAVER, MAGIC, scVI). epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-12630-7
skills.summary: Benchmark denoising/imputation of sparse single-cell data by running SCALE's VAE-GMM imputation (--impute) on a scATAC-seq dataset such as Forebrain and evaluating cell-wise Pearson correlations against per-cell-type meta-cells, in comparison with scRNA-seq methods (scImpute, SAVER, MAGIC, scVI).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is explicit identification and removal of batch effects or other technical artifacts — the paper states SCALE 'is not specifically designed to identify and remove these artifacts from the input data' Input is scRNA-seq data without an scATAC-seq sparsity/binary structure concern; the benchmark rationale rests on scATAC-seq 'missingness' and close-to-binary data Only a small preview of denoised values is needed — use the storage-efficient --binary option instead of numerical --impute imputation

skills.description: Use when a raw, sparse scATAC-seq peak matrix has been denoised with SCALE and the task requires the numerical imputed matrix (adata.obsm['imputed']) as input to downstream tools like chromVAR.
skills.name: imputed-accessibility-matrix-handling
skills.search_text: imputed-accessibility-matrix-handling Use when a raw, sparse scATAC-seq peak matrix has been denoised with SCALE and the task requires the numerical imputed matrix (adata.obsm['imputed']) as input to downstream tools like chromVAR. Only a binarized imputation is needed for storage-constrained workflows — the README recommends adata.obsm['binary'] with --binary for saving storage instead The analysis requires individual-peak resolution or explicit batch-effect removal — the article notes chromVAR 'only analyzes peaks in groups and lacks the resolution of individual peaks' and SCALE 'is not specifically designed to identify and remove these artifacts from the input data' http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_0769 Handles the numerical imputed scATAC-seq peak-count matrix produced by SCALE's --impute option (stored as adata.obsm['imputed'] in adata.h5ad) so it can be used for downstream analyses such as chromVAR motif deviation scoring instead of the sparse raw matrix. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-12630-7
skills.summary: Handles the numerical imputed scATAC-seq peak-count matrix produced by SCALE's --impute option (stored as adata.obsm['imputed'] in adata.h5ad) so it can be used for downstream analyses such as chromVAR motif deviation scoring instead of the sparse raw matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a binarized imputation is needed for storage-constrained workflows — the README recommends adata.obsm['binary'] with --binary for saving storage instead The analysis requires individual-peak resolution or explicit batch-effect removal — the article notes chromVAR 'only analyzes peaks in groups and lacks the resolution of individual peaks' and SCALE 'is not specifically designed to identify and remove these artifacts from the input data'

skills.description: Use when benchmarking single-cell epigenomic clustering methods on scChIP-seq/scATAC-seq data where no natural labels exist and a ground-truth cell-type mix with known labels is required to compute ARIs.
skills.name: in-silico-cell-mixing-assembly
skills.search_text: in-silico-cell-mixing-assembly Use when benchmarking single-cell epigenomic clustering methods on scChIP-seq/scATAC-seq data where no natural labels exist and a ground-truth cell-type mix with known labels is required to compute ARIs. The dataset already contains biological labels or annotated cell types, so clustering performance can be evaluated directly without constructing a synthetic mix The analysis targets discovery of novel sub-populations rather than method benchmarking — an in-silico mix imposes artificial, perfectly separable cell identities Input data are not count matrices from sparse single-cell epigenomic assays (e.g. they are bulk ChIP-seq or scRNA-seq); the assembly procedure and QC thresholds are calibrated for scChIP-seq/scATAC-seq sparsity http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Assemble a controlled in-silico mixture of single-cell H3K27me3 scChIP-seq count matrices from four known cell lines (Jurkat, Ramos, HBCx-22, MDA-MB-468) so that clustering/benchmarking methods can be evaluated against a known ground-truth label vector using the adjusted Rand index. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-19542-x
skills.summary: Assemble a controlled in-silico mixture of single-cell H3K27me3 scChIP-seq count matrices from four known cell lines (Jurkat, Ramos, HBCx-22, MDA-MB-468) so that clustering/benchmarking methods can be evaluated against a known ground-truth label vector using the adjusted Rand index.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset already contains biological labels or annotated cell types, so clustering performance can be evaluated directly without constructing a synthetic mix The analysis targets discovery of novel sub-populations rather than method benchmarking — an in-silico mix imposes artificial, perfectly separable cell identities Input data are not count matrices from sparse single-cell epigenomic assays (e.g. they are bulk ChIP-seq or scRNA-seq); the assembly procedure and QC thresholds are calibrated for scChIP-seq/scATAC-seq sparsity

skills.description: Use when you need to rank functional genomic elements (CTF sites, promoters, enhancers) by their predicted impact on chromatin interactions, i.e. identify which elements underlie genome folding patterns from sequence.
skills.name: in-silico-deletion-perturbation-prediction
skills.search_text: in-silico-deletion-perturbation-prediction Use when you need to rank functional genomic elements (CTF sites, promoters, enhancers) by their predicted impact on chromatin interactions, i.e. identify which elements underlie genome folding patterns from sequence. You need experimentally measured Hi-C interaction changes rather than sequence-based predicted perturbation effects Your question is single-nucleotide variant impact rather than whole-element (CTCF/promoter/enhancer) deletion effects — use deepC's SNP-level variant scoring instead You lack a trained deepC model for the relevant cell type and suitable tissue-specific Hi-C training data http://edamontology.org/topic_3678 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 A genome-wide in silico deletion screen that scores regulatory elements (CTCF sites, promoters, enhancers, shuffled backgrounds) by the predicted change in chromatin interaction maps when the element is removed from megabase-scale sequence windows, using deepC to quantify each element's contribution to 3D genome folding. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41592-020-0960-3
skills.summary: A genome-wide in silico deletion screen that scores regulatory elements (CTCF sites, promoters, enhancers, shuffled backgrounds) by the predicted change in chromatin interaction maps when the element is removed from megabase-scale sequence windows, using deepC to quantify each element's contribution to 3D genome folding.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need experimentally measured Hi-C interaction changes rather than sequence-based predicted perturbation effects Your question is single-nucleotide variant impact rather than whole-element (CTCF/promoter/enhancer) deletion effects — use deepC's SNP-level variant scoring instead You lack a trained deepC model for the relevant cell type and suitable tissue-specific Hi-C training data

skills.description: Use when you have a trained CITRUS model output (hid_tmr TF activities), a binary SGA alteration matrix, and want to predict which TFs are associated with specific somatic alterations per cancer type.
skills.name: in-silico-gene-knockout-perturbation
skills.search_text: in-silico-gene-knockout-perturbation Use when you have a trained CITRUS model output (hid_tmr TF activities), a binary SGA alteration matrix, and want to predict which TFs are associated with specific somatic alterations per cancer type. You lack a trained CITRUS model or its output pickle files (dataset_CITRUS.pkl / output_dataset_CITRUS.pkl); the knock out requires propagating perturbed SGA through this specific model Your goal is differential expression between mutant and wild-type tumors from raw data rather than model-inferred causal TF activity associations TFs of interest belong to the same motif family that CITRUS cannot disambiguate, or you need TF activation/repression directionality or co-binding (e.g. AP-1-IRF complexes) represented http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Systematic in silico knock out analysis that zeroes a somatic alteration (SGA) gene in carrier tumors and propagates the perturbed input through the trained CITRUS model to obtain knockout TF activities, then tests mutant versus wild-type TF activity differences to identify TFs causally associated with alterations such as PIK3CA, PTEN, KRAS, TP53 and CTNNB1. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkac881
skills.summary: Systematic in silico knock out analysis that zeroes a somatic alteration (SGA) gene in carrier tumors and propagates the perturbed input through the trained CITRUS model to obtain knockout TF activities, then tests mutant versus wild-type TF activity differences to identify TFs causally associated with alterations such as PIK3CA, PTEN, KRAS, TP53 and CTNNB1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You lack a trained CITRUS model or its output pickle files (dataset_CITRUS.pkl / output_dataset_CITRUS.pkl); the knock out requires propagating perturbed SGA through this specific model Your goal is differential expression between mutant and wild-type tumors from raw data rather than model-inferred causal TF activity associations TFs of interest belong to the same motif family that CITRUS cannot disambiguate, or you need TF activation/repression directionality or co-binding (e.g. AP-1-IRF complexes) represented

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a methylation deconvolution tool (e.g., DXM) and ground-truth subpopulation profiles and prevalences are needed that cannot be obtained from real mixed samples.
skills.name: in-silico-mixture-generation-from-reference-profiles
skills.search_text: in-silico-mixture-generation-from-reference-profiles Use when benchmarking a methylation deconvolution tool (e.g., DXM) and ground-truth subpopulation profiles and prevalences are needed that cannot be obtained from real mixed samples. The goal is to validate deconvolution on real heterogeneous biological samples with unknown ground truth (e.g., DLBCL patient cohorts), where simulated binarized profiles do not reflect biological methylation distributions The reference profiles contain partial methylation values that must be preserved rather than binarized to 0/1, since this skill specifically generates idealized binarized mixtures The tool under test models copy-number variation or allele-specific methylation, which DXM and this idealized mixture design do not account for http://edamontology.org/topic_3674 http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 Generates idealized simulated heterogeneous methylation samples by mixing binarized reference cell-type methylation profiles (e.g., HMEC with CD4+ T or HCC1954) at fixed subpopulation prevalences and sequencing coverages using numpy, to benchmark deconvolution methods like DXM. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab516
skills.summary: Generates idealized simulated heterogeneous methylation samples by mixing binarized reference cell-type methylation profiles (e.g., HMEC with CD4+ T or HCC1954) at fixed subpopulation prevalences and sequencing coverages using numpy, to benchmark deconvolution methods like DXM.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to validate deconvolution on real heterogeneous biological samples with unknown ground truth (e.g., DLBCL patient cohorts), where simulated binarized profiles do not reflect biological methylation distributions The reference profiles contain partial methylation values that must be preserved rather than binarized to 0/1, since this skill specifically generates idealized binarized mixtures The tool under test models copy-number variation or allele-specific methylation, which DXM and this idealized mixture design do not account for

skills.description: Use when benchmarking methylation read aligners (e.g., Msuite vs Bismark vs BWA-meth) on ground-truth data, or when stratifying mapping performance by region composition such as CT/GA-rich bins.
skills.name: in-silico-read-simulation
skills.search_text: in-silico-read-simulation Use when benchmarking methylation read aligners (e.g., Msuite vs Bismark vs BWA-meth) on ground-truth data, or when stratifying mapping performance by region composition such as CT/GA-rich bins. Analyzing real sequencing data or biological conclusions — simulation is only valid for in-silico benchmarking against known truth coordinates Data generated by BS-seq protocol where 4-letter mode is not applicable (README: 4-letter mode ONLY supports TAPS/5hmC-CATCH data) Reads longer or shorter than the tested 36-/100-bp paired-/single-end configurations without re-validating the benchmark parameters http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Generate simulated methylome sequencing reads with the SHERMAN script under the TAPS protocol (C->T conversion 20% at CpG, 0.5% at CpH, 0.1% sequencing error) so that aligner mapping efficiency and accuracy can be benchmarked against known ground truth. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2020.100127
skills.summary: Generate simulated methylome sequencing reads with the SHERMAN script under the TAPS protocol (C->T conversion 20% at CpG, 0.5% at CpH, 0.1% sequencing error) so that aligner mapping efficiency and accuracy can be benchmarked against known ground truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Analyzing real sequencing data or biological conclusions — simulation is only valid for in-silico benchmarking against known truth coordinates Data generated by BS-seq protocol where 4-letter mode is not applicable (README: 4-letter mode ONLY supports TAPS/5hmC-CATCH data) Reads longer or shorter than the tested 36-/100-bp paired-/single-end configurations without re-validating the benchmark parameters

skills.description: Use when you need to dissect which bases and sequence motifs around a non-coding SNP drive a predicted chromatin activity change (e.g., transcription factor binding) for a single variant, at single-base resolution.
skills.name: in-silico-saturated-mutagenesis-analysis
skills.search_text: in-silico-saturated-mutagenesis-analysis Use when you need to dissect which bases and sequence motifs around a non-coding SNP drive a predicted chromatin activity change (e.g., transcription factor binding) for a single variant, at single-base resolution. The goal is to annotate many variants genome-scale rather than dissect one sequence/variant — use DeepFun's SNP Activity Difference (SAD) profiles via tutorials/sad.ipynb instead The variant's effect depends on long-range interactions such as 3D DNA contact, which the DeepFun model does not consider You need quantitative (non-binarized) epigenomic signal predictions — DeepFun trained with peaks treated as binary format and ignores quantitative information http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Runs DeepFun/Basset in silico saturated mutagenesis to predict the effect of every single-nucleotide substitution within a sequence window (e.g., ±200 bp around a query SNP) on a specific chromatin profile, and renders SAD-style heat maps that reveal informative motifs (e.g., the NFE2 motif TGACTCAGCA at rs6426833). epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab429
skills.summary: Runs DeepFun/Basset in silico saturated mutagenesis to predict the effect of every single-nucleotide substitution within a sequence window (e.g., ±200 bp around a query SNP) on a specific chromatin profile, and renders SAD-style heat maps that reveal informative motifs (e.g., the NFE2 motif TGACTCAGCA at rs6426833).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to annotate many variants genome-scale rather than dissect one sequence/variant — use DeepFun's SNP Activity Difference (SAD) profiles via tutorials/sad.ipynb instead The variant's effect depends on long-range interactions such as 3D DNA contact, which the DeepFun model does not consider You need quantitative (non-binarized) epigenomic signal predictions — DeepFun trained with peaks treated as binary format and ignores quantitative information

skills.description: Use when building a supervised nc-sindel classifier for tissue-specific regulatory indels and you need to convert indel position/ref/alt files into a CADD + DanQ multi-omics feature table for model training.
skills.name: indel-training-data-preparation
skills.search_text: indel-training-data-preparation Use when building a supervised nc-sindel classifier for tissue-specific regulatory indels and you need to convert indel position/ref/alt files into a CADD + DanQ multi-omics feature table for model training. You only need precomputed tissue-specific functional scores for known nc-sindels — use R/TIVAN-indel.R with the precomputed 44-GTEx-tissue score files instead of rebuilding features. Your variants are SNVs rather than small indels — the CADD.indel.rda annotations and the sequence-injecting prepare.R logic are specific to indels. Input is already a feature table (annot.csv plus seq_features.h5 exist) — skip preparation and go directly to train.py or predict.py. http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Generates the labeled training features for TIVAN-indel by combining 45 CADD annotations (via an R rda file covering 1000 Genomes indels) with 919 multi-omics features predicted from reference/alternative indel sequences using the pretrained DanQ model, producing annot.csv and seq_features.h5 in a target folder. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad060
skills.summary: Generates the labeled training features for TIVAN-indel by combining 45 CADD annotations (via an R rda file covering 1000 Genomes indels) with 919 multi-omics features predicted from reference/alternative indel sequences using the pretrained DanQ model, producing annot.csv and seq_features.h5 in a target folder.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need precomputed tissue-specific functional scores for known nc-sindels — use R/TIVAN-indel.R with the precomputed 44-GTEx-tissue score files instead of rebuilding features. Your variants are SNVs rather than small indels — the CADD.indel.rda annotations and the sequence-injecting prepare.R logic are specific to indels. Input is already a feature table (annot.csv plus seq_features.h5 exist) — skip preparation and go directly to train.py or predict.py.

skills.description: Use when you have CscoreTool-M *_cscore.txt probability outputs and need to measure how heterogeneous sub-compartment localization is across cells, e.g. comparing proliferating vs terminally differentiated cells or G1 vs S/G2 stages.
skills.name: information-content-heterogeneity-quantification
skills.search_text: information-content-heterogeneity-quantification Use when you have CscoreTool-M *_cscore.txt probability outputs and need to measure how heterogeneous sub-compartment localization is across cells, e.g. comparing proliferating vs terminally differentiated cells or G1 vs S/G2 stages. Input is bulk Hi-C from a single homogeneous cell population with no cell-cycle or cell-type mixture to compare — heterogeneity quantification over probability scores has little meaning You need discrete sub-compartment labels or GO enrichment of sub-compartment genes rather than a continuous heterogeneity measure per window The *_cscore.txt probabilities were computed with mismatched N_subcompartment across conditions being compared (e.g. 5 vs 10), since entropy values are not comparable across different numbers of sub-compartments http://edamontology.org/topic_3912 Quantifies genome-organization heterogeneity within a cell population by computing Shannon information content over CscoreTool-M sub-compartment probability scores (from *_cscore.txt outputs) per genomic window, then aggregating by cell type and cell-cycle stage. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad314
skills.summary: Quantifies genome-organization heterogeneity within a cell population by computing Shannon information content over CscoreTool-M sub-compartment probability scores (from *_cscore.txt outputs) per genomic window, then aggregating by cell type and cell-cycle stage.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is bulk Hi-C from a single homogeneous cell population with no cell-cycle or cell-type mixture to compare — heterogeneity quantification over probability scores has little meaning You need discrete sub-compartment labels or GO enrichment of sub-compartment genes rather than a continuous heterogeneity measure per window The *_cscore.txt probabilities were computed with mismatched N_subcompartment across conditions being compared (e.g. 5 vs 10), since entropy values are not comparable across different numbers of sub-compartments

skills.description: Use when filtering CNN-derived motif detectors and their TFBS candidate sets from DESSO predict.py output, to discard weak or degenerate motifs before downstream motif comparison or TFBS calling.
skills.name: information-content-motif-filtering
skills.search_text: information-content-motif-filtering Use when filtering CNN-derived motif detectors and their TFBS candidate sets from DESSO predict.py output, to discard weak or degenerate motifs before downstream motif comparison or TFBS calling. Motif discovery from raw ChIP-seq peaks without trained DESSO CNN detectors — this skill only filters and optimizes detector-derived candidate sets Ranking motifs by enrichment alone when instance-level TFBS coordinates are needed — the binomial model selects a per-motif optimal cutoff, not just a significance call Genomes/backgrounds other than the GC-matched 101-bp human ENCODE background without re-estimating occurrence probabilities, since P-values depend on the 500,000-bin background set http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Retention filtering of DESSO-predicted motif detectors using the binomial-distribution TFBS identification model: motifs are kept only if their optimal-cutoff candidate set passes P < 1e-4, contains more than 5 motif instances, and has at least 3 positions with information content > 1. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz672
skills.summary: Retention filtering of DESSO-predicted motif detectors using the binomial-distribution TFBS identification model: motifs are kept only if their optimal-cutoff candidate set passes P < 1e-4, contains more than 5 motif instances, and has at least 3 positions with information content > 1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Motif discovery from raw ChIP-seq peaks without trained DESSO CNN detectors — this skill only filters and optimizes detector-derived candidate sets Ranking motifs by enrichment alone when instance-level TFBS coordinates are needed — the binomial model selects a per-motif optimal cutoff, not just a significance call Genomes/backgrounds other than the GC-matched 101-bp human ENCODE background without re-estimating occurrence probabilities, since P-values depend on the 500,000-bin background set

skills.description: Use when calibrating observed/apparent methylation levels from bisulfite amplicon sequencing of standard controls (known AMP percentages) across multiple CpGs in a CGI or DMR, and a joint Bayesian model with latent Gaussian field inference is needed.
skills.name: inla-approximate-bayesian-inference
skills.search_text: inla-approximate-bayesian-inference Use when calibrating observed/apparent methylation levels from bisulfite amplicon sequencing of standard controls (known AMP percentages) across multiple CpGs in a CGI or DMR, and a joint Bayesian model with latent Gaussian field inference is needed. Data are ordinary case/control methylation measurements without standard controls of known AMP — MethylCal calibration curves require five or more standard controls with known methylation percentages The goal is one-at-a-time CpG calibration or calibration of average methylation — MethylCal explicitly analyses all CpGs in a CGI/DMR jointly to avoid this You need a different calibration method than the Bayesian one — the package separately provides WarneckeCalibrationPlot and MoskalevCorrection/MoskalevCalibrationPlot http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 Fit MethylCal's joint Bayesian calibration models (M1–M4) for bisulfite amplicon sequencing standard controls using INLA's approximate Bayesian inference, avoiding MCMC while yielding posterior mean calibration curves and goodness-of-fit measures (mlik, DIC, RSS) per assay. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz325
skills.summary: Fit MethylCal's joint Bayesian calibration models (M1–M4) for bisulfite amplicon sequencing standard controls using INLA's approximate Bayesian inference, avoiding MCMC while yielding posterior mean calibration curves and goodness-of-fit measures (mlik, DIC, RSS) per assay.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are ordinary case/control methylation measurements without standard controls of known AMP — MethylCal calibration curves require five or more standard controls with known methylation percentages The goal is one-at-a-time CpG calibration or calibration of average methylation — MethylCal explicitly analyses all CpGs in a CGI/DMR jointly to avoid this You need a different calibration method than the Bayesian one — the package separately provides WarneckeCalibrationPlot and MoskalevCorrection/MoskalevCalibrationPlot

skills.description: Use when processing paired-end cfMeDIP-seq (or cfDNA) BAM alignments within a Snakemake QC pipeline and you need fragment-size distributions and windowed short/long fragmentation ratios as quality-control metrics.
skills.name: insert-size-metrics-profiling
skills.search_text: insert-size-metrics-profiling Use when processing paired-end cfMeDIP-seq (or cfDNA) BAM alignments within a Snakemake QC pipeline and you need fragment-size distributions and windowed short/long fragmentation ratios as quality-control metrics. Data are single-end — MEDIPIPE runs Picard CollectInsertSizeMetrics and computes fragmentation size ratios for paired-end data only Alignment stage is incomplete — the BAM must already be filtered and duplicate-removed; running insert-size metrics on unfiltered or un-deduplicated alignments produces inflated fragment-size estimates http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Estimate cfDNA fragment-size distributions from paired-end cfMeDIP-seq alignments using Picard CollectInsertSizeMetrics, and derive short-to-long fragmentation size ratios in consecutive 1 Mb and 5 Mb genomic windows (Cristiano et al. 2019) as MEDIPIPE QC metrics. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad423
skills.summary: Estimate cfDNA fragment-size distributions from paired-end cfMeDIP-seq alignments using Picard CollectInsertSizeMetrics, and derive short-to-long fragmentation size ratios in consecutive 1 Mb and 5 Mb genomic windows (Cristiano et al. 2019) as MEDIPIPE QC metrics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are single-end — MEDIPIPE runs Picard CollectInsertSizeMetrics and computes fragmentation size ratios for paired-end data only Alignment stage is incomplete — the BAM must already be filtered and duplicate-removed; running insert-size metrics on unfiltered or un-deduplicated alignments produces inflated fragment-size estimates

skills.description: Use when a cfMeDIP-seq (or MeDIP-seq) pipeline has produced per-sample QC outputs (FASTQC, SAMtools, Picard, MEDIPS reports) and they must be aggregated into one interactive HTML summary across samples, groups, or batches.
skills.name: interactive-html-qc-report-generation
skills.search_text: interactive-html-qc-report-generation Use when a cfMeDIP-seq (or MeDIP-seq) pipeline has produced per-sample QC outputs (FASTQC, SAMtools, Picard, MEDIPS reports) and they must be aggregated into one interactive HTML summary across samples, groups, or batches. Input is raw FASTQ only and no upstream QC (FASTQC/SAMtools/Picard/MEDIPS) outputs exist yet — run the upstream QC pipeline stages first The goal is methylation quantification aggregation (bin-sample TXT matrices) rather than QC metric summarization — use the aggregation/filtering skill instead A single-sample run where a per-tool native QC report already suffices and no cross-sample or cross-batch comparison is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Aggregates per-sample QC metrics from cfMeDIP-seq processing (FASTQC, SAMtools, Picard, MEDIPS) with MultiQC plus an embedded script into a summarized HTML report that allows interactive examination of sample QC metrics across different groups or batches. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad423
skills.summary: Aggregates per-sample QC metrics from cfMeDIP-seq processing (FASTQC, SAMtools, Picard, MEDIPS) with MultiQC plus an embedded script into a summarized HTML report that allows interactive examination of sample QC metrics across different groups or batches.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTQ only and no upstream QC (FASTQC/SAMtools/Picard/MEDIPS) outputs exist yet — run the upstream QC pipeline stages first The goal is methylation quantification aggregation (bin-sample TXT matrices) rather than QC metric summarization — use the aggregation/filtering skill instead A single-sample run where a per-tool native QC report already suffices and no cross-sample or cross-batch comparison is needed

skills.description: Use when comparing multiple epigenomic peak files (e.g. ATAC-seq vs DNase-seq, or CUT&Tag/CUT&Run vs ENCODE ChIP-seq H3K27ac reference) and you need QC, overlap statistics, and functional annotation collated in one report.
skills.name: interactive-html-report-generation
skills.search_text: interactive-html-report-generation Use when comparing multiple epigenomic peak files (e.g. ATAC-seq vs DNase-seq, or CUT&Tag/CUT&Run vs ENCODE ChIP-seq H3K27ac reference) and you need QC, overlap statistics, and functional annotation collated in one report. Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ/BAM) — EpiCompare operates on peak files (narrowPeak/BED) and Picard summaries, not raw reads or alignment You need single-sample QC only with no comparison reference or second dataset — the skill's core value is contrasting datasets, and overlap/precision-recall sections require multiple peak files Peak files have not been blacklist-filtered and you plan downstream analyses on the peaks themselves — EpiCompare removes blacklisted and non-standard-chromosome peaks internally, so its outputs should not be used as a substitute for returning cleaned peak files http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Generate a single collated interactive HTML report of epigenomic peak-file QC and benchmarking using the Bioconductor R package EpiCompare, which wraps peak overlap, ChromHMM/ChIPseeker annotation, and Picard-derived metrics into one knitr/rmarkdown (BiocStyle::html_document) document. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad049
skills.summary: Generate a single collated interactive HTML report of epigenomic peak-file QC and benchmarking using the Bioconductor R package EpiCompare, which wraps peak overlap, ChromHMM/ChIPseeker annotation, and Picard-derived metrics into one knitr/rmarkdown (BiocStyle::html_document) document.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ/BAM) — EpiCompare operates on peak files (narrowPeak/BED) and Picard summaries, not raw reads or alignment You need single-sample QC only with no comparison reference or second dataset — the skill's core value is contrasting datasets, and overlap/precision-recall sections require multiple peak files Peak files have not been blacklist-filtered and you plan downstream analyses on the peaks themselves — EpiCompare removes blacklisted and non-standard-chromosome peaks internally, so its outputs should not be used as a substitute for returning cleaned peak files

skills.description: Use when a time-series regulatory network has been constructed in TSMiner and you need to visually navigate time-specific network maps to identify which TFs interact with pathways and quantify overlaps between pathway-connected TF sets.
skills.name: interactive-network-visualization-exploration
skills.search_text: interactive-network-visualization-exploration Use when a time-series regulatory network has been constructed in TSMiner and you need to visually navigate time-specific network maps to identify which TFs interact with pathways and quantify overlaps between pathway-connected TF sets. The expression data are not time-series, since TSMiner networks are specifically time-point-resolved and clustering-only designs cannot evaluate temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways. You need repressor (negative TF–TG) interaction results as the primary signal; known repressors are limited, so negative-interaction networks are much sparser. You require a static whole-network topology analysis rather than identifying which TFs interact with specific pathways at specific time points. http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Explores TSMiner's interactive time-specific TF–pathway network maps to trace regulatory cascades (e.g., the late-stage mouse liver regeneration immune cascade at 36 h, 48 h and 168 h) and record which transcription factors are shared between pathways at each stage. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: Explores TSMiner's interactive time-specific TF–pathway network maps to trace regulatory cascades (e.g., the late-stage mouse liver regeneration immune cascade at 36 h, 48 h and 168 h) and record which transcription factors are shared between pathways at each stage.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The expression data are not time-series, since TSMiner networks are specifically time-point-resolved and clustering-only designs cannot evaluate temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways. You need repressor (negative TF–TG) interaction results as the primary signal; known repressors are limited, so negative-interaction networks are much sparser. You require a static whole-network topology analysis rather than identifying which TFs interact with specific pathways at specific time points.

skills.search_text: inverse-normal-transformation-of-pvalues Use when combining non-independent p-values (e.g. correlated methylation promoter/track p-values within a genomic interval) and you need a valid Stouffer-style combination: convert p to Z with qnorm(1 - p/2), then decorrelate using the Cholesky factor of Sigma. P-values are already independent — plain Stouffer/Fisher combination suffices and Cholesky whitening is unnecessary Sigma is not symmetric positive-definite (e.g. too few samples relative to correlated features) — chol() will fail and the whitening is invalid P-values are one-sided or have unknown directionality — the Phi^{-1}(1 - p/2) two-sided mapping would miscode the effect direction http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3940 Transforms two-sided p-values into signed Z-scores via the inverse normal CDF (Phi^{-1}(1 - p/2), qnorm in R) and, when the p-values are correlated as in SMITE's methylation contexts, whitens them with the inverse Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix (Sigma = C^T C) so the resulting Z* scores are approximately independent and can be combined as if from independent experiments. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-017-1477-3

When no matched negative control dataset exists, since DiNAMO is a discriminative method requiring a positive/control FASTA pair When the motif of interest is position-variable but must be modeled as a PWM/probability matrix rather than an IUPAC consensus (e.g. MEME-style EM discovery is expected instead) When searching only exact (non-degenerate) string motifs — the paper notes exact-string tools like RSAT exist, and DiNAMO's advantage lies in degenerate IUPAC motifs http://edamontology.org/topic_0160 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Exhaustive discovery of over-represented degenerate IUPAC DNA motifs between a positive (signal) and negative (control) FASTA dataset using DiNAMO, which builds an IUPAC motif lattice, simplifies it with mutual information, and filters by Holm-Bonferroni-adjusted Fisher's exact test (default P-value threshold 0.05). epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2215-1

skills.name: iupac-lattice-construction
skills.search_text: iupac-lattice-construction Use when you need to enumerate all degenerate IUPAC motifs of a given length L (e.g., 6-mers for TFBS discovery) from counted L-mers of DNA sequences, ensuring no candidate motif is missed. You are searching for motifs with unrestricted positions in sequences where a scanning-window enumeration is too costly and a heuristic/EM approach (MEME, Weeder, HOMER) is acceptable — this skill is specific to exact IUPAC enumeration Motifs are not of fixed length L, or you cannot tolerate the degeneracy cap d — the lattice is built only for motifs of a fixed length bounded by the degenerate-letter threshold You need PSSM/frequency-matrix motif models rather than discrete IUPAC consensus motifs http://edamontology.org/topic_3125 Constructs the exact lattice of degenerate IUPAC motifs of length L by generalizing all L-mers observed in a positive dataset position by position along the 4-level IUPAC character hierarchy, keeping only motifs whose every exact instance exists in the L-mer hashtable. This is DiNAMO's core mechanism for exploring the full motif space without heuristic restriction. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2215-1
skills.summary: Constructs the exact lattice of degenerate IUPAC motifs of length L by generalizing all L-mers observed in a positive dataset position by position along the 4-level IUPAC character hierarchy, keeping only motifs whose every exact instance exists in the L-mer hashtable. This is DiNAMO's core mechanism for exploring the full motif space without heuristic restriction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are searching for motifs with unrestricted positions in sequences where a scanning-window enumeration is too costly and a heuristic/EM approach (MEME, Weeder, HOMER) is acceptable — this skill is specific to exact IUPAC enumeration Motifs are not of fixed length L, or you cannot tolerate the degeneracy cap d — the lattice is built only for motifs of a fixed length bounded by the degenerate-letter threshold You need PSSM/frequency-matrix motif models rather than discrete IUPAC consensus motifs

skills.description: Use when you have an IUPAC motif lattice built from a positive and a negative FASTA dataset and need to score, rank, and prune over-represented degenerate motifs without bias toward occurrence count.
skills.name: iupac-motif-lattice-simplification
skills.search_text: iupac-motif-lattice-simplification Use when you have an IUPAC motif lattice built from a positive and a negative FASTA dataset and need to score, rank, and prune over-represented degenerate motifs without bias toward occurrence count. You need statistical significance assessment rather than dominance-based pruning — DiNAMO applies Fisher's exact test with Holm–Bonferroni adjustment as a separate downstream filtering step The input is raw unfiltered reads rather than a lattice whose motifs have all instances present in the positive dataset — the final lattice contains exactly the IUPAC motifs whose instances are all present in the positive dataset, so it must be built first You need position-specific motif search via expectation maximization (e.g. MEME-style) instead of exhaustive discriminative IUPAC enumeration http://edamontology.org/topic_0160 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Simplifies the DiNAMO IUPAC motif lattice by ranking all candidate degenerate motifs with a mutual-information (MI) objective function computed from per-node 2x2 contingency tables, then greedily retaining non-dominated motifs. MI captures motif–dataset dependency independently of occurrence count, unlike Fisher's exact test P-value, so short degenerate ancestors do not outrank their specific descendants. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2215-1
skills.summary: Simplifies the DiNAMO IUPAC motif lattice by ranking all candidate degenerate motifs with a mutual-information (MI) objective function computed from per-node 2x2 contingency tables, then greedily retaining non-dominated motifs. MI captures motif–dataset dependency independently of occurrence count, unlike Fisher's exact test P-value, so short degenerate ancestors do not outrank their specific descendants.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need statistical significance assessment rather than dominance-based pruning — DiNAMO applies Fisher's exact test with Holm–Bonferroni adjustment as a separate downstream filtering step The input is raw unfiltered reads rather than a lattice whose motifs have all instances present in the positive dataset — the final lattice contains exactly the IUPAC motifs whose instances are all present in the positive dataset, so it must be built first You need position-specific motif search via expectation maximization (e.g. MEME-style) instead of exhaustive discriminative IUPAC enumeration

skills.description: Use when each candidate degenerate IUPAC motif carries a 2x2 contingency table (a,b,c,d counts in positive/negative datasets) and you need an occurrence-count-independent score such as MI for ranking or lattice simplification.
skills.name: joint-probability-estimation
skills.search_text: joint-probability-estimation Use when each candidate degenerate IUPAC motif carries a 2x2 contingency table (a,b,c,d counts in positive/negative datasets) and you need an occurrence-count-independent score such as MI for ranking or lattice simplification. You only need a statistical significance call rather than a rank/score — use DiNAMO's Fisher's exact test with Holm–Bonferroni adjustment instead, which is the paper's downstream filtering step The lattice has not been built yet and L-mer counts/contingency tables are unavailable — MI estimation cannot proceed without the per-motif contingency tables Motifs are not represented as degenerate IUPAC models with all instances present in the positive dataset (e.g. PWM/EM approaches like MEME), since the contingency-table-based MI is defined for this exact IUPAC lattice http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Estimate joint probabilities p(O_i, C_j) between binary motif presence/absence (O) and dataset condition (C: positive vs negative) from 2x2 contingency tables attached to each vertex of the IUPAC motif lattice, then compute mutual information MI(O;C) to score motifs independently of their occurrence count. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2215-1
skills.summary: Estimate joint probabilities p(O_i, C_j) between binary motif presence/absence (O) and dataset condition (C: positive vs negative) from 2x2 contingency tables attached to each vertex of the IUPAC motif lattice, then compute mutual information MI(O;C) to score motifs independently of their occurrence count.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need a statistical significance call rather than a rank/score — use DiNAMO's Fisher's exact test with Holm–Bonferroni adjustment instead, which is the paper's downstream filtering step The lattice has not been built yet and L-mer counts/contingency tables are unavailable — MI estimation cannot proceed without the per-motif contingency tables Motifs are not represented as degenerate IUPAC models with all instances present in the positive dataset (e.g. PWM/EM approaches like MEME), since the contingency-table-based MI is defined for this exact IUPAC lattice

The dataset has no matched scRNA-seq reference available for anchor-based label transfer, so no labels exist to overlay on the ATAC embedding The goal is quantitative comparison of embedding quality (e.g., connectivity-index benchmarking against LSA/cisTopic) rather than visual presentation — the t-SNE panel is a qualitative output The analysis requires scaling to ~a million cells, where t-SNE visualization becomes impractical even though SnapATAC itself scales via the ensemble Nyström method http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Projects cell-type labels transferred from a scRNA-seq reference onto the scATAC-seq t-SNE embedding computed by SnapATAC's runViz, producing a joint RNA/ATAC visualization panel (e.g., PBMC_ATAC_RNA.png). skills.description: Use when calling or benchmarking chromatin loops from pooled scHi-C contact matrices: run Juicer HiCCUPS on .hic files built from ~371-cell mESC halves at 10KB resolution under both default and optimal parameters, then score replicate overlap against SnapHiC.
skills.name: juicer-hiccups-loop-detection
skills.search_text: juicer-hiccups-loop-detection Use when calling or benchmarking chromatin loops from pooled scHi-C contact matrices: run Juicer HiCCUPS on .hic files built from ~371-cell mESC halves at 10KB resolution under both default and optimal parameters, then score replicate overlap against SnapHiC. Only raw per-cell contact lists are available with no aggregated .hic matrix — HiCCUPS runs on .hic files, so the SnapHiC 'bin rwr' + 'hic' steps must build the pooled matrix first Loops must be called from individual sparse scHi-C cells without pooling — the paper benchmarks SnapHiC (50.8% reproducibility) as superior to pooled HiCCUPS (38.7–39.7%) on such data The goal is cell-type-specific loop discovery from single-nucleus methyl-3C-seq (e.g., 2,869 human prefrontal cortical cells) — the paper applies SnapHiC there, not the HiCCUPS baseline http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Runs Juicer's HiCCUPS loop caller on pseudo-bulk .hic contact matrices built from pooled single-cell Hi-C contacts; in the SnapHiC paper it is the pooled-baseline benchmark run on two 371-cell mESC halves (mm10, 10KB bins) with default and optimal parameters, yielding 38.7%/39.7% replicate loop reproducibility versus SnapHiC's 50.8%. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41592-021-01231-2
skills.summary: Runs Juicer's HiCCUPS loop caller on pseudo-bulk .hic contact matrices built from pooled single-cell Hi-C contacts; in the SnapHiC paper it is the pooled-baseline benchmark run on two 371-cell mESC halves (mm10, 10KB bins) with default and optimal parameters, yielding 38.7%/39.7% replicate loop reproducibility versus SnapHiC's 50.8%.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only raw per-cell contact lists are available with no aggregated .hic matrix — HiCCUPS runs on .hic files, so the SnapHiC 'bin rwr' + 'hic' steps must build the pooled matrix first Loops must be called from individual sparse scHi-C cells without pooling — the paper benchmarks SnapHiC (50.8% reproducibility) as superior to pooled HiCCUPS (38.7–39.7%) on such data The goal is cell-type-specific loop discovery from single-nucleus methyl-3C-seq (e.g., 2,869 human prefrontal cortical cells) — the paper applies SnapHiC there, not the HiCCUPS baseline

skills.name: kmeans-trajectory-clustering
skills.search_text: kmeans-trajectory-clustering Use when a normalized feature-by-donor abundance matrix (peaks or genes) has samples ordered by age and you need to detect and classify features showing genuine monotonic or non-monotonic temporal trends over adult lifespan. skills.description: Use when preparing uPBM training data for DNAffinity's random-forest regressor: 35-mer affinities are dominated by weak binders and the PWM-defined high-affinity motif must be emphasized (10x weight) after MEME-based trimming.
skills.name: kmer-undersampling-for-affinity-training-sets
skills.search_text: kmer-undersampling-for-affinity-training-sets Use when preparing uPBM training data for DNAffinity's random-forest regressor: 35-mer affinities are dominated by weak binders and the PWM-defined high-affinity motif must be emphasized (10x weight) after MEME-based trimming. Input is gcPBM or HT-SELEX data: those techniques use different preprocessing (gcPBM `proteins/{protein}/{protein}_{concentration}.txt` plus `_freq_matrix_6.txt`; HT-SELEX cycle files with SVM removal of inconsistent enrichments between cycles), not uPBM MEME-trimming plus undersampling/weighting. The `{protein}_training.txt` file is already the preprocessed template consumed by `upbm_regressor.py` (e.g. test_data `Gata4_training.txt`) — launch the regressor directly instead of re-balancing. The goal is in vivo TFBS discovery in yeast (DNAffinity predictions combined with yeast G1 nucleosome maps) rather than rebuilding an in vitro uPBM training set. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Balances uPBM 35-mer affinity training sets before DNAffinity random-forest training by undersampling low-affinity k-mers and giving 10x weight to sequences matching the PWM-derived high-affinity motif, after trimming to the MEME-derived motif region. This keeps the regression focused on the informative high-affinity regime and reproduces the paper's benchmark R2 = 0.69 ± 0.17 across 66 mouse TFs. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkac708

This keeps the regression focused on the informative high-affinity regime and reproduces the paper's benchmark R2 = 0.69 ± 0.17 across 66 mouse TFs.
