skills.description: Use when multi-region tumour epiallele presence/absence profiles (post purity correction) need to be converted into an evolutionary tree relating tumour regions and matched normal tissue.
skills.name: newick-tree-export
skills.search_text: newick-tree-export Use when multi-region tumour epiallele presence/absence profiles (post purity correction) need to be converted into an evolutionary tree relating tumour regions and matched normal tissue. Epiallele profiles have not been decontaminated — normal tissue contamination (parameter rho) must first be estimated and profiles corrected and clipped to [0,1] Reads cannot be phased between disjoint loci, so this tree inference is unsuitable when the goal requires phasing epialleles across distant loci Only one tumour sample region is available — the method requires multiple tissue samples to build pairwise distance matrices http://edamontology.org/topic_3292 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Infers a tumour phylogenetic tree from decontaminated epiallele profiles by averaging per-locus Euclidean distance matrices across samples and fitting a balanced minimum evolution tree with fastme.bal (ape R package), exported in Newick format. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-017-1753-2
skills.summary: Infers a tumour phylogenetic tree from decontaminated epiallele profiles by averaging per-locus Euclidean distance matrices across samples and fitting a balanced minimum evolution tree with fastme.bal (ape R package), exported in Newick format.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Epiallele profiles have not been decontaminated — normal tissue contamination (parameter rho) must first be estimated and profiles corrected and clipped to [0,1] Reads cannot be phased between disjoint loci, so this tree inference is unsuitable when the goal requires phasing epialleles across distant loci Only one tumour sample region is available — the method requires multiple tissue samples to build pairwise distance matrices

skills.description: Use when fitting CscoreTool-M's probabilistic sub-compartment model (Ci, alpha, beta) to Hi-C interaction data and you need to reproduce or re-implement its non-convex likelihood optimization and convergence loop.
skills.name: newton-based-maximum-likelihood-parameter-updating
skills.search_text: newton-based-maximum-likelihood-parameter-updating Use when fitting CscoreTool-M's probabilistic sub-compartment model (Ci, alpha, beta) to Hi-C interaction data and you need to reproduce or re-implement its non-convex likelihood optimization and convergence loop. Input is not Hi-C interaction data (e.g. ChIP-seq or RNA-seq counts); CscoreTool-M's likelihood model is defined over Hi-C summary interactions Genomic windows are not equal-length with a defined Rabl position (relative centromere-telomere coordinate); the Rabl-effect term of the model cannot be specified You only need simple compartment calls (A/B) rather than multiple probabilistic sub-compartments within a cell population CscoreTool-M's maximum-likelihood optimization loop for Hi-C sub-compartment inference: it sequentially solves convex sub-problems for the per-window sub-compartment probabilities Ci on each chromosome using a primal-dual interior point method with Newton search as the inner solver, then updates alpha and beta by Newton updates, iterating until the likelihood converges to a local maximum. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad314
skills.summary: CscoreTool-M's maximum-likelihood optimization loop for Hi-C sub-compartment inference: it sequentially solves convex sub-problems for the per-window sub-compartment probabilities Ci on each chromosome using a primal-dual interior point method with Newton search as the inner solver, then updates alpha and beta by Newton updates, iterating until the likelihood converges to a local maximum.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not Hi-C interaction data (e.g. ChIP-seq or RNA-seq counts); CscoreTool-M's likelihood model is defined over Hi-C summary interactions Genomic windows are not equal-length with a defined Rabl position (relative centromere-telomere coordinate); the Rabl-effect term of the model cannot be specified You only need simple compartment calls (A/B) rather than multiple probabilistic sub-compartments within a cell population

skills.description: Use when fitting penalized GAM-type regression models (e.g. smooth functions of genomic position s(x) on ChIP-Seq counts) where the Hessian of the penalized negative-binomial likelihood is sparse and a direct sparse solve is preferable to forming the inverse.
skills.name: newton-raphson-maximum-likelihood-optimization
skills.search_text: newton-raphson-maximum-likelihood-optimization Use when fitting penalized GAM-type regression models (e.g. smooth functions of genomic position s(x) on ChIP-Seq counts) where the Hessian of the penalized negative-binomial likelihood is sparse and a direct sparse solve is preferable to forming the inverse. The analysis requires data-driven smoothing hyperparameter estimation by cross-validation — fixing lambda and theta (as in the vignette fit) skips that objective estimation The target is position-wise significance testing (computeSignificance()) or plotting (plotGenoGAM()); those are downstream steps operating on an already-fitted GenoGAM object The problem is dense (no exploitable sparsity in the Hessian), in which case the SuperLU sparse direct solver offers no advantage http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Fits the penalized negative-binomial generalized additive model per genomic tile in GenoGAM 2.0 via Newton-Raphson iteration, solving the sparse linear system with the SuperLU direct solver so the inverse Hessian is never formed. This exploitation of model sparsity is what makes whole-genome fits (ca. 300 million parameters) tractable. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2238-7
skills.summary: Fits the penalized negative-binomial generalized additive model per genomic tile in GenoGAM 2.0 via Newton-Raphson iteration, solving the sparse linear system with the SuperLU direct solver so the inverse Hessian is never formed. This exploitation of model sparsity is what makes whole-genome fits (ca. 300 million parameters) tractable.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis requires data-driven smoothing hyperparameter estimation by cross-validation — fixing lambda and theta (as in the vignette fit) skips that objective estimation The target is position-wise significance testing (computeSignificance()) or plotting (plotGenoGAM()); those are downstream steps operating on an already-fitted GenoGAM object The problem is dense (no exploitable sparsity in the Hessian), in which case the SuperLU sparse direct solver offers no advantage

skills.description: Use when raw single- or pair-ended FASTQ datasets for one or more NGS assays must be processed reproducibly end-to-end via Nextflow, or when comparing pipeline runtime/user-input burden against alternatives.
skills.name: nextflow-workflow-execution
skills.search_text: nextflow-workflow-execution Use when raw single- or pair-ended FASTQ datasets for one or more NGS assays must be processed reproducibly end-to-end via Nextflow, or when comparing pipeline runtime/user-input burden against alternatives. You need to run only a subset of tools rather than an entire workflow — the article states 'CIPHER currently only runs entire workflows, but we are aware that individuals may prefer to use only a subset of tools'. You need to mix single-ended and pair-ended data in one run — the README warns 'DO NOT MIX AND MATCH SINGLE AND PAIR ENDED DATA INTO THE SAME CONFIG FILE. CIPHER DOES NOT HANDLE THIS USE-CASE YET.' You need multi-factor or time-series RNA-seq differential designs — CIPHER's RNA-seq pipeline is largely optimized for two-type experimental designs (e.g. WT versus KO). http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Execute CIPHER's Nextflow-based NGS workflow platform (ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, DNase-seq, MNase-seq, ATAC-seq, GRO-seq) with containerization, running entire pipelines from raw FASTQ evaluation through QC, peak calling, or differential expression with parallel dataset processing. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-017-1770-1
skills.summary: Execute CIPHER's Nextflow-based NGS workflow platform (ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, DNase-seq, MNase-seq, ATAC-seq, GRO-seq) with containerization, running entire pipelines from raw FASTQ evaluation through QC, peak calling, or differential expression with parallel dataset processing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to run only a subset of tools rather than an entire workflow — the article states 'CIPHER currently only runs entire workflows, but we are aware that individuals may prefer to use only a subset of tools'. You need to mix single-ended and pair-ended data in one run — the README warns 'DO NOT MIX AND MATCH SINGLE AND PAIR ENDED DATA INTO THE SAME CONFIG FILE. CIPHER DOES NOT HANDLE THIS USE-CASE YET.' You need multi-factor or time-series RNA-seq differential designs — CIPHER's RNA-seq pipeline is largely optimized for two-type experimental designs (e.g. WT versus KO).

skills.description: Use when an aligner-evaluation experiment needs synthetic bisulfite-seq FASTQ read sets with a controlled per-base error rate (e.g. 0%, 1%, 2%) and known genomic origin, so mapping quality can be scored against ground truth.
skills.name: ngs-error-model-parameterization
skills.search_text: ngs-error-model-parameterization Use when an aligner-evaluation experiment needs synthetic bisulfite-seq FASTQ read sets with a controlled per-base error rate (e.g. 0%, 1%, 2%) and known genomic origin, so mapping quality can be scored against ground truth. The evaluation requires real experimental read data (e.g. a WGBS dataset like GEO GSE80911) rather than simulated reads with a known ground truth. The aligner under test is not a bisulfite-seq aligner — Sherman generates bisulfite-treated reads that would not exercise normal aligner behavior. Only alignment throughput/scalability is being measured and error-rate-dependent accuracy is irrelevant; a single simulated or real read set suffices. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 Parameterize an NGS sequencing-error model by simulating bisulfite-treated reads with Sherman at controlled error rates (0%, 1%, 2%) so that aligner accuracy (mappability, precision, sensitivity, accuracy) can be evaluated against a known ground truth. In the BiSpark study this produced three simulated read sets from human chromosome 1 (hg19) that served as shared input for mapping-quality and alignment-time reproductions. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2498-2
skills.summary: Parameterize an NGS sequencing-error model by simulating bisulfite-treated reads with Sherman at controlled error rates (0%, 1%, 2%) so that aligner accuracy (mappability, precision, sensitivity, accuracy) can be evaluated against a known ground truth. In the BiSpark study this produced three simulated read sets from human chromosome 1 (hg19) that served as shared input for mapping-quality and alignment-time reproductions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The evaluation requires real experimental read data (e.g. a WGBS dataset like GEO GSE80911) rather than simulated reads with a known ground truth. skills.description: Use when multiple nucleosome-positioning methods have been run on the same ATAC-seq and/or MNase-seq data and their predicted nucleosome calls must be compared on an identical validation set using AUPR.
skills.name: nucleosome-positioning-aupr-evaluation
skills.search_text: nucleosome-positioning-aupr-evaluation Use when multiple nucleosome-positioning methods have been run on the same ATAC-seq and/or MNase-seq data and their predicted nucleosome calls must be compared on an identical validation set using AUPR. Only a single method's nucleosome predictions are available with no baseline calls (e.g. NucleoATAC or DANPOS2) to compare against The validation annotations differ between methods being compared — AUPR is only interpretable when all methods are scored on the identical validation set The goal is comparing DNA-binding-factor (TF) binding site predictions rather than nucleosome positioning; that requires ChIP-chip/ChIP-exo/ORGANIC annotations instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmarking protocol for comparing predicted nucleosome positions from multiple chromatin-occupancy methods (e.g. RoboCOP with ATAC-seq or MNase+ATAC, DANPOS2, NucleoATAC) by computing nucleosome-position AUPR against a common high-precision validation set, such as chemical-cleavage annotations in S. cerevisiae. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab553
skills.summary: Benchmarking protocol for comparing predicted nucleosome positions from multiple chromatin-occupancy methods (e.g. RoboCOP with ATAC-seq or MNase+ATAC, DANPOS2, NucleoATAC) by computing nucleosome-position AUPR against a common high-precision validation set, such as chemical-cleavage annotations in S. cerevisiae.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single method's nucleosome predictions are available with no baseline calls (e.g. NucleoATAC or DANPOS2) to compare against The validation annotations differ between methods being compared — AUPR is only interpretable when all methods are scored on the identical validation set The goal is comparing DNA-binding-factor (TF) binding site predictions rather than nucleosome positioning; that requires ChIP-chip/ChIP-exo/ORGANIC annotations instead

skills.description: Use when a genome-wide nucleosome positioning prediction (dyad calls or occupancy-derived dyads) must be validated quantitatively against gold-standard chemical-cleavage dyad annotations, e.g. reproducing Figure 4C.
skills.name: nucleosome-positioning-benchmarking-against-chemical-cleavage-annotations
skills.search_text: nucleosome-positioning-benchmarking-against-chemical-cleavage-annotations Use when a genome-wide nucleosome positioning prediction (dyad calls or occupancy-derived dyads) must be validated quantitatively against gold-standard chemical-cleavage dyad annotations, e.g. reproducing Figure 4C. Validating transcription factor (DBF) binding site predictions, which are benchmarked against ChIP-chip, ChIP-exo, and ORGANIC annotations rather than chemical-cleavage dyads The input is raw MNase-seq reads with no dyad predictions extracted yet — first run RoboCOP occupancy inference before benchmarking dyads Benchmarking ATAC-seq-based predictions against MNase-specific dyad score expectations, since the article reports markedly better performance with MNase-seq than ATAC-seq http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_3176 http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 Benchmarks computationally predicted nucleosome dyad positions (e.g., from RoboCOP_MNase) against high-precision chemical-cleavage dyad annotations (Brogaard et al., ref 24) using precision-recall analysis over a 50 bp match tolerance. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab553
skills.summary: Benchmarks computationally predicted nucleosome dyad positions (e.g., from RoboCOP_MNase) against high-precision chemical-cleavage dyad annotations (Brogaard et al., ref 24) using precision-recall analysis over a 50 bp match tolerance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Validating transcription factor (DBF) binding site predictions, which are benchmarked against ChIP-chip, ChIP-exo, and ORGANIC annotations rather than chemical-cleavage dyads The input is raw MNase-seq reads with no dyad predictions extracted yet — first run RoboCOP occupancy inference before benchmarking dyads Benchmarking ATAC-seq-based predictions against MNase-specific dyad score expectations, since the article reports markedly better performance with MNase-seq than ATAC-seq

skills.description: Use when reproducing or sanity-checking the motif-scanning sensitivity of a BOM/FIMO CRE classification workflow, e.g. verifying that ~83% of CRE nucleotides are annotated at q<=0.5 before ablation or retraining.
skills.name: nucleotide-annotation-fraction-quantification
skills.search_text: nucleotide-annotation-fraction-quantification Use when reproducing or sanity-checking the motif-scanning sensitivity of a BOM/FIMO CRE classification workflow, e.g. verifying that ~83% of CRE nucleotides are annotated at q<=0.5 before ablation or retraining. Input is already a per-sequence motif-count feature table or trained model — this skill only quantifies raw annotation coverage from coordinates and a motif library. The analysis requires motif order, orientation, or spacing information — BOM's representation is explicitly unordered counts of motifs, independent of grammar. The genome or motif library differs from mm10/gimme.vertebrate.v5.0.meme without revalidating the coverage expectation — the ~83% figure is dataset- and library-specific. http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Quantifies the fraction of CRE nucleotides covered by at least one FIMO motif annotation at escalating q-value cutoffs (0.1, 0.3, 0.5), using the gimme.vertebrate.v5.0.meme library and BOM pipeline. It serves as a sensitivity check that motif-scan sensitivity is sufficient before motif-count features are used for classification. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-65362-2
skills.summary: Quantifies the fraction of CRE nucleotides covered by at least one FIMO motif annotation at escalating q-value cutoffs (0.1, 0.3, 0.5), using the gimme.vertebrate.v5.0.meme library and BOM pipeline. It serves as a sensitivity check that motif-scan sensitivity is sufficient before motif-count features are used for classification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a per-sequence motif-count feature table or trained model — this skill only quantifies raw annotation coverage from coordinates and a motif library. The analysis requires motif order, orientation, or spacing information — BOM's representation is explicitly unordered counts of motifs, independent of grammar. The genome or motif library differs from mm10/gimme.vertebrate.v5.0.meme without revalidating the coverage expectation — the ~83% figure is dataset- and library-specific.

skills.description: Use when converting fixed-length 41-nt DNA sequences (A/C/G/T) into per-position binary features for the csDMA 6mA classifier, when Motif and Kmer features alone underperform, or when a purely chemical-dichotomy encoding of nucleotides is needed.
skills.name: nucleotide-chemical-dichotomy-encoding
skills.search_text: nucleotide-chemical-dichotomy-encoding Use when converting fixed-length 41-nt DNA sequences (A/C/G/T) into per-position binary features for the csDMA 6mA classifier, when Motif and Kmer features alone underperform, or when a purely chemical-dichotomy encoding of nucleotides is needed. Input sequences are not 41 nt or contain ambiguous bases beyond A/C/G/T, since the three dichotomy rules only partition A, C, G, and T. Input is already a numeric feature table (e.g. existing Kmer/Motif matrix or precomputed binary features) — re-encoding would duplicate features rather than add the dichotomy representation. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Binary nucleotide encoding scheme from csDMA that turns each nucleotide of a 41-nt DNA 6mA sample into three chemical-dichotomy indicators (purine/pyrimidine, A/T vs C/G, A/C vs G/T), producing a 3 × 41 = 123-element feature vector per sequence. It is one of the three feature blocks (Motif, Kmer, Binary) whose combination gave csDMA's best feature-subset AUC of 0.871. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-019-49430-4
skills.summary: Binary nucleotide encoding scheme from csDMA that turns each nucleotide of a 41-nt DNA 6mA sample into three chemical-dichotomy indicators (purine/pyrimidine, A/T vs C/G, A/C vs G/T), producing a 3 × 41 = 123-element feature vector per sequence. It is one of the three feature blocks (Motif, Kmer, Binary) whose combination gave csDMA's best feature-subset AUC of 0.871.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences are not 41 nt or contain ambiguous bases beyond A/C/G/T, since the three dichotomy rules only partition A, C, G, and T. Input is already a numeric feature table (e.g. existing Kmer/Motif matrix or precomputed binary features) — re-encoding would duplicate features rather than add the dichotomy representation.

skills.description: Use when comparing motif discovery tools (e.g. DiNAMO vs MEME-CHIP, HOMER, Discrover) on data where ground-truth implanted motifs exist and per-nucleotide recovery quality must be quantified.
skills.name: nucleotide-level-correlation-coefficient-evaluation
skills.search_text: nucleotide-level-correlation-coefficient-evaluation Use when comparing motif discovery tools (e.g. DiNAMO vs MEME-CHIP, HOMER, Discrover) on data where ground-truth implanted motifs exist and per-nucleotide recovery quality must be quantified. Real datasets with no known implanted ground-truth motifs — nCC against implanted motifs cannot be computed Evaluating tools on motif properties other than nucleotide-level recovery (e.g. runtime, memory) where the article reports separate metrics (Table 3) Motif lengths other than the benchmarked L=6 without re-validating the pipeline http://edamontology.org/topic_0160 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark DNA motif discovery tools by implanting known IUPAC motifs into synthetic positive/control FASTA pairs and scoring each tool's predicted motifs with the nucleotide level correlation coefficient (nCC), the metric used to show DiNAMO outperforming MEME-CHIP, HOMER and Discrover on degenerate motifs. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2215-1
skills.summary: Benchmark DNA motif discovery tools by implanting known IUPAC motifs into synthetic positive/control FASTA pairs and scoring each tool's predicted motifs with the nucleotide level correlation coefficient (nCC), the metric used to show DiNAMO outperforming MEME-CHIP, HOMER and Discrover on degenerate motifs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Real datasets with no known implanted ground-truth motifs — nCC against implanted motifs cannot be computed Evaluating tools on motif properties other than nucleotide-level recovery (e.g. runtime, memory) where the article reports separate metrics (Table 3) Motif lengths other than the benchmarked L=6 without re-validating the pipeline

skills.description: Use when converting labeled DNA sequences (e.g., FASTA of 41-nt 6mA positives/negatives) into a fixed-length numeric feature matrix via k-mer relative-frequency encoding before classifier training.
skills.name: nucleotide-pattern-counting
skills.search_text: nucleotide-pattern-counting Use when converting labeled DNA sequences (e.g., FASTA of 41-nt 6mA positives/negatives) into a fixed-length numeric feature matrix via k-mer relative-frequency encoding before classifier training. Input is already a numeric feature matrix or the downstream model expects motif/binary encodings rather than k-mer frequencies Sequences vary widely in length and window-count normalization by k-mer length would distort relative frequencies (csDMA uses fixed 41-nt samples) http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Encodes fixed-length DNA sequences (e.g., 41-nt 6mA benchmark samples) by computing relative frequencies of contiguous k-mer nucleotide patterns; in csDMA, k=2,3,4 yields 16+64+256=336 features per sample. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-019-49430-4
skills.summary: Encodes fixed-length DNA sequences (e.g., 41-nt 6mA benchmark samples) by computing relative frequencies of contiguous k-mer nucleotide patterns; in csDMA, k=2,3,4 yields 16+64+256=336 features per sample.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a numeric feature matrix or the downstream model expects motif/binary encodings rather than k-mer frequencies Sequences vary widely in length and window-count normalization by k-mer length would distort relative frequencies (csDMA uses fixed 41-nt samples)

skills.description: Use when testing whether genomic ranges (peaks, QTLs, CREs) show significant enrichment or correlation with features (genes, cell types) and a null that preserves local genomic correlation structure is required.
skills.name: null-distribution-hypothesis-testing
skills.search_text: null-distribution-hypothesis-testing Use when testing whether genomic ranges (peaks, QTLs, CREs) show significant enrichment or correlation with features (genes, cell types) and a null that preserves local genomic correlation structure is required. When simple random shuffling/permutation of ranges is sufficient and computational cost must be minimized — though note shuffling may yield overly narrow null distributions and over-estimated significance When the input is not genomic ranges or range-associated statistics (e.g., a feature table without coordinates), since bootRanges requires GRanges input http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Generates null sets of genomic ranges via segmented block bootstrap (bootRanges/nullranges) to test whether observed range-based statistics — overlap enrichment or cross-omic correlations — exceed a genomic-structure-aware null. Used here to show observed gene-peak correlations in 10x single-cell multiome data (0.33) far exceed the bootstrap null (0.007). epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad190
skills.summary: Generates null sets of genomic ranges via segmented block bootstrap (bootRanges/nullranges) to test whether observed range-based statistics — overlap enrichment or cross-omic correlations — exceed a genomic-structure-aware null. Used here to show observed gene-peak correlations in 10x single-cell multiome data (0.33) far exceed the bootstrap null (0.007).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When simple random shuffling/permutation of ranges is sufficient and computational cost must be minimized — though note shuffling may yield overly narrow null distributions and over-estimated significance When the input is not genomic ranges or range-associated statistics (e.g., a feature table without coordinates), since bootRanges requires GRanges input

skills.description: Use when testing enrichment of overlap between two genomic range sets (e.g., ATAC-seq caQTL peaks and GWAS SNPs) and you need to compare block-bootstrap vs. shuffling nulls via z scores of the overlap rate.
skills.name: null-distribution-z-score-computation
skills.search_text: null-distribution-z-score-computation Use when testing enrichment of overlap between two genomic range sets (e.g., ATAC-seq caQTL peaks and GWAS SNPs) and you need to compare block-bootstrap vs. shuffling nulls via z scores of the overlap rate. When the analysis goal is optimizing DEG logFC thresholds via generalized splines on overlap counts (use the macrophage.R workflow instead) When comparing running time of bootRanges vs. GSC on genome-scale statistics (use bootranges_vs_GSC.R) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Compute z scores measuring how far an observed genomic range overlap statistic (e.g., liver caQTL peaks overlapping total cholesterol GWAS SNPs) falls from a null distribution generated by segmented block bootstrap (bootRanges) versus conventional shuffling, revealing that shuffling produces overly narrow nulls and inflated significance. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad190
skills.summary: Compute z scores measuring how far an observed genomic range overlap statistic (e.g., liver caQTL peaks overlapping total cholesterol GWAS SNPs) falls from a null distribution generated by segmented block bootstrap (bootRanges) versus conventional shuffling, revealing that shuffling produces overly narrow nulls and inflated significance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the analysis goal is optimizing DEG logFC thresholds via generalized splines on overlap counts (use the macrophage.R workflow instead) When comparing running time of bootRanges vs. GSC on genome-scale statistics (use bootranges_vs_GSC.R)

skills.description: Use when testing enrichment/overlap of genomic ranges (e.g. caQTLs, CREs, differential peaks) where naive shuffling or permutation would over-estimate statistical significance due to genomic correlation.
skills.name: null-range-generation-for-enrichment-testing
skills.search_text: null-range-generation-for-enrichment-testing Use when testing enrichment/overlap of genomic ranges (e.g. caQTLs, CREs, differential peaks) where naive shuffling or permutation would over-estimate statistical significance due to genomic correlation. When the analysis goal permits conventional shuffling/permutation and genomic correlation structure is not a concern — the paper shows shuffling can yield overly narrow null distributions, but bootRanges is specifically the alternative for correlated genomic data When benchmarking running time against GSC — this skill covers null range generation, not the bootranges_vs_GSC.R timing comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Generates null sets of genomic ranges via segmented block bootstrap (bootRanges from the nullranges R/Bioconductor package) to test enrichment of query ranges against a genome segmentation, preserving local genomic correlation structure instead of using shuffling or permutation. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad190
skills.summary: Generates null sets of genomic ranges via segmented block bootstrap (bootRanges from the nullranges R/Bioconductor package) to test enrichment of query ranges against a genome segmentation, preserving local genomic correlation structure instead of using shuffling or permutation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the analysis goal permits conventional shuffling/permutation and genomic correlation structure is not a concern — the paper shows shuffling can yield overly narrow null distributions, but bootRanges is specifically the alternative for correlated genomic data When benchmarking running time against GSC — this skill covers null range generation, not the bootranges_vs_GSC.R timing comparison

skills.description: Use when implementing or re-deriving a probabilistic model of Hi-C interaction counts that requires a centromere-telomere (Rabl) positional term, bias factors, and sub-compartment probability products feeding a Poisson likelihood.
skills.name: numerical-model-implementation
skills.search_text: numerical-model-implementation Use when implementing or re-deriving a probabilistic model of Hi-C interaction counts that requires a centromere-telomere (Rabl) positional term, bias factors, and sub-compartment probability products feeding a Poisson likelihood. The analysis targets cis interactions or single-cell Hi-C rather than population-level trans-interaction counts modeled by the Rabl term Observed reads fall in ENCODE blacklisted regions or span regions with translocations listed in ExcludedInteractions.txt, which the model excludes from both counts and expectations Only a two-compartment (A/B) assignment is needed and no sub-compartment probability model is required http://edamontology.org/topic_3420 Implements the CscoreTool-M generative model for Hi-C trans interactions: a Rabl-effect modifier Rij = 1 + alpha*ri*rj + beta*(ri+rj)*ri*rj combined with window biases Bi/Bj and sub-compartment probabilities to yield expected counts Fij evaluated under a Poisson log-likelihood. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad314
skills.summary: Implements the CscoreTool-M generative model for Hi-C trans interactions: a Rabl-effect modifier Rij = 1 + alpha*ri*rj + beta*(ri+rj)*ri*rj combined with window biases Bi/Bj and sub-compartment probabilities to yield expected counts Fij evaluated under a Poisson log-likelihood.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis targets cis interactions or single-cell Hi-C rather than population-level trans-interaction counts modeled by the Rabl term Observed reads fall in ENCODE blacklisted regions or span regions with translocations listed in ExcludedInteractions.txt, which the model excludes from both counts and expectations Only a two-compartment (A/B) assignment is needed and no sub-compartment probability model is required

skills.description: Use when the goal is to benchmark or extrapolate dimensionality-reduction scalability of scATAC-seq data beyond the available cell count (e.g., 20k-80k measured cells up to a simulated 1M cells) using the ensemble Nyström approximation.
skills.name: nystrom-approximation-large-scale-simulation
skills.search_text: nystrom-approximation-large-scale-simulation Use when the goal is to benchmark or extrapolate dimensionality-reduction scalability of scATAC-seq data beyond the available cell count (e.g., 20k-80k measured cells up to a simulated 1M cells) using the ensemble Nyström approximation. The dataset is small enough (<~100k cells) that an exact eigendecomposition of the Jaccard matrix is feasible and approximation error is not worth trading off Input is already a peak-based feature matrix or the analysis requires population-level peak annotation prior to clustering, which is the design SnapATAC's bin-based Jaccard/Nyström path avoids The environment cannot satisfy the original SnapATAC runtime constraints (Python >= 2.7 & < 3.0 for SnapTools; R >= 3.4.0 & < 3.6.0 because 3.6 breaks the rhdf5 package) — use SnapATAC2 instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Applies the ensemble Nyström method within SnapATAC to approximate dimensionality reduction of the cell-by-cell Jaccard similarity matrix, enabling runtime-scaling benchmarks and simulated 1M-cell scATAC-seq analysis on regular hardware. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-21583-9
skills.summary: Applies the ensemble Nyström method within SnapATAC to approximate dimensionality reduction of the cell-by-cell Jaccard similarity matrix, enabling runtime-scaling benchmarks and simulated 1M-cell scATAC-seq analysis on regular hardware.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is small enough (<~100k cells) that an exact eigendecomposition of the Jaccard matrix is feasible and approximation error is not worth trading off Input is already a peak-based feature matrix or the analysis requires population-level peak annotation prior to clustering, which is the design SnapATAC's bin-based Jaccard/Nyström path avoids The environment cannot satisfy the original SnapATAC runtime constraints (Python >= 2.7 & < 3.0 for SnapTools; R >= 3.4.0 & < 3.6.0 because 3.6 breaks the rhdf5 package) — use SnapATAC2 instead

skills.description: Use when you have ChIP-seq peak/occupancy data for many transcription factors and need to partition regions into HOT, MILD and COLD percentile classes to test whether apparent high occupancy correlates with control or artifact signal.
skills.name: occupancy-class-stratification
skills.search_text: occupancy-class-stratification Use when you have ChIP-seq peak/occupancy data for many transcription factors and need to partition regions into HOT, MILD and COLD percentile classes to test whether apparent high occupancy correlates with control or artifact signal. The analysis goal is calling individual TF peaks or motifs rather than comparing signal enrichment between occupancy classes Input is already a per-class feature/enrichment table with no underlying bigWig signal or region intervals to extract from The ChIP-seq data lack matched mock/IgG control experiments, so class-wise artifact signal cannot be assessed http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Stratifies genomic regions into occupancy classes — HOT (top >99th percentile of transcription factor binding events), MILD (75th–99th) and COLD (<75th) — so that per-class enrichment of ChIP-seq signal (e.g., IgG mock controls) can be computed and compared to test whether high occupancy reflects ChIP-seq artifacts. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz460
skills.summary: Stratifies genomic regions into occupancy classes — HOT (top >99th percentile of transcription factor binding events), MILD (75th–99th) and COLD (<75th) — so that per-class enrichment of ChIP-seq signal (e.g., IgG mock controls) can be computed and compared to test whether high occupancy reflects ChIP-seq artifacts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is calling individual TF peaks or motifs rather than comparing signal enrichment between occupancy classes Input is already a per-class feature/enrichment table with no underlying bigWig signal or region intervals to extract from The ChIP-seq data lack matched mock/IgG control experiments, so class-wise artifact signal cannot be assessed

skills.description: Use when you have a time-course expression dataset (e.g. GSE6865 B. subtilis) plus a candidate regulon list and need to infer direct regulator–target interactions with an ODE model rather than correlation or co-expression methods.
skills.name: ode-based-gene-regulation-model-fitting
skills.search_text: ode-based-gene-regulation-model-fitting Use when you have a time-course expression dataset (e.g. GSE6865 B. subtilis) plus a candidate regulon list and need to infer direct regulator–target interactions with an ODE model rather than correlation or co-expression methods. The dataset is a single-sample or steady-state expression profile with no time dimension, since the ODE model requires a continuous expression time series You need a fully validated method for eukaryotic regulatory networks without caution — the paper states Genexpi was designed for bacterial regulons and eukaryotic use requires care Genes whose expression does not change over the time course or are explainable by the constant-synthesis model — these must be filtered out before model fitting, not fitted as targets http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Fit Genexpi's ordinary-differential-equation regulation model to smoothed time-course expression profiles to infer which candidate regulators (e.g. sigma factors) control each gene, using simulated annealing parameter search in an OpenCL core. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2138-x
skills.summary: Fit Genexpi's ordinary-differential-equation regulation model to smoothed time-course expression profiles to infer which candidate regulators (e.g. sigma factors) control each gene, using simulated annealing parameter search in an OpenCL core.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is a single-sample or steady-state expression profile with no time dimension, since the ODE model requires a continuous expression time series You need a fully validated method for eukaryotic regulatory networks without caution — the paper states Genexpi was designed for bacterial regulons and eukaryotic use requires care Genes whose expression does not change over the time course or are explainable by the constant-synthesis model — these must be filtered out before model fitting, not fitted as targets

skills.description: Use when inferring regulatory interactions from time-course gene expression data and per-gene ODE parameters (synthesis rate, decay rate, regulator weights) must be fitted to a sigmoidal activation model, e.g. Bacillus subtilis SigA regulon with GSE6865 series.
skills.name: ode-model-parameter-fitting
skills.search_text: ode-model-parameter-fitting Use when inferring regulatory interactions from time-course gene expression data and per-gene ODE parameters (synthesis rate, decay rate, regulator weights) must be fitted to a sigmoidal activation model, e.g. Bacillus subtilis SigA regulon with GSE6865 series. Genes whose expression does not change significantly over the whole time range — the no-change model excludes them as the Genexpi model contains no information for them Genes fitted adequately by the constant synthesis model (w = 0, large b) — they must be excluded as targets since any regulator could fit them http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 Fit Genexpi's ODE regulation model — mRNA synthesis dz/dt = k1*f(rho) - k2*z with a logistic (sigmoidal) activation of regulator inputs and a per-gene decay rate — to smoothed time-course expression data, yielding per-gene/regulator parameters (k1, k2, b, weights) and a fit-quality score. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2138-x
skills.summary: Fit Genexpi's ODE regulation model — mRNA synthesis dz/dt = k1*f(rho) - k2*z with a logistic (sigmoidal) activation of regulator inputs and a per-gene decay rate — to smoothed time-course expression data, yielding per-gene/regulator parameters (k1, k2, b, weights) and a fit-quality score.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Genes whose expression does not change significantly over the whole time range — the no-change model excludes them as the Genexpi model contains no information for them Genes fitted adequately by the constant synthesis model (w = 0, large b) — they must be excluded as targets since any regulator could fit them

skills.description: Use when time-course gene expression profiles must be fitted with an ODE regulatory model to decide which candidate gene–regulator interactions are real, as in Genexpi/CyGenexpi regulon inference.
skills.name: ode-parameter-fitting-simulated-annealing
skills.search_text: ode-parameter-fitting-simulated-annealing Use when time-course gene expression profiles must be fitted with an ODE regulatory model to decide which candidate gene–regulator interactions are real, as in Genexpi/CyGenexpi regulon inference. The gene's expression does not change significantly over the whole time range — the Genexpi model contains no information for such genes and they are excluded as regulators and targets. The gene is better explained by the constant synthesis model — such genes are excluded as targets because any regulator can fit them with w = 0 and large b. Eukaryotic data involving transcription factors that regulate in complexes (e.g. MBP1, SWI4, SWI6), which breaks Genexpi's expected single-regulator model and yields random-indistinguishable results. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_2258 Fits Genexpi's ordinary differential equation model of gene regulation to smoothed time-course expression data by minimizing the error function with simulated annealing in OpenCL, running 128 annealing runs per gene–regulator set with regularization r(beta) and a fit-quality threshold of 0.8. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2138-x
skills.summary: Fits Genexpi's ordinary differential equation model of gene regulation to smoothed time-course expression data by minimizing the error function with simulated annealing in OpenCL, running 128 annealing runs per gene–regulator set with regularization r(beta) and a fit-quality threshold of 0.8.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The gene's expression does not change significantly over the whole time range — the Genexpi model contains no information for such genes and they are excluded as regulators and targets. The gene is better explained by the constant synthesis model — such genes are excluded as targets because any regulator can fit them with w = 0 and large b. Eukaryotic data involving transcription factors that regulate in complexes (e.g. MBP1, SWI4, SWI6), which breaks Genexpi's expected single-regulator model and yields random-indistinguishable results.

skills.description: Use when validating a ranked list of predicted cis driver genes (e.g., iEDGE Rank-1 genes from amplifications/deletions) against curated cancer driver compendia to confirm that top-ranked genes are enriched for known oncogenes or tumor suppressors.
skills.name: oncogene-tumor-suppressor-classification
skills.search_text: oncogene-tumor-suppressor-classification Use when validating a ranked list of predicted cis driver genes (e.g., iEDGE Rank-1 genes from amplifications/deletions) against curated cancer driver compendia to confirm that top-ranked genes are enriched for known oncogenes or tumor suppressors. The candidate driver list has no alteration-direction information (amplification vs deletion), so OG/TN labels cannot be assigned to reference genes The goal is pathway-level annotation of cis/trans effects, which is handled by iEDGE's run_hyperEnrichment pathway enrichment module rather than driver-database overlap testing Validation target is functional essentiality against genetic screens (DepMap), not enrichment in curated driver compendia http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Validates iEDGE-predicted cis drivers by classifying reference driver genes by alteration direction — amplified genes as candidate oncogenes (OG), deleted genes as candidate tumor suppressors (TN) — and testing whether Rank-1 cis genes are enriched for known drivers from TUSON, OMIM, COSMIC CGC, and UniProt using one-sided Fisher exact tests. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-019-52886-z
skills.summary: Validates iEDGE-predicted cis drivers by classifying reference driver genes by alteration direction — amplified genes as candidate oncogenes (OG), deleted genes as candidate tumor suppressors (TN) — and testing whether Rank-1 cis genes are enriched for known drivers from TUSON, OMIM, COSMIC CGC, and UniProt using one-sided Fisher exact tests.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The candidate driver list has no alteration-direction information (amplification vs deletion), so OG/TN labels cannot be assigned to reference genes The goal is pathway-level annotation of cis/trans effects, which is handled by iEDGE's run_hyperEnrichment pathway enrichment module rather than driver-database overlap testing Validation target is functional essentiality against genetic screens (DepMap), not enrichment in curated driver compendia

skills.summary: Retrieve hg19 genomic sequence in successive (1 Mb + bin) sliding windows with pysam/pybedtools and one-hot encode the A/C/G/T bases into the 4-channel input format required by deepC, which predicts chromatin interactions from megabase-scale DNA sequence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a one-hot encoded sequence track or numeric feature matrix rather than raw hg19 FASTA plus interval coordinates The target sequence is not A/C/G/T reference DNA (e.g. pre-collapsed consensus, protein, or multi-base variant haplotypes) where single-base one-hot encoding does not apply The downstream model expects a different window length or base alphabet than deepC's (1 Mb + bin) windows of A/C/G/T

skills.search_text: one-sided-fisher-gene-set-enrichment Use when validating a ranked or predicted driver gene list by testing its overlap against a curated functional gene set, e.g., reproducing the P = 3.53e-5 enrichment of BRCA Rank-1 cis genes among amplification-driven dependency genes. The gene list has not been ranked or filtered by a driver-prediction step (e.g., iEDGE mediation analysis), so enrichment lacks a meaningful hypothesis The gene universe (ntotal) or set membership is undefined, since Fisher exact counts depend critically on the correct background The functional gene set is already the same compendium used to build the driver list, making enrichment circular http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Tests whether a candidate driver gene list (e.g., iEDGE Rank-1 cis genes from TCGA breast cancer) is significantly over-represented in a functional gene set (e.g., amplification-driven DepMap dependency genes) using a one-sided Fisher exact / hypergeometric test as implemented in iEDGE's run_hyperEnrichment. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-019-52886-z

skills.when_to_use_negative: The gene list has not been ranked or filtered by a driver-prediction step (e.g., iEDGE mediation analysis), so enrichment lacks a meaningful hypothesis The gene universe (ntotal) or set membership is undefined, since Fisher exact counts depend critically on the correct background The functional gene set is already the same compendium used to build the driver list, making enrichment circular

skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is driver discovery from patient tumor data (iEDGE's cis/trans DE + Sobel mediation analysis on TCGA SCNA/expression), not in-silico validation against cell-line dependency screens Dependency and copy-number matrices cannot be paired by common cell lines, so the per-gene regression of dependency on copy number is not well defined Testing amplification only is inappropriate — for deletion-driven dependencies the one-sided 'alpha < 0' alternative would need to be reversed, which this skill does not cover as specified

skills.description: Use when raw ONT FAST5 current signals must be converted into per-base translocation times (seconds per genomic position) for sequencing-speed or non-B DNA structure analyses.
skills.name: ont-signal-event-segmentation
skills.search_text: ont-signal-event-segmentation Use when raw ONT FAST5 current signals must be converted into per-base translocation times (seconds per genomic position) for sequencing-speed or non-B DNA structure analyses. Input is already basecalled FASTQ or a pre-computed event table with fixed block strides — Albacore's fixed stride assumption is precisely what Tombo re-squiggling is meant to overcome The analysis targets base modifications detected directly from current signal rather than translocation timing No reference genome is available, since Tombo re-squiggling requires a reference (hg38.fa) to correct spurious variation and segment events http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Reconstructs per-base translocation times from raw Oxford Nanopore FAST5 current signals by basecalling with Albacore and re-squiggling with Tombo, then computing each position's duration as the ratio of current measurements to the ONT sampling rate. This converts raw signal into per-position translocation times suitable for downstream non-B DNA modelling. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad220
skills.summary: Reconstructs per-base translocation times from raw Oxford Nanopore FAST5 current signals by basecalling with Albacore and re-squiggling with Tombo, then computing each position's duration as the ratio of current measurements to the ONT sampling rate. This converts raw signal into per-position translocation times suitable for downstream non-B DNA modelling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already basecalled FASTQ or a pre-computed event table with fixed block strides — Albacore's fixed stride assumption is precisely what Tombo re-squiggling is meant to overcome The analysis targets base modifications detected directly from current signal rather than translocation timing No reference genome is available, since Tombo re-squiggling requires a reference (hg38.fa) to correct spurious variation and segment events

skills.description: Use when you have a 10 kb-binned .cool/.hic Hi-C matrix (e.g., GM12878) and need to benchmark predicted loops against enrichment-based callers or validate loop sets against orthogonal data such as H3K27ac HiChIP or ENCODE ChIP-Seq peaks.
skills.name: orthogonal-loop-validation-enrichment-assessment
skills.search_text: orthogonal-loop-validation-enrichment-assessment Use when you have a 10 kb-binned .cool/.hic Hi-C matrix (e.g., GM12878) and need to benchmark predicted loops against enrichment-based callers or validate loop sets against orthogonal data such as H3K27ac HiChIP or ENCODE ChIP-Seq peaks. Very low sequencing depth (e.g., 1.5% down-sample rate): Fit-Hi-C yields no interactions at q < 1e-5 and the cutoff must be relaxed to 0.1, so the standard comparison is not reproducible Enrichment-only questions where supervised benchmarking is unnecessary (e.g., you only need one caller's loops without overlap/validation assessment) Platforms lacking dedicated loop-detection algorithms or compatible formats, such as DNA SPRITE matrices Compares supervised (Peakachu) chromatin loop calls against enrichment-based methods (HiCCUPS, Fit-Hi-C) on the same 10 kb Hi-C matrix, building a three-way Venn overlap and computing method-specific validation ratios against orthogonal ChIA-PET/HiChIP/ChIP-Seq evidence. It quantifies that Peakachu recovers a unique, well-validated loop set (72% overlap, 58% vs 48%/40% validation). epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-17239-9
skills.summary: Compares supervised (Peakachu) chromatin loop calls against enrichment-based methods (HiCCUPS, Fit-Hi-C) on the same 10 kb Hi-C matrix, building a three-way Venn overlap and computing method-specific validation ratios against orthogonal ChIA-PET/HiChIP/ChIP-Seq evidence. It quantifies that Peakachu recovers a unique, well-validated loop set (72% overlap, 58% vs 48%/40% validation).

skills.summary: Validates cross-species regulatory element mappings (e.g., AdaLiftOver SNP-to-target maps) by checking that a known human promoter SNP lands in the orthologous mouse promoter region, using reciprocal-best UCSC chain liftOver plus epigenomic and sequence-grammar scoring as the mapping engine.

skills.description: Use when you need to identify orthologous non-coding regulatory elements across species (e.g., human-mouse or rat-human ENCODE ChIP-seq/DNase-seq peaks) and existing sequence-conservation liftOver suffers from multi-mapping, low precision, or low mapping rate.
skills.name: orthologous-region-mapping-chip-seq
skills.search_text: orthologous-region-mapping-chip-seq Use when you need to identify orthologous non-coding regulatory elements across species (e.g., human-mouse or rat-human ENCODE ChIP-seq/DNase-seq peaks) and existing sequence-conservation liftOver suffers from multi-mapping, low precision, or low mapping rate. The query regions are coding sequences or the species pair has no available UCSC reciprocal-best chain file or BSgenome object. No orthologous epigenomic datasets exist for the species pair, so epigenomic signal similarity cannot be computed and parameters cannot be trained. The task is simple synteny-based coordinate conversion of uniquely mappable regions where candidate prioritization is unnecessary — plain UCSC liftOver suffices. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Maps query regulatory regions (e.g., ChIP-seq / DNase-seq peaks) from one species to orthologous target regions in another using AdaLiftOver, which extends query regions via the UCSC liftOver framework and prioritizes candidates by epigenomic signal and sequence grammar similarity. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad149
skills.summary: Maps query regulatory regions (e.g., ChIP-seq / DNase-seq peaks) from one species to orthologous target regions in another using AdaLiftOver, which extends query regions via the UCSC liftOver framework and prioritizes candidates by epigenomic signal and sequence grammar similarity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query regions are coding sequences or the species pair has no available UCSC reciprocal-best chain file or BSgenome object. No orthologous epigenomic datasets exist for the species pair, so epigenomic signal similarity cannot be computed and parameters cannot be trained. skills.search_text: overdispersion-estimation-from-replicates Use when calling enriched CLIP/eCLIP windows from tiled transcriptomic or repetitive-element windows, where per-window read-start counts in IP and matched input are available and counts are overdispersed and GC-biased. skills.description: Use when quantifying significance of an observed SNP–peak (or range–range) overlap against block-bootstrapped null ranges, i.e. when per-bootstrap overlap rates, their variance, and a z-score are needed.
skills.name: overlap-rate-variance-estimation
skills.search_text: overlap-rate-variance-estimation Use when quantifying significance of an observed SNP–peak (or range–range) overlap against block-bootstrapped null ranges, i.e. when per-bootstrap overlap rates, their variance, and a z-score are needed. The null sets come from conventional shuffling or permutation rather than block bootstrapping, since those schemes may produce overly narrow null distributions and over-estimated significance. The goal is threshold optimization or DEG–peak overlap counts (macrophage.R with generalized spline fitting) rather than SNP–peak overlap-rate significance testing. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Computes the proportion of SNPs with a peak overlap within a 10 kb window (the overlap rate), the variance of this rate across block-bootstrapped null sets, and a z-score standardizing the observed rate against the bootRanges null distribution. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad190
skills.summary: Computes the proportion of SNPs with a peak overlap within a 10 kb window (the overlap rate), the variance of this rate across block-bootstrapped null sets, and a z-score standardizing the observed rate against the bootRanges null distribution.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The null sets come from conventional shuffling or permutation rather than block bootstrapping, since those schemes may produce overly narrow null distributions and over-estimated significance. skills.description: Use when a set of null genomic range iterations (from bootRanges block bootstrap or conventional shuffling) must be converted into an overlap-rate statistic with variance and z-score for false-positive-rate or significance assessment.
skills.name: overlap-statistic-zscore-computation
skills.search_text: overlap-statistic-zscore-computation Use when a set of null genomic range iterations (from bootRanges block bootstrap or conventional shuffling) must be converted into an overlap-rate statistic with variance and z-score for false-positive-rate or significance assessment. The goal is generating the null range sets themselves rather than scoring them — use bootRanges (segBootranges.R) or bootstrap.R first; this skill only computes the overlap-rate statistic. The analysis requires overlap counts for threshold optimization (e.g. DEG logFC thresholds with generalized splines in macrophage.R) rather than overlap-rate variance/z-score significance testing. Input is not genomic ranges or the comparison target lacks a defined overlap definition (e.g. continuous genome-scale statistics compared for running time in bootranges_vs_GSC.R). http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Computes the rate of overlap between two genomic range sets (e.g. null-bootstrapped ranges and observed ranges), its variance across null iterations, and a z-score statistic, as implemented in var.R from the bootRanges paper. This statistic is what allows calibrated (bootRanges block bootstrap) vs over-narrow (shuffling) null distributions to be compared at a nominal alpha threshold. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad190
skills.summary: Computes the rate of overlap between two genomic range sets (e.g. null-bootstrapped ranges and observed ranges), its variance across null iterations, and a z-score statistic, as implemented in var.R from the bootRanges paper. This statistic is what allows calibrated (bootRanges block bootstrap) vs over-narrow (shuffling) null distributions to be compared at a nominal alpha threshold.

skills.search_text: overlapping-regional-element-clustering-crem Use when StitchIt has produced REMs per gene (from paired DNase1-seq and RNA-seq samples) and you need to consolidate overlapping or directly adjacent REMs into CREMs with unique IDs for database-level annotation or counting. Input is a set of peaks or REMs not derived from the StitchIt gene-centric linear model (e.g. plain DNase1-seq peak calls), where overlap-merging into EpiRegio CREMs would not correspond to the published definition You need cell type- or tissue-specific REM activity rather than consolidated CREM loci — EpiRegio's Cell type score and Cell type DNase1 signal operate at the REM level Groups REMs inferred by the StitchIt algorithm into Clusters of Regulatory EleMents (CREMs) by merging REMs that overlap or are directly adjacent, assigning each CREM a unique ID. skills.description: Use when integrating p-values/scores from multiple genomic assays whose distributions occupy different ranges — e.g. before SMITE scorePval — and you need scores comparable to a reference (expression) without changing within-feature ranking.
skills.name: p-value-distribution-normalization
skills.search_text: p-value-distribution-normalization Use when integrating p-values/scores from multiple genomic assays whose distributions occupy different ranges — e.g. before SMITE scorePval — and you need scores comparable to a reference (expression) without changing within-feature ranking. Input data are raw effect sizes or unannotated assay outputs rather than p-values already attached to genes via annotateExpression/annotateModification — normalizePval expects a populated PvalueAnnotation. You need to change cross-feature ranking or apply non-monotonic calibration; the rescale method is monotonic by design and cannot reorder scores within a modification-context pairing. Only a single data type is present and no cross-type comparability problem exists — distribution rescaling against a reference is unnecessary. http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Normalizes component p-value distributions from different data types (expression, methylation promoter/body, H3K4me1) onto a common reference scale using SMITE's logit-transform + rescale pipeline, while preserving the rank order of scores so downstream module detection compares features fairly. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-017-1477-3
skills.summary: Normalizes component p-value distributions from different data types (expression, methylation promoter/body, H3K4me1) onto a common reference scale using SMITE's logit-transform + rescale pipeline, while preserving the rank order of scores so downstream module detection compares features fairly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data are raw effect sizes or unannotated assay outputs rather than p-values already attached to genes via annotateExpression/annotateModification — normalizePval expects a populated PvalueAnnotation. You need to change cross-feature ranking or apply non-monotonic calibration; the rescale method is monotonic by design and cannot reorder scores within a modification-context pairing. Only a single data type is present and no cross-type comparability problem exists — distribution rescaling against a reference is unnecessary.

skills.description: Use when comparing stability of consensus subgroup classifications on a gene expression matrix — e.g., judging whether row sampling outperforms column sampling, or whether ATC/skmeans yields more consistent partitions than alternatives.

skills.search_text: pac-clustering-stability-evaluation Use when comparing stability of consensus subgroup classifications on a gene expression matrix — e.g., judging whether row sampling outperforms column sampling, or whether ATC/skmeans yields more consistent partitions than alternatives. skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw unprocessed expression data — missing values, outliers, and low-variance rows must be handled by adjust_matrix() before partitioning, so raw stability comparisons are not meaningful ScRNA-Seq datasets with several thousands of cells, where cola runtime and memory usage may be unacceptable The goal is detecting very small clusters — downsampling (row/column sampling) may miss small cell clusters, so PAC-based stability on sampled partitions can be misleading

skills.description: Use when validating that a method's scientific conclusions do not depend on its tunable parameters — e.g., sweeping DNA fragment size and window size in RECOGNICER and checking whether total domain length and read counts remain stable.
skills.name: parameter-sensitivity-analysis
skills.search_text: parameter-sensitivity-analysis Use when validating that a method's scientific conclusions do not depend on its tunable parameters — e.g., sweeping DNA fragment size and window size in RECOGNICER and checking whether total domain length and read counts remain stable. The goal is assessing sensitivity to sequencing depth rather than model parameters — the paper handles depth robustness by random downsampling of reads, not by parameter sweeps. The analysis goal is calling domains with one fixed, recommended configuration rather than testing robustness — RECOGNICER defaults (FRAGMENT_SIZE=150, WINDOW_SIZE=200) should simply be used. The user intends to tune the many internal coarse-graining parameters beyond fragment/window size, which the README strongly discourages ('strongly NOT recommended to change other parameters'). http://edamontology.org/topic_3674 Sweeps tunable model parameters of a computational method (here RECOGNICER's FRAGMENT_SIZE and WINDOW_SIZE for ChIP-seq broad domain calling) and tabulates an output summary metric per setting to demonstrate robustness or sensitivity, as done for human CD4+ T cell H3K27me3 Chromosome 1 data. epigenomics/v2 10.1007/s40484-020-0225-2

skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is assessing sensitivity to sequencing depth rather than model parameters — the paper handles depth robustness by random downsampling of reads, not by parameter sweeps. The analysis goal is calling domains with one fixed, recommended configuration rather than testing robustness — RECOGNICER defaults (FRAGMENT_SIZE=150, WINDOW_SIZE=200) should simply be used. skills.description: Use when a scored sequence set (e.g. FASTA with sequence scores in headers) plus a JASPAR motif library must be tested for motif enrichment at each position relative to an anchor (TSS, other motifs) while controlling for GC bias.
skills.name: partial-correlation-covariate-control
skills.search_text: partial-correlation-covariate-control Use when a scored sequence set (e.g. FASTA with sequence scores in headers) plus a JASPAR motif library must be tested for motif enrichment at each position relative to an anchor (TSS, other motifs) while controlling for GC bias. The goal is de novo motif recognition/assembly — MEPP currently only functions with a fixed motif library, and de novo motif assembly is left to future work. Position-agnostic motif enrichment is sufficient (e.g. ZOOPs-style presence/absence tests as in HOMER or MEIRLOP) — the positional partial-correlation machinery adds no value there. No continuous biological score is available per sequence — the partial Pearson correlation requires a scored sequence vector, not binary labels alone. Computes MEPP's positional enrichment profile by calculating, at each heatmap position column, the partial Pearson correlation (pXY·Z) of the motif score matrix against the sequence score vector while regressing out per-sequence GC content, then deriving permutation-based confidence intervals and Benjamini-Yekutieli-corrected P-values. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nargab/lqac075
skills.summary: Computes MEPP's positional enrichment profile by calculating, at each heatmap position column, the partial Pearson correlation (pXY·Z) of the motif score matrix against the sequence score vector while regressing out per-sequence GC content, then deriving permutation-based confidence intervals and Benjamini-Yekutieli-corrected P-values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is de novo motif recognition/assembly — MEPP currently only functions with a fixed motif library, and de novo motif assembly is left to future work. Position-agnostic motif enrichment is sufficient (e.g. ZOOPs-style presence/absence tests as in HOMER or MEIRLOP) — the positional partial-correlation machinery adds no value there. No continuous biological score is available per sequence — the partial Pearson correlation requires a scored sequence vector, not binary labels alone.

skills.description: Use when estimating gene-expression vs drug-response associations from pharmacogenomic data (CCLE-style expression, copy number, mutation, and pharmacology profiles) where CNV effects and confounding mutations (kinase/tumor-suppressor genes) must be adjusted before correlation.
skills.name: partial-correlation-drug-response-analysis
skills.search_text: partial-correlation-drug-response-analysis Use when estimating gene-expression vs drug-response associations from pharmacogenomic data (CCLE-style expression, copy number, mutation, and pharmacology profiles) where CNV effects and confounding mutations (kinase/tumor-suppressor genes) must be adjusted before correlation. No mutation or copy-number data are available for the cohort, so confounders cannot be identified or CNV effects regressed out — plain correlation would be mislabeled as confounder-adjusted. The goal is downstream transcriptional-regulator selection (uniP/multiP/GSEA) rather than gene-level drug-response association estimation — use the later RePhine steps instead. Reliable target/ChIP-seq information is absent — the article notes RePhine overall 'is restricted to the cases where reliable target information is available' (relevant when extending this step to TR identification). http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 RePhine's Step 1 module that estimates noise- and confounder-robust gene–drug associations: expression is first adjusted for copy number by linear-regression residuals, drug-response mutation confounders are selected with an adaptive lasso plus likelihood ratio test, and per-gene partial correlations (computed with the R ppcor package) quantify CNV-adjusted expression vs drug response (e.g., PLX4720 in CCLE). epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2019.09.008
skills.summary: RePhine's Step 1 module that estimates noise- and confounder-robust gene–drug associations: expression is first adjusted for copy number by linear-regression residuals, drug-response mutation confounders are selected with an adaptive lasso plus likelihood ratio test, and per-gene partial correlations (computed with the R ppcor package) quantify CNV-adjusted expression vs drug response (e.g., PLX4720 in CCLE).
skills.when_to_use_negative: No mutation or copy-number data are available for the cohort, so confounders cannot be identified or CNV effects regressed out — plain correlation would be mislabeled as confounder-adjusted. The goal is downstream transcriptional-regulator selection (uniP/multiP/GSEA) rather than gene-level drug-response association estimation — use the later RePhine steps instead. Reliable target/ChIP-seq information is absent — the article notes RePhine overall 'is restricted to the cases where reliable target information is available' (relevant when extending this step to TR identification).

skills.description: Use when per-sample A/B compartment scores must be computed from Hi-C contact maps (resolutions down to 5-10 kb) and full eigen-decomposition is infeasible due to memory limits on large chromosome matrices.
skills.name: partial-svd-compartment-calling-on-filebacked-big-matrices
skills.search_text: partial-svd-compartment-calling-on-filebacked-big-matrices Use when per-sample A/B compartment scores must be computed from Hi-C contact maps (resolutions down to 5-10 kb) and full eigen-decomposition is infeasible due to memory limits on large chromosome matrices. Input is single-cell Hi-C without pseudo-bulk aggregation — single-cell contact maps are too sparse for reliable compartment identification; aggregate ~100+ cells per condition first The goal is comparing compartmentalization across multiple (>2) Hi-C datasets rather than calling compartments per sample — use dcHiC's quantile normalization and Mahalanobis-distance differential step instead Resolution finer than ~5 kb is required — the FBM-based partial SVD is validated up to 5-10 kb http://edamontology.org/topic_3912 Computes A/B compartment scores from Hi-C contact maps by distance-normalizing (observed/expected) each chromosome matrix, converting it to a correlation matrix, and running a parallelized partial SVD (only the first few singular vectors) over a memory-efficient Filebacked Big Matrix (FBM) via bigstatsr, with automated PC and sign selection based on GC content and gene density. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-34626-6
skills.summary: Computes A/B compartment scores from Hi-C contact maps by distance-normalizing (observed/expected) each chromosome matrix, converting it to a correlation matrix, and running a parallelized partial SVD (only the first few singular vectors) over a memory-efficient Filebacked Big Matrix (FBM) via bigstatsr, with automated PC and sign selection based on GC content and gene density.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is single-cell Hi-C without pseudo-bulk aggregation — single-cell contact maps are too sparse for reliable compartment identification; aggregate ~100+ cells per condition first The goal is comparing compartmentalization across multiple (>2) Hi-C datasets rather than calling compartments per sample — use dcHiC's quantile normalization and Mahalanobis-distance differential step instead Resolution finer than ~5 kb is required — the FBM-based partial SVD is validated up to 5-10 kb

skills.search_text: partition-jaccard-concordance-comparison Decision support for choosing the number of subgroups k from cola consensus partitioning results, when per-k consensus matrices and partitions are available and a reproducible, threshold-based k-selection rule is needed. Samples already have trusted subgroup labels, so no k-selection is needed Only a single k was tested — the Jaccard redundancy rule requires consecutive pairs of k values (k-1 vs k) The input is an scRNA-Seq dataset with several thousands of cells, where cola's runtime and memory usage may be unacceptable http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reconstructs cola's best-k selection decision procedure by computing four per-k metrics — 1-PAC (proportion of ambiguous pairs, with the 5% most unstable samples excluded), mean silhouette, partition-concordance, and consecutive-k Jaccard indices — and applying cola's three-rule decision procedure to choose the optimal number of subgroups. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa1146

skills.name: partition-size-imbalance-statistics
skills.search_text: partition-size-imbalance-statistics Use when a distributed Spark pipeline (e.g. BiSpark-style bisulfite alignment on WGBS FASTQ reads) shows uneven per-partition loads across executors, and you need to quantify imbalance and verify that hash-based re-partitioning balances record counts. Input is not distributed Spark RDD data (e.g. a single-node aligner output such as a Bismark SAM file) — partition-size balance statistics have no meaning there When the goal is alignment accuracy or mappability assessment rather than data-distribution skew across nodes When shuffling cost dominates and the pipeline is single-node: the paper notes load balancing and shuffling are a trade-off and it is hard to conclude theoretically whether performance would improve http://edamontology.org/topic_0769 A diagnostic skill for quantifying data skew across Spark RDD partitions during bisulfite read alignment, using per-partition record counts and max/min ratios before and after hash-partitioning re-distribution. skills.search_text: pc-selection-and-sign-orientation-with-genomic-features Use when computing A/B compartment scores from a Hi-C contact map and you need to decide which eigenvector (PC1 vs PC2) is the compartment component and which sign corresponds to the A-type compartment. skills.summary: Selects the principal component (PC1 or PC2) representing A/B compartments from a Hi-C contact map and orients its sign so compartment scores correlate positively with GC content and gene density, as implemented in dcHiC via a parallelized partial SVD on a Filebacked Big Matrix.

skills.description: Use when each sample contributes a windowed multi-variable profile over age (e.g., epigenomic/ATAC-seq or RNA-seq features in moving windows spanning ~10-20 years) and a multivariate test such as MANOVA needs a compact, low-dimensional representation of each window before testing.
skills.name: pca-based-dimensionality-reduction-of-windowed-profiles
skills.search_text: pca-based-dimensionality-reduction-of-windowed-profiles Use when each sample contributes a windowed multi-variable profile over age (e.g., epigenomic/ATAC-seq or RNA-seq features in moving windows spanning ~10-20 years) and a multivariate test such as MANOVA needs a compact, low-dimensional representation of each window before testing. The data are not ordered along a temporal/age axis, so there are no before/after windows to compare (e.g., a static cross-sectional feature table). The windowed profiles are already low-dimensional (fewer than ~4 variables per window), making PCA reduction unnecessary before MANOVA. The goal is differential analysis between sexes or cell types rather than detecting ages of rapid change along the lifespan. Reduces each age-windowed epigenomic profile from the PBMC aging time series to 3 principal components so that MANOVA can test age-related shifts in the breakpoint analysis. It is the intermediate step between moving-window profile extraction and MANOVA p-value computation in the trajectory/breakpoint pipeline of the Sexual-dimorphism in human immune system aging study (Nature Communications, 2020). epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-14396-9
skills.summary: Reduces each age-windowed epigenomic profile from the PBMC aging time series to 3 principal components so that MANOVA can test age-related shifts in the breakpoint analysis. It is the intermediate step between moving-window profile extraction and MANOVA p-value computation in the trajectory/breakpoint pipeline of the Sexual-dimorphism in human immune system aging study (Nature Communications, 2020).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are not ordered along a temporal/age axis, so there are no before/after windows to compare (e.g., a static cross-sectional feature table). The windowed profiles are already low-dimensional (fewer than ~4 variables per window), making PCA reduction unnecessary before MANOVA. The goal is differential analysis between sexes or cell types rather than detecting ages of rapid change along the lifespan.

Input is raw count data that has not passed QC and correlation filtering — ChromSCape normalizes and runs PCA only after quality control filtering of outlier cells Analysis goal is peak-level feature extraction with motif/topic models (e.g. CisTopic, SnapATAC, Cusanovich2018), which the article benchmarks as alternative featurization methods rather than PCA Regions have not been filtered (e.g. regions not detected in at least 1% of cells, or user-excluded BED regions such as CNV segments not yet removed) http://edamontology.org/topic_0204 Dimensionality reduction of filtered, normalized single-cell H3K27me3 scChIP-seq count matrices by PCA with centering, retaining the first 50 PCs as the feature space used downstream for clustering (ConsensusClusterPlus), visualization, and differential enrichment analysis in ChromSCape. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-19542-x
skills.summary: Dimensionality reduction of filtered, normalized single-cell H3K27me3 scChIP-seq count matrices by PCA with centering, retaining the first 50 PCs as the feature space used downstream for clustering (ConsensusClusterPlus), visualization, and differential enrichment analysis in ChromSCape.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw count data that has not passed QC and correlation filtering — ChromSCape normalizes and runs PCA only after quality control filtering of outlier cells Analysis goal is peak-level feature extraction with motif/topic models (e.g. CisTopic, SnapATAC, Cusanovich2018), which the article benchmarks as alternative featurization methods rather than PCA Regions have not been filtered (e.g. regions not detected in at least 1% of cells, or user-excluded BED regions such as CNV segments not yet removed)
