skills.name: roc-auc-binding-site-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-binding-site-evaluation Use when you need to quantify whether a triplex-prediction tool (e.g. 3plex, Triplexator) enriches real RNA:DNA binding peaks over matched negative regions, and to tier lncRNAs by AUC evidence. You lack a defined positive peak set or cannot generate length-matched negatives — AUC comparison is meaningless without both classes You only need raw triplex coordinates/annotations rather than a quantitative enrichment assessment of predictions against binding data Comparing against TriplexFPP CNN-based classifications, where the source study found no good agreement with 3plex predictions and missed known TPX-forming lncRNAs (CDKN2B-AS1, lncSmad7, MEG3, NEAT1, TERC) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3524 Evaluation strategy that scores triplex (TPX) prediction enrichment of experimentally determined lncRNA binding sites by computing ROC curves and AUC values for positive peaks versus matched shuffled genomic negatives, using the pROC R package with one-sided Mann-Whitney tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.05.016
skills.summary: Evaluation strategy that scores triplex (TPX) prediction enrichment of experimentally determined lncRNA binding sites by computing ROC curves and AUC values for positive peaks versus matched shuffled genomic negatives, using the pROC R package with one-sided Mann-Whitney tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You lack a defined positive peak set or cannot generate length-matched negatives — AUC comparison is meaningless without both classes You only need raw triplex coordinates/annotations rather than a quantitative enrichment assessment of predictions against binding data Comparing against TriplexFPP CNN-based classifications, where the source study found no good agreement with 3plex predictions and missed known TPX-forming lncRNAs (CDKN2B-AS1, lncSmad7, MEG3, NEAT1, TERC)

skills.description: Use when evaluating binary sgRNA high-activity classifiers (e.g., labeled via phenotype scores below -0.1 or activity scores above 0.75) and you need a threshold-independent ROC-AUC metric to compare prediction models.
skills.name: roc-auc-classification-scoring
skills.search_text: roc-auc-classification-scoring Use when evaluating binary sgRNA high-activity classifiers (e.g., labeled via phenotype scores below -0.1 or activity scores above 0.75) and you need a threshold-independent ROC-AUC metric to compare prediction models. The evaluation goal is ordinal/rank agreement on continuous activity scores rather than binary classification — use Spearman correlation instead, as the paper does for its regression schema (Fig. 3b). Ground-truth labels are not available for the held-out sgRNAs, so a supervised classification metric such as ROC-AUC cannot be computed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Scores sgRNA-activity classification performance with the area under the ROC curve (ROC-AUC) using scikit-learn, as done in EpiCas-DL to benchmark deep-learning models against Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, DeepHF, and C-RNNcrispr on independent CRISPRi/CRISPRoff/CRISPRa screening datasets. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.11.034
skills.summary: Scores sgRNA-activity classification performance with the area under the ROC curve (ROC-AUC) using scikit-learn, as done in EpiCas-DL to benchmark deep-learning models against Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, DeepHF, and C-RNNcrispr on independent CRISPRi/CRISPRoff/CRISPRa screening datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The evaluation goal is ordinal/rank agreement on continuous activity scores rather than binary classification — use Spearman correlation instead, as the paper does for its regression schema (Fig. 3b). Ground-truth labels are not available for the held-out sgRNAs, so a supervised classification metric such as ROC-AUC cannot be computed.

skills.description: Use when binary-classifying sgRNAs as highly active vs. inactive (e.g., phenotype score < −0.1 labeled '1') and you need cross-validated ROC-AUC comparison of a CNN against classical ML baselines on sequence-plus-epigenetic features.
skills.name: roc-auc-cross-validation-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-cross-validation-evaluation Use when binary-classifying sgRNAs as highly active vs. inactive (e.g., phenotype score < −0.1 labeled '1') and you need cross-validated ROC-AUC comparison of a CNN against classical ML baselines on sequence-plus-epigenetic features. The task is regression of continuous sgRNA activity scores (e.g., Spearman correlation) rather than binary highly-active/inactive classification Input sgRNAs lack positional coordinates or cell-type epigenetic tracks, so the 11 x 40 sequence-plus-epigenetic matrix cannot be assembled Evaluating on datasets outside CRISPRoff/CRISPRi/CRISPRa screening data where the phenotype-score cutoff and normalization were validated http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmark sgRNA activity prediction models by computing ROC-AUC under cross-validation on a 90%/10% train-test split, comparing a deep-learning model (e.g., EpiCas-DL CNN) against Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, DeepHF, and C-RNNcrispr baselines fit with scikit-learn. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.11.034
skills.summary: Benchmark sgRNA activity prediction models by computing ROC-AUC under cross-validation on a 90%/10% train-test split, comparing a deep-learning model (e.g., EpiCas-DL CNN) against Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, DeepHF, and C-RNNcrispr baselines fit with scikit-learn.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is regression of continuous sgRNA activity scores (e.g., Spearman correlation) rather than binary highly-active/inactive classification Input sgRNAs lack positional coordinates or cell-type epigenetic tracks, so the 11 x 40 sequence-plus-epigenetic matrix cannot be assembled Evaluating on datasets outside CRISPRoff/CRISPRi/CRISPRa screening data where the phenotype-score cutoff and normalization were validated

skills.description: Use when comparing how sensitively and accurately multiple methods (e.g., TSMiner vs clustering tools) recover a known positive set of pathways/TFs from time-series expression data, and a negative set can be defined.
skills.name: roc-auc-curve-analysis
skills.search_text: roc-auc-curve-analysis Use when comparing how sensitively and accurately multiple methods (e.g., TSMiner vs clustering tools) recover a known positive set of pathways/TFs from time-series expression data, and a negative set can be defined. Input lacks a defined positive reference set (e.g., no list of known LR-associated pathways or known TFs) — ROC/AUC against an arbitrary negative set is meaningless. The goal is to construct time-specific regulatory networks itself, not to evaluate detection sensitivity/accuracy across competing methods. Only one method's predictions exist with no comparable ranked predictions from other methods — there is no ranking to sweep thresholds over for a fair AUC comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmark sensitivity and accuracy of pathway-detection methods (TSMiner, DREM v2.0, hclust, k-means, STEM, WGCNA) by sweeping P-value thresholds 0–0.05 against known LR-associated pathways and building ROC curves with AUC against a defined negative pathway set. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: Benchmark sensitivity and accuracy of pathway-detection methods (TSMiner, DREM v2.0, hclust, k-means, STEM, WGCNA) by sweeping P-value thresholds 0–0.05 against known LR-associated pathways and building ROC curves with AUC against a defined negative pathway set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input lacks a defined positive reference set (e.g., no list of known LR-associated pathways or known TFs) — ROC/AUC against an arbitrary negative set is meaningless. The goal is to construct time-specific regulatory networks itself, not to evaluate detection sensitivity/accuracy across competing methods. Only one method's predictions exist with no comparable ranked predictions from other methods — there is no ranking to sweep thresholds over for a fair AUC comparison.

skills.description: Use when predictions of genomic binding regions must be scored against curated positive peaks and matched negative regions, and you need AUC comparison across parameter settings plus significance testing of parameter effects.
skills.name: roc-auc-evaluation-of-genomic-predictions
skills.search_text: roc-auc-evaluation-of-genomic-predictions Use when predictions of genomic binding regions must be scored against curated positive peaks and matched negative regions, and you need AUC comparison across parameter settings plus significance testing of parameter effects. When you need tool-vs-tool prediction agreement rather than accuracy against experimental peaks — the article notes no good agreement was found between 3plex and TriplexFPP predictions When your positives are not replicate-filtered peaks and negatives are not length-matched shuffled regions — the AUC comparison assumes the described evaluation-set construction http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Evaluates genomic interaction predictions (e.g. ssRNA:dsDNA triplex predictions from 3plex/Triplexator) by computing ROC curves and AUC values per parameter combination with the pROC R package, then testing which parameters (peak filtering method, minimal TPX length, ssRNA masking) affect accuracy via linear-model ANOVA and a 10,000-permutation randomisation test. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.05.016
skills.summary: Evaluates genomic interaction predictions (e.g. ssRNA:dsDNA triplex predictions from 3plex/Triplexator) by computing ROC curves and AUC values per parameter combination with the pROC R package, then testing which parameters (peak filtering method, minimal TPX length, ssRNA masking) affect accuracy via linear-model ANOVA and a 10,000-permutation randomisation test.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you need tool-vs-tool prediction agreement rather than accuracy against experimental peaks — the article notes no good agreement was found between 3plex and TriplexFPP predictions When your positives are not replicate-filtered peaks and negatives are not length-matched shuffled regions — the AUC comparison assumes the described evaluation-set construction

skills.description: Use when comparing tools that predict transcription factors from time-series expression data (e.g. liver-regeneration RNA-seq) and you must quantify sensitivity/accuracy against a curated list of known TFs.
skills.name: roc-auc-evaluation-of-tf-prediction
skills.search_text: roc-auc-evaluation-of-tf-prediction Use when comparing tools that predict transcription factors from time-series expression data (e.g. liver-regeneration RNA-seq) and you must quantify sensitivity/accuracy against a curated list of known TFs. The expression data are not time-series (TSMiner/DREM require time-course profiles to build tree-structure or time-specific models). No curated set of known TFs exists for the studied process, making recovery counting and ROC/AUC analysis impossible. The goal is clustering of expression modules rather than TF-level benchmarking — clustering tools cannot evaluate temporal dynamics of regulators. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Benchmark a time-specific regulatory network method (e.g. TSMiner vs DREM v2.0) on its ability to recover known LR-associated TFs, counting recovered and unique TFs at P-value cut-offs of 0.01 and 0.05 and computing sensitivity curves and ROC/AUC scores across P-value cut-offs spanning 0 to 1. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: Benchmark a time-specific regulatory network method (e.g. TSMiner vs DREM v2.0) on its ability to recover known LR-associated TFs, counting recovered and unique TFs at P-value cut-offs of 0.01 and 0.05 and computing sensitivity curves and ROC/AUC scores across P-value cut-offs spanning 0 to 1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The expression data are not time-series (TSMiner/DREM require time-course profiles to build tree-structure or time-specific models). No curated set of known TFs exists for the studied process, making recovery counting and ROC/AUC analysis impossible. The goal is clustering of expression modules rather than TF-level benchmarking — clustering tools cannot evaluate temporal dynamics of regulators.

skills.description: Use when a trained variant- or gene-prioritization classifier (positive disease variants/genes vs. negatives) must be validated, and discriminative performance on held-out or cross-validated test sets must be reported as ROC curves with AUC values.
skills.name: roc-auc-model-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-model-evaluation Use when a trained variant- or gene-prioritization classifier (positive disease variants/genes vs. negatives) must be validated, and discriminative performance on held-out or cross-validated test sets must be reported as ROC curves with AUC values. When the goal is ranking or prioritization output quality rather than binary discrimination — e.g. the iMEGES gene score evaluation compares disease vs non-disease genes but proxies come from imputed GWAS P-values where hits may be proxy markers, not causal variants When class labels are absent or unreliable (no positives of known disease variants/genes), since ROC/AUC requires labeled positive and negative sets When input is raw sequencing data (VCF/BED) rather than model scores or an already-trained classifier — run the ncDeepBrain variant score step first http://edamontology.org/topic_3399 Evaluates a trained deep learning prioritization model (e.g. iMEGES/ncDeepBrain) by ten-fold cross-validation, generating sensitivity-vs-specificity ROC curves and AUC scores that quantify how well the model discriminates disease variants or genes from non-disease counterparts. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2469-7
skills.summary: Evaluates a trained deep learning prioritization model (e.g. iMEGES/ncDeepBrain) by ten-fold cross-validation, generating sensitivity-vs-specificity ROC curves and AUC scores that quantify how well the model discriminates disease variants or genes from non-disease counterparts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is ranking or prioritization output quality rather than binary discrimination — e.g. the iMEGES gene score evaluation compares disease vs non-disease genes but proxies come from imputed GWAS P-values where hits may be proxy markers, not causal variants When class labels are absent or unreliable (no positives of known disease variants/genes), since ROC/AUC requires labeled positive and negative sets When input is raw sequencing data (VCF/BED) rather than model scores or an already-trained classifier — run the ncDeepBrain variant score step first

skills.description: Use when a statistical test or predictor (e.g., a mediation test) must be validated on simulated data with known true positives/negatives, and you need AUC, sensitivity, and specificity as a function of controlled parameters such as effect strength and sample size.
skills.name: roc-auc-performance-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-performance-evaluation Use when a statistical test or predictor (e.g., a mediation test) must be validated on simulated data with known true positives/negatives, and you need AUC, sensitivity, and specificity as a function of controlled parameters such as effect strength and sample size. The data are real observational data without known ground-truth mediation labels — simulation with known true/false pairs is required for this skill The question is applying mediation testing to discover drivers (use the iEDGE run_iEDGE workflow), not benchmarking the test's statistical performance Conditions of adequate sample size and strong correlation are already guaranteed, so a full performance grid adds little Simulation-based evaluation of a binary classifier's discriminative power by sweeping a parameter grid (here, correlation between independent variable and mediator vs. sample size N) and computing AUC, sensitivity, and specificity per cell — used in iEDGE to validate the Sobel test of mediation against known true/false mediation labels. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-019-52886-z
skills.summary: Simulation-based evaluation of a binary classifier's discriminative power by sweeping a parameter grid (here, correlation between independent variable and mediator vs. sample size N) and computing AUC, sensitivity, and specificity per cell — used in iEDGE to validate the Sobel test of mediation against known true/false mediation labels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are real observational data without known ground-truth mediation labels — simulation with known true/false pairs is required for this skill The question is applying mediation testing to discover drivers (use the iEDGE run_iEDGE workflow), not benchmarking the test's statistical performance Conditions of adequate sample size and strong correlation are already guaranteed, so a full performance grid adds little

skills.description: Use when comparing two or more Hi-C significance-calling or normalization methods on replicate datasets, and you need quantitative reproducibility (replicate overlap fractions) and ROC AUC of significance scores.
skills.name: roc-auc-reproducibility-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-reproducibility-evaluation Use when comparing two or more Hi-C significance-calling or normalization methods on replicate datasets, and you need quantitative reproducibility (replicate overlap fractions) and ROC AUC of significance scores. Input is raw FASTQ/BAM Hi-C data that has not yet been processed into binned fragment-pair coverage tables (.feature format) The goal is map-level reproducibility (HiC-spector score) or compartment A/B profile correlation rather than significant-interaction overlap and ROC AUC Only a single replicate is available, so reproducible-interaction labels cannot be defined across replicates http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 A benchmarking skill that evaluates Hi-C normalization/significance-calling methods (covNorm vs Fit-Hi-C) by the fraction of significant long-range chromatin contacts reproducible across biological replicates and by ROC AUC of significance scores for discriminating reproducible interactions. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.05.041
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill that evaluates Hi-C normalization/significance-calling methods (covNorm vs Fit-Hi-C) by the fraction of significant long-range chromatin contacts reproducible across biological replicates and by ROC AUC of significance scores for discriminating reproducible interactions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTQ/BAM Hi-C data that has not yet been processed into binned fragment-pair coverage tables (.feature format) The goal is map-level reproducibility (HiC-spector score) or compartment A/B profile correlation rather than significant-interaction overlap and ROC AUC Only a single replicate is available, so reproducible-interaction labels cannot be defined across replicates

skills.description: Use when multiple TPX-prediction tools or scoring functions must be compared quantitatively on the same positive (Top1000 RNA:DNA peaks) and negative (bedtools-shuffled genomic) region sets.
skills.name: roc-auc-tool-comparison
skills.search_text: roc-auc-tool-comparison Use when multiple TPX-prediction tools or scoring functions must be compared quantitatively on the same positive (Top1000 RNA:DNA peaks) and negative (bedtools-shuffled genomic) region sets. When the goal is de novo TPX discovery on a single transcript rather than a head-to-head accuracy benchmark against experimental positive/negative peaks. When no experimentally validated positive regions (e.g. RADICL-seq Top1000 peaks) exist for the lncRNAs, since ROC/AUC labels cannot be defined. When comparing TriplexFPP predictions, since the article reports no good agreement between TriplexFPP and rule-based tool outputs. Benchmark triplex (TPX) prediction tools by scoring positive vs negative regions, computing ROC curves and AUC with the pROC R package (v1.17.0.1), and comparing AUCs across tools and scoring strategies. epigenomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.05.016
skills.summary: Benchmark triplex (TPX) prediction tools by scoring positive vs negative regions, computing ROC curves and AUC with the pROC R package (v1.17.0.1), and comparing AUCs across tools and scoring strategies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is de novo TPX discovery on a single transcript rather than a head-to-head accuracy benchmark against experimental positive/negative peaks. When no experimentally validated positive regions (e.g. RADICL-seq Top1000 peaks) exist for the lncRNAs, since ROC/AUC labels cannot be defined. When comparing TriplexFPP predictions, since the article reports no good agreement between TriplexFPP and rule-based tool outputs.

skills.description: Use when predicted functional scores for nc-sindels and gold-standard positive/negative eQTL labels are available and you must compare classifier performance (AUROC/AUPRC) across multiple tissues or cell types.
skills.name: roc-auprc-performance-benchmarking
skills.search_text: roc-auprc-performance-benchmarking Use when predicted functional scores for nc-sindels and gold-standard positive/negative eQTL labels are available and you must compare classifier performance (AUROC/AUPRC) across multiple tissues or cell types. Input is already a feature table (annot.csv CADD annotations or seq_features.h5 multi-omics features) rather than predicted scores — feature generation, not benchmarking, is needed The goal is within-GTEx tissue prediction rather than the independent DICE cross-study evaluation described here No labeled positive/negative sindel sets exist for the test cell types, since AUROC/AUPRC cannot be computed without ground truth http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark TIVAN-indel's predicted functional scores against competing indel-prioritization methods (CADD/FATHMM-indel SVM and DanQ/DeepSEA with Boosted LR) by computing median AUROC and AUPRC across 15 independent DICE immune cell types. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad060
skills.summary: Benchmark TIVAN-indel's predicted functional scores against competing indel-prioritization methods (CADD/FATHMM-indel SVM and DanQ/DeepSEA with Boosted LR) by computing median AUROC and AUPRC across 15 independent DICE immune cell types.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table (annot.csv CADD annotations or seq_features.h5 multi-omics features) rather than predicted scores — feature generation, not benchmarking, is needed The goal is within-GTEx tissue prediction rather than the independent DICE cross-study evaluation described here No labeled positive/negative sindel sets exist for the test cell types, since AUROC/AUPRC cannot be computed without ground truth

skills.description: Use when comparing differential occupancy / peak-calling methods on a dosage-responsive ChIP-seq benchmark with a gold-standard positive set defined at a signal quantile, and you need ROC curves and AUC-vs-cutoff comparisons.
skills.name: roc-curve-auc-benchmarking
skills.search_text: roc-curve-auc-benchmarking Use when comparing differential occupancy / peak-calling methods on a dosage-responsive ChIP-seq benchmark with a gold-standard positive set defined at a signal quantile, and you need ROC curves and AUC-vs-cutoff comparisons. Input is not a ChIP-seq differential occupancy setting with a defined gold-standard positive set — the benchmark quantile-based truth labels do not transfer to other data types You need a genome-wide production fit rather than a method comparison — use the standard GenoGAM workflow (GenoGAMDataSet → computeSizeFactors → genogam → computeSignificance) without ROC/AUC benchmarking http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark a differential ChIP-seq occupancy caller (e.g. GenoGAM 2.0) against competitors (csaw, DESeq2, GenoGAM 1.0) by sweeping signal-quantile cutoffs to build ROC curves and AUC-vs-cutoff tables, reproducing the original GenoGAM study benchmark (doi:10.1186/s13059-014-0550-8). epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2238-7
skills.summary: Benchmark a differential ChIP-seq occupancy caller (e.g. GenoGAM 2.0) against competitors (csaw, DESeq2, GenoGAM 1.0) by sweeping signal-quantile cutoffs to build ROC curves and AUC-vs-cutoff tables, reproducing the original GenoGAM study benchmark (doi:10.1186/s13059-014-0550-8).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not a ChIP-seq differential occupancy setting with a defined gold-standard positive set — the benchmark quantile-based truth labels do not transfer to other data types You need a genome-wide production fit rather than a method comparison — use the standard GenoGAM workflow (GenoGAMDataSet → computeSizeFactors → genogam → computeSignificance) without ROC/AUC benchmarking

skills.description: Use when a modified-vs-unmodified region caller on broad histone marks (e.g. H3K27me3) must be ranked against competitors using an independent qPCR-validated ground-truth region set rather than simulated data.
skills.name: roc-evaluation-against-qpcr-validated-regions
skills.search_text: roc-evaluation-against-qpcr-validated-regions Use when a modified-vs-unmodified region caller on broad histone marks (e.g. H3K27me3) must be ranked against competitors using an independent qPCR-validated ground-truth region set rather than simulated data. The task is differential calling between two samples (the bivariate histoneHMM use case) rather than single-sample modified-vs-unmodified detection benchmarking No independent qPCR-validated or otherwise experimentally validated region set exists, so sensitivity/specificity cannot be computed against ground truth (the article used simulation studies, Additional file 1, in that setting) The histone mark of interest forms sharp peak-like features rather than broad diffuse footprints like H3K27me3/H3K9me3, where peak-style callers are appropriate and this broad-mark benchmark does not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0160 Benchmark a ChIP-seq peak caller or HMM-based caller by sweeping its score thresholds and building per-base-pair ROC curves of sensitivity versus specificity against an independent qPCR-validated region set (here 197 H3K27me3 regions from GSM721294/GSM721306), as done to show histoneHMM outperforms MACS2 broad, Zinba, SICER, BroadPeak and Rseg in Figure 5a. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-015-0491-6
skills.summary: Benchmark a ChIP-seq peak caller or HMM-based caller by sweeping its score thresholds and building per-base-pair ROC curves of sensitivity versus specificity against an independent qPCR-validated region set (here 197 H3K27me3 regions from GSM721294/GSM721306), as done to show histoneHMM outperforms MACS2 broad, Zinba, SICER, BroadPeak and Rseg in Figure 5a.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is differential calling between two samples (the bivariate histoneHMM use case) rather than single-sample modified-vs-unmodified detection benchmarking No independent qPCR-validated or otherwise experimentally validated region set exists, so sensitivity/specificity cannot be computed against ground truth (the article used simulation studies, Additional file 1, in that setting) The histone mark of interest forms sharp peak-like features rather than broad diffuse footprints like H3K27me3/H3K9me3, where peak-style callers are appropriate and this broad-mark benchmark does not apply

skills.description: Use when you need to justify or tune the number of random samplings (repetitions) in cola consensus partitioning, or to show that a low sampling count already yields a stable partition.
skills.name: row-sampling-perturbation-benchmarking
skills.search_text: row-sampling-perturbation-benchmarking Use when you need to justify or tune the number of random samplings (repetitions) in cola consensus partitioning, or to show that a low sampling count already yields a stable partition. Input is single-cell data with several thousands of cells — cola runtime and memory usage may be unacceptable, and downsampling may miss small cell clusters The goal is feature selection method comparison (e.g., ATC vs SD/MAD/CV) rather than sampling-size sensitivity of partition stability http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A benchmarking skill that varies the number of random row samplings (e.g., 25, 50, 100, 200) in cola consensus partitioning to quantify how sampling effort affects partition stability (SD of 1-PAC) and concordance between settings, using the TCGA GBM expression dataset as the exemplar input. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa1146
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill that varies the number of random row samplings (e.g., 25, 50, 100, 200) in cola consensus partitioning to quantify how sampling effort affects partition stability (SD of 1-PAC) and concordance between settings, using the TCGA GBM expression dataset as the exemplar input.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is single-cell data with several thousands of cells — cola runtime and memory usage may be unacceptable, and downsampling may miss small cell clusters The goal is feature selection method comparison (e.g., ATC vs SD/MAD/CV) rather than sampling-size sensitivity of partition stability

skills.description: Use when running cola consensus partitioning on a high-dimensional matrix and you need to decide whether to resample rows or columns during bootstrapping, or to verify that both sampling types yield comparable subgroupings.
skills.name: row-vs-column-sampling-comparison
skills.search_text: row-vs-column-sampling-comparison Use when running cola consensus partitioning on a high-dimensional matrix and you need to decide whether to resample rows or columns during bootstrapping, or to verify that both sampling types yield comparable subgroupings. The dataset is single-cell RNA-Seq with several thousands of cells, where cola runtime and memory usage may be unacceptable and downsampling may miss small cell clusters You only need a single consensus partition for one sampling scheme rather than an explicit row-versus-column sampling stability comparison The input is a methylation matrix needing probe-level filters (sex chromosomes, SNP-overlapping probes) that this GBM expression workflow does not include http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 A cola-based benchmark that contrasts randomly sampling rows (features) versus columns (samples) during consensus partitioning, quantifying stability via 1-PAC and cross-sampling-type concordance. skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is single-cell RNA-Seq with several thousands of cells, where cola runtime and memory usage may be unacceptable and downsampling may miss small cell clusters You only need a single consensus partition for one sampling scheme rather than an explicit row-versus-column sampling stability comparison The input is a methylation matrix needing probe-level filters (sex chromosomes, SNP-overlapping probes) that this GBM expression workflow does not include

skills.description: Use when starting CIPHER's enhancer-prediction or element-feature computation and you have ENCODE ChIP-seq/DNase-seq data that must be converted to RPM-normalized bedGraph signal tracks before genomic elements are classified.

skills.search_text: rpm-normalized-bedgraph-processing Use when starting CIPHER's enhancer-prediction or element-feature computation and you have ENCODE ChIP-seq/DNase-seq data that must be converted to RPM-normalized bedGraph signal tracks before genomic elements are classified. skills.summary: A CIPHER workflow pattern in which RPM-normalized bedGraph signal files of DNase-seq and ChIP-seq (H3K4me1, H3K4me3, H3K27ac) data are consumed as standardized coverage inputs for the random-forest enhancer predictor ('--function predictEnhancers') and for computing chromatin-signature features over genomic elements.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need only a subset of CIPHER's tools rather than a whole workflow — the article notes 'CIPHER currently only runs entire workflows, not subsets of tools' Your data are raw reads and you expect the enhancer model itself to handle mapping/normalization — RPM-normalized bedGraph signal must be produced by the upstream CIPHER pre-processing steps first You mix single-ended and pair-ended data in the same config file, which CIPHER does not handle

skills.description: Use when RRBS reads from multi-region tumour samples plus matched normal tissue have been fitted with bed_fit and per-locus epiallele proportions are needed, purity (rho) must be estimated from the xi density, or tumour profiles must be decontaminated before phylogeny/entropy analysis.
skills.name: rrbs-methylation-data-analysis
skills.search_text: rrbs-methylation-data-analysis Use when RRBS reads from multi-region tumour samples plus matched normal tissue have been fitted with bed_fit and per-locus epiallele proportions are needed, purity (rho) must be estimated from the xi density, or tumour profiles must be decontaminated before phylogeny/entropy analysis. The sample has no matched normal tissue, so n cannot be marginalised and xi cannot separate tumour from contaminating signal Loci fail the article's filters (median read depth < 100, fewer than 6 CpGs, > 25% missing data, or chromosomes X/Y), where phi and n are unreliable The goal is differential methylation testing between sample groups rather than purity estimation and decontamination of epiallele profiles http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Estimates tumour sample purity (rho) from RRBS-derived epiallele distributions by comparing tumour vs matched-normal per-locus epiallele profiles, then decontaminates profiles with t_q = (phi_q - (1-rho)*n_q)/rho. Applied with the R 'bed' Bayesian Epiallele Detection package. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-017-1753-2
skills.summary: Estimates tumour sample purity (rho) from RRBS-derived epiallele distributions by comparing tumour vs matched-normal per-locus epiallele profiles, then decontaminates profiles with t_q = (phi_q - (1-rho)*n_q)/rho. Applied with the R 'bed' Bayesian Epiallele Detection package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample has no matched normal tissue, so n cannot be marginalised and xi cannot separate tumour from contaminating signal Loci fail the article's filters (median read depth < 100, fewer than 6 CpGs, > 25% missing data, or chromosomes X/Y), where phi and n are unreliable The goal is differential methylation testing between sample groups rather than purity estimation and decontamination of epiallele profiles

skills.search_text: runtime-memory-benchmarking Use when reproducing or auditing SCALE's scalability claims on a large scATAC-seq input (e.g. the ~80k-cell mouse_atlas.h5ad), where reported runtime (~1.5 h), memory (~2 GB), and clustering F1 (0.419) must be measured and compared. skills.search_text: sakoe-chiba-band-constrained-warping Use when aligning two or more epigenomic tracks (or other multivariate time series of binned coverage vectors) by shape similarity, where the warping path must be bounded near the diagonal and strand orientation must be handled. Input regions contain no enrichment structure to align, or peaks are shorter than 5 or longer than 1000 bins — the paper's filtering excludes such peaks before alignment The sequences are already aligned or the analysis requires point-wise positional comparison without local rescaling — DTW would warp away genuine positional differences A tighter or looser warping constraint is required by the application — the width-12 band is a paper-specific tuning, not a universal default http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Constrained multidimensional Dynamic Time Warping that aligns sequences of binned epigenomic coverage vectors using a Sakoe-Chiba band of width 12, capping the warping path's departure from the diagonal so that epigenomic marks can be matched by shape with O(k*max(N,M)) run-time. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-016-1306-0
skills.summary: Constrained multidimensional Dynamic Time Warping that aligns sequences of binned epigenomic coverage vectors using a Sakoe-Chiba band of width 12, capping the warping path's departure from the diagonal so that epigenomic marks can be matched by shape with O(k*max(N,M)) run-time.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input regions contain no enrichment structure to align, or peaks are shorter than 5 or longer than 1000 bins — the paper's filtering excludes such peaks before alignment The sequences are already aligned or the analysis requires point-wise positional comparison without local rescaling — DTW would warp away genuine positional differences A tighter or looser warping constraint is required by the application — the width-12 band is a paper-specific tuning, not a universal default

skills.description: Use when planning an interindividual single-cell DE (or eQTL) study and you need to pick sample size, cells per cell type, and read depth by comparing power across a design grid rather than guessing a single design.

skills.search_text: sample-size-and-cells-per-sample-design-grid-evaluation Use when planning an interindividual single-cell DE (or eQTL) study and you need to pick sample size, cells per cell type, and read depth by comparing power across a design grid rather than guessing a single design. The planned sample size far exceeds the pilot/reference study the priors were derived from — data-driven priors only reliably assess power at sample sizes smaller or roughly equal to the pilot data sets The study is a simulation-based power check of a single fixed design with complex cell-type annotation needs, where tools like muscat or powsimR are more appropriate (despite their 35–48 GB memory footprint) The comparison design is unbalanced or non-two-group (e.g. continuous covariates or pseudo-time), which the balanced pseudobulk NB power model here does not cover directly http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Grid-based evaluation of sample size and cells-per-sample combinations using scPower's analytic pseudobulk power model, computing overall detection power as expression probability × DE power for each design point to identify the optimal experimental parameter combination. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-26779-7
skills.summary: Grid-based evaluation of sample size and cells-per-sample combinations using scPower's analytic pseudobulk power model, computing overall detection power as expression probability × DE power for each design point to identify the optimal experimental parameter combination.

skills.description: Use when aligned BAM files from a mapped ChIPseq/RNAseq run must be filtered by fragment-size bounds and duplicate-read policy before peakcalling or downstream normalization.
skills.name: samtools-bam-filtering
skills.search_text: samtools-bam-filtering Use when aligned BAM files from a mapped ChIPseq/RNAseq run must be filtered by fragment-size bounds and duplicate-read policy before peakcalling or downstream normalization. Input is still raw FASTQ or has not been mapped — the NEAT pipeline runs 'unzip', 'rename', 'QC' and 'map' before 'filter' The goal is adapter or quality trimming of reads rather than fragment-size and duplicate filtering of aligned reads (that belongs to the 'QC' module) The task is peak calling itself or reorganizing/storing .bam and .bai files — use NEAT's 'peakcalling' or 'cleanfiles' modules instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Filter aligned ChIPseq/RNAseq BAM files with SAMtools according to user-specified NEAT parameters (duplicate-read management policy, minimum and maximum fragment sizes), as implemented in NEAT's 'filter' module that runs after 'map' and before 'peakcalling'. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-016-0902-3
skills.summary: Filter aligned ChIPseq/RNAseq BAM files with SAMtools according to user-specified NEAT parameters (duplicate-read management policy, minimum and maximum fragment sizes), as implemented in NEAT's 'filter' module that runs after 'map' and before 'peakcalling'.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still raw FASTQ or has not been mapped — the NEAT pipeline runs 'unzip', 'rename', 'QC' and 'map' before 'filter' The goal is adapter or quality trimming of reads rather than fragment-size and duplicate filtering of aligned reads (that belongs to the 'QC' module) The task is peak calling itself or reorganizing/storing .bam and .bai files — use NEAT's 'peakcalling' or 'cleanfiles' modules instead

You need to call loops on the full cell population rather than benchmark subsample reproducibility — run the pipeline once on all cells instead Input is bulk Hi-C or already-aggregated contact matrices with no per-cell files to split Comparing reproducibility across different cell types or conditions rather than random splits of the same population — use differential loop analysis instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Randomly partition a pool of single-cell Hi-C contact files into two equal, disjoint replicate halves to benchmark loop-calling reproducibility (symmetric overlap) between methods such as SnapHiC and Juicer HiCCUPS on identical cell subsets. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41592-021-01231-2
skills.summary: Randomly partition a pool of single-cell Hi-C contact files into two equal, disjoint replicate halves to benchmark loop-calling reproducibility (symmetric overlap) between methods such as SnapHiC and Juicer HiCCUPS on identical cell subsets.

skills.description: Use when evaluating a distributed aligner or Spark-based pipeline's scale-out behavior: you have access to clusters of differing node counts (e.g. 10, 20, 40 slaves) and need to quantify throughput gain or loss as nodes are added.
skills.name: scalability-curve-analysis
skills.search_text: scalability-curve-analysis Use when evaluating a distributed aligner or Spark-based pipeline's scale-out behavior: you have access to clusters of differing node counts (e.g. 10, 20, 40 slaves) and need to quantify throughput gain or loss as nodes are added. You only have access to a single cluster size — a two-point (or one-point) throughput measurement cannot reveal a scaling gradient or the balance-vs-shuffle trade-off. The benchmark question is per-node performance against single-node tools (e.g. BiSpark vs Bismark or CloudAligner timing) rather than scale-out behavior of one tool across cluster sizes. Input data or reference indexing time varies between runs — including non-alignment pre-processing (reference transformation/indexing, input distribution) will confound the elapsed-time comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Measures how a distributed tool's throughput scales with cluster size by running identical workloads on clusters of increasing node counts and plotting throughput (reads/second) versus number of slave nodes. Used in the BiSpark evaluation to show that load balancing (BiSpark-balance) costs throughput on small clusters but gains it on large ones. epigenomics/v2 10.1186/s12859-018-2498-2
skills.summary: Measures how a distributed tool's throughput scales with cluster size by running identical workloads on clusters of increasing node counts and plotting throughput (reads/second) versus number of slave nodes. Used in the BiSpark evaluation to show that load balancing (BiSpark-balance) costs throughput on small clusters but gains it on large ones.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have access to a single cluster size — a two-point (or one-point) throughput measurement cannot reveal a scaling gradient or the balance-vs-shuffle trade-off. The benchmark question is per-node performance against single-node tools (e.g. BiSpark vs Bismark or CloudAligner timing) rather than scale-out behavior of one tool across cluster sizes. Input data or reference indexing time varies between runs — including non-alignment pre-processing (reference transformation/indexing, input distribution) will confound the elapsed-time comparison.

skills.description: Use when a scATAC-seq accessibility matrix clusters primarily by copy number state and you need to test whether CNVs confound clustering: drop CNV-chromosome peaks, recluster, and compare assignments via AMI.
skills.name: scatac-accessibility-matrix-processing
skills.search_text: scatac-accessibility-matrix-processing Use when a scATAC-seq accessibility matrix clusters primarily by copy number state and you need to test whether CNVs confound clustering: drop CNV-chromosome peaks, recluster, and compare assignments via AMI. Clustering is already based on motif activity scores (e.g., ChromVAR), where CNV-driven effects are less pronounced Tumors driven primarily by single nucleotide variants with no or rare CNVs, where Copy-scAT cannot infer meaningful CNVs You need a definitive correction for CNV effects rather than a diagnostic of confounding — the optimal correction approach is undetermined http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 A Copy-scAT (CopyscAT R package) workflow that removes peaks mapping to CNV-bearing chromosomes from a single-cell ATAC-seq accessibility matrix, reclusters cells on the CNV-free peak matrix (identifyCNVClusters + fastcluster hierarchical clustering), and quantifies how much clustering was CNV-driven by computing adjusted mutual information (AMI) against the original assignments. epigenomics/v2 10.1126/sciadv.abg6045
skills.summary: A Copy-scAT (CopyscAT R package) workflow that removes peaks mapping to CNV-bearing chromosomes from a single-cell ATAC-seq accessibility matrix, reclusters cells on the CNV-free peak matrix (identifyCNVClusters + fastcluster hierarchical clustering), and quantifies how much clustering was CNV-driven by computing adjusted mutual information (AMI) against the original assignments.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Clustering is already based on motif activity scores (e.g., ChromVAR), where CNV-driven effects are less pronounced Tumors driven primarily by single nucleotide variants with no or rare CNVs, where Copy-scAT cannot infer meaningful CNVs You need a definitive correction for CNV effects rather than a diagnostic of confounding — the optimal correction approach is undetermined

skills.description: Use when you already have single-cell cluster assignments for scATAC-seq data (e.g., from a SnapATAC snap file with barcodes and the FM fragment session) and need to generate pseudo-bulk signal per cluster for peak calling.
skills.name: scatac-fragment-aggregation-per-cluster
skills.search_text: scatac-fragment-aggregation-per-cluster Use when you already have single-cell cluster assignments for scATAC-seq data (e.g., from a SnapATAC snap file with barcodes and the FM fragment session) and need to generate pseudo-bulk signal per cluster for peak calling. Cluster labels are not yet available or unreliable — the article warns that peaks in rare populations may be underrepresented when crude clusters reflect only dominant cell types You need a population-level reference independent of iterative clustering; iterative clustering requires multiple rounds of clustering, aggregation, and peak calling, hindering large-scale datasets Input is already a processed peak or feature matrix (cell-by-peak matrix in the PM session) rather than raw fragments needing aggregation http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Aggregates single-nucleus ATAC-seq fragments from cells assigned to each cluster into pseudo-bulk accessibility profiles, which are then used for per-cluster MACS2 peak calling to build a cell-type-specific atlas of candidate cis-regulatory elements. This is how SnapATAC-derived clusters (e.g., the 55,592-nucleus mouse secondary motor cortex atlas) are converted into discrete regulatory element sets. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-21583-9
skills.summary: Aggregates single-nucleus ATAC-seq fragments from cells assigned to each cluster into pseudo-bulk accessibility profiles, which are then used for per-cluster MACS2 peak calling to build a cell-type-specific atlas of candidate cis-regulatory elements. This is how SnapATAC-derived clusters (e.g., the 55,592-nucleus mouse secondary motor cortex atlas) are converted into discrete regulatory element sets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Cluster labels are not yet available or unreliable — the article warns that peaks in rare populations may be underrepresented when crude clusters reflect only dominant cell types You need a population-level reference independent of iterative clustering; iterative clustering requires multiple rounds of clustering, aggregation, and peak calling, hindering large-scale datasets Input is already a processed peak or feature matrix (cell-by-peak matrix in the PM session) rather than raw fragments needing aggregation

skills.search_text: scatac-fragment-genome-binning Use when raw scATAC-seq fragment files (e.g., cellranger-atac output) must be converted into a per-cell genomic bin count matrix prior to CNV or copy number inference with Copy-scAT. Input is already a binned or normalized count matrix rather than a raw fragment file Malignancy is driven primarily by SNVs with no or rare CNVs, so fragment pileup-based CNV inference provides little signal http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Converts raw cellranger-atac fragment files into a filtered, edgeR-normalized barcode-by-bin read-depth matrix (1-Mbp bins, ≥5000 fragments per barcode) as the first stage of Copy-scAT's CNV inference workflow. epigenomics/v2 10.1126/sciadv.abg6045

Input is already a feature matrix (cell-by-peak or cell-by-gene counts) rather than raw fragments/reads — depth reduction cannot be applied meaningfully post-quantification The goal is accuracy benchmarking on full-depth data rather than assessing robustness to reduced sequencing depth Working in SnapATAC2 (Python/Rust), which is designed to scale to millions of cells and uses its own matrix-free spectral embedding pipeline instead of the SnapTools/snap-file workflow http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Downsamples scATAC-seq reads to a reduced sequencing depth (e.g., 10% of the original, a 90% reduction) with SnapTools so that clustering reproducibility of a method can be scored against its full-depth results, as done in the SnapATAC scalability/reproducibility benchmark. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-21583-9

skills.description: Use when scATAC-seq cells lack annotations and a matched or related scRNA-seq reference with known cell types is available, e.g. predicting PBMC cell types from a ~10k-cell scRNA reference.
skills.name: scatac-scrna-integration-label-transfer
skills.search_text: scatac-scrna-integration-label-transfer Use when scATAC-seq cells lack annotations and a matched or related scRNA-seq reference with known cell types is available, e.g. predicting PBMC cell types from a ~10k-cell scRNA reference. The scATAC and scRNA data come from unrelated tissues/species with no shared features, so CCA anchors cannot be meaningfully established The goal is de novo scATAC clustering without any annotated reference — use SnapATAC's own runDimReduct/runCluster workflow instead Working in R >= 3.6.0, where the rhdf5 dependency breaks the original SnapATAC (R must be >= 3.4.0 & < 3.6.0); consider SnapATAC2 in Python instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Transfers cell-type labels from a scRNA-seq reference onto a scATAC-seq dataset by exporting a SnapATAC embedding into Seurat (snapToSeurat) and applying Seurat's CCA-based anchor label transfer, as demonstrated on the 10X PBMC scATAC/scRNA pair. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-21583-9
skills.summary: Transfers cell-type labels from a scRNA-seq reference onto a scATAC-seq dataset by exporting a SnapATAC embedding into Seurat (snapToSeurat) and applying Seurat's CCA-based anchor label transfer, as demonstrated on the 10X PBMC scATAC/scRNA pair.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The scATAC and scRNA data come from unrelated tissues/species with no shared features, so CCA anchors cannot be meaningfully established The goal is de novo scATAC clustering without any annotated reference — use SnapATAC's own runDimReduct/runCluster workflow instead Working in R >= 3.6.0, where the rhdf5 dependency breaks the original SnapATAC (R must be >= 3.4.0 & < 3.6.0); consider SnapATAC2 in Python instead

skills.search_text: scatac-seq-cell-type-prediction Use when both a labeled scATAC-seq reference dataset (gene score matrix + cell-type metadata) and an unlabeled target scATAC-seq dataset are available and per-cell cell-type labels must be transferred without joint reference-target integration. The reference is scRNA-seq rather than scATAC-seq — Cellcano is designed for scATAC-seq-as-reference; cross-modality prediction (scRNA-seq reference) and multimodal references are planned but not implemented Input is already a feature table of non-gene-score features (e.g. bin counts) chosen deliberately — although gene scores work as equally well or better than bin counts, the workflow as described assumes ArchR-derived gene scores Only unsupervised cluster discovery is needed and no labeled reference exists — supervised Cellcano requires reference cell-type labels http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Predict single-cell ATAC-seq cell types in a target dataset using Cellcano's two-round supervised learning: an MLP trained on reference gene scores, followed by a self-Knowledge Distiller (KD) model trained on low-entropy anchor cells from the target. Using a scATAC-seq reference outperforms unsupervised clustering and cross-modality label transfer in accuracy, robustness and scalability.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reference is scRNA-seq rather than scATAC-seq — Cellcano is designed for scATAC-seq-as-reference; cross-modality prediction (scRNA-seq reference) and multimodal references are planned but not implemented Input is already a feature table of non-gene-score features (e.g. bin counts) chosen deliberately — although gene scores work as equally well or better than bin counts, the workflow as described assumes ArchR-derived gene scores Only unsupervised cluster discovery is needed and no labeled reference exists — supervised Cellcano requires reference cell-type labels

skills.search_text: scatac-seq-celltyping-benchmark-evaluation Use when benchmarking cell-typing predictions for scATAC-seq data — e.g., comparing Cellcano's predicted labels against FACS-derived ground truth for a human PBMC target dataset to quantify per-type accuracy. Input lacks a reference scATAC-seq dataset with known labels, so no supervised celltyping predictions (and hence no true-vs-predicted evaluation) can be produced The goal is cross-modality prediction using scRNA-seq as reference or multimodal (joint scRNA-/scATAC-seq) references — the article states these are planned but not implemented in Cellcano Input is already a labeled prediction-vs-truth table; then only the crosstab step is needed, not the full celltyping pipeline http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Evaluates supervised scATAC-seq cell-typing predictions (e.g., Cellcano's two-round MLP/Knowledge Distiller outputs) against ground-truth labels by building a true-vs-predicted confusion matrix and checking diagonal counts, as in the Cellcano human PBMC quick-start demo. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-37439-3
skills.summary: Evaluates supervised scATAC-seq cell-typing predictions (e.g., Cellcano's two-round MLP/Knowledge Distiller outputs) against ground-truth labels by building a true-vs-predicted confusion matrix and checking diagonal counts, as in the Cellcano human PBMC quick-start demo.

skills.description: Use when the input is a raw scATAC-seq count matrix (h5ad, txt/tsv/csv, or mtx folder with count/peak/barcode files) and the goal is cell-type clustering, visualization, or denoising/imputation with benchmarked accuracy against scABC, scVI, cisTopic, and SC3.
skills.name: scatac-seq-latent-feature-clustering
skills.search_text: scatac-seq-latent-feature-clustering Use when the input is a raw scATAC-seq count matrix (h5ad, txt/tsv/csv, or mtx folder with count/peak/barcode files) and the goal is cell-type clustering, visualization, or denoising/imputation with benchmarked accuracy against scABC, scVI, cisTopic, and SC3. The task is to identify and remove batch effects or other technical artifacts from input data — the authors state SCALE is 'not specifically designed to identify and remove these artifacts from the input data'; explicit batch-effect modeling is deferred to future work (or use SCALEX for integration). The analysis needs single-peak motif resolution via grouped motif activity alone — chromVAR evaluates groups of peaks sharing motifs without individual peak resolution, and this skill is for whole-dataset latent-feature clustering instead. The input is scRNA-seq expression data — scRNA-seq tools like scVI apply a single Gaussian prior in that setting and are not designed for the close-to-binary, sparse scATAC-seq count matrix this skill expects. http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Cluster sparse single-cell ATAC-seq data by learning latent features with SCALE, a variational autoencoder (VAE) with a probabilistic Gaussian Mixture Model prior, then annotate clusters via Leiden and UMAP embeddings. SCALE is applied because the close-to-binary, high-dimensional scATAC-seq data suffer from 'missingness', making direct scRNA-seq methods unsuitable. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-12630-7
skills.summary: Cluster sparse single-cell ATAC-seq data by learning latent features with SCALE, a variational autoencoder (VAE) with a probabilistic Gaussian Mixture Model prior, then annotate clusters via Leiden and UMAP embeddings. SCALE is applied because the close-to-binary, high-dimensional scATAC-seq data suffer from 'missingness', making direct scRNA-seq methods unsuitable.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is to identify and remove batch effects or other technical artifacts from input data — the authors state SCALE is 'not specifically designed to identify and remove these artifacts from the input data'; explicit batch-effect modeling is deferred to future work (or use SCALEX for integration). The analysis needs single-peak motif resolution via grouped motif activity alone — chromVAR evaluates groups of peaks sharing motifs without individual peak resolution, and this skill is for whole-dataset latent-feature clustering instead. The input is scRNA-seq expression data — scRNA-seq tools like scVI apply a single Gaussian prior in that setting and are not designed for the close-to-binary, sparse scATAC-seq count matrix this skill expects.

skills.description: Use when sparse scATAC-seq peak-by-cell data (h5ad) needs transcription factor motif activity scoring, especially to test whether SCALE-imputed data recovers more cluster-specific motifs than the raw matrix.
skills.name: scatac-seq-motif-activity-analysis
skills.search_text: scatac-seq-motif-activity-analysis Use when sparse scATAC-seq peak-by-cell data (h5ad) needs transcription factor motif activity scoring, especially to test whether SCALE-imputed data recovers more cluster-specific motifs than the raw matrix.
