skills.name: tf-activation-repression-time-point-detection
skills.search_text: tf-activation-repression-time-point-detection Use when you have a time-series expression matrix plus TF-gene interaction data and need to determine, per time point, which TFs significantly regulate tree-structure subpaths and whether each TF is activated or repressed. Input lacks time-series structure (e.g., single-condition expression profiles) — TFs cannot be assigned to specific time points without temporal resolution No TF-gene interaction (TF-TG) annotations are available for the organism — both positive and negative interaction evidence is required for subpath regulation tests Goal is clustering of expression modules without temporal dynamics of regulators — clustering methods cannot evaluate the temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 TSMiner's TF prediction module identifies which transcription factors (TFs) significantly regulate each subpath of the tree-structure model at each time point, using a hypergeometric test plus a permutation test, and then labels each TF as activated or repressed based on the average fold change of its target genes. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: TSMiner's TF prediction module identifies which transcription factors (TFs) significantly regulate each subpath of the tree-structure model at each time point, using a hypergeometric test plus a permutation test, and then labels each TF as activated or repressed based on the average fold change of its target genes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input lacks time-series structure (e.g., single-condition expression profiles) — TFs cannot be assigned to specific time points without temporal resolution No TF-gene interaction (TF-TG) annotations are available for the organism — both positive and negative interaction evidence is required for subpath regulation tests Goal is clustering of expression modules without temporal dynamics of regulators — clustering methods cannot evaluate the temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways

skills.description: Use when you need to quantitatively compare genome-wide TF binding site predictors (e.g., RoboCOP vs COMPETE vs FIMO baselines) using probabilistic occupancy scores and ChIP-based ground-truth binding annotations.
skills.name: tf-binding-site-precision-recall-evaluation
skills.search_text: tf-binding-site-precision-recall-evaluation Use when you need to quantitatively compare genome-wide TF binding site predictors (e.g., RoboCOP vs COMPETE vs FIMO baselines) using probabilistic occupancy scores and ChIP-based ground-truth binding annotations. The goal is validating nucleosome positioning rather than TF binding sites — the article validates nucleosome predictions with chemical cleavage method annotations, not ChIP-based TF annotations. No ground-truth TF binding annotations (ChIP-chip/ChIP-exo/ORGANIC) are available for the organism/TFs, making AUPR at single-nucleotide resolution impossible. Only a single predictor is available with no competing methods — the skill's core is a comparative AUPR benchmark across RoboCOP, COMPETE, and MACS2+FIMO baselines. http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Benchmarking protocol that ranks predicted TF binding sites from RoboCOP (MNase-seq, ATAC-seq, or joint), COMPETE variants, and MACS2+FIMO baselines by their probabilistic scores and scores them as per-TF AUPR at single-nucleotide resolution against ChIP-chip/ChIP-exo/ORGANIC ground-truth annotations, with Mann-Whitney U tests on the per-TF AUPR distributions. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab553
skills.summary: Benchmarking protocol that ranks predicted TF binding sites from RoboCOP (MNase-seq, ATAC-seq, or joint), COMPETE variants, and MACS2+FIMO baselines by their probabilistic scores and scores them as per-TF AUPR at single-nucleotide resolution against ChIP-chip/ChIP-exo/ORGANIC ground-truth annotations, with Mann-Whitney U tests on the per-TF AUPR distributions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is validating nucleosome positioning rather than TF binding sites — the article validates nucleosome predictions with chemical cleavage method annotations, not ChIP-based TF annotations. No ground-truth TF binding annotations (ChIP-chip/ChIP-exo/ORGANIC) are available for the organism/TFs, making AUPR at single-nucleotide resolution impossible. Only a single predictor is available with no competing methods — the skill's core is a comparative AUPR benchmark across RoboCOP, COMPETE, and MACS2+FIMO baselines.

skills.description: Use when quantifying how well individual or combined DNA shape features (HelT, MGW, ProT, Roll) or sequences predict TF-DNA binding specificity across ENCODE ChIP-seq datasets, using test AUC from a trained DESSO CNN.
skills.name: tf-dna-binding-auc-evaluation
skills.search_text: tf-dna-binding-auc-evaluation Use when quantifying how well individual or combined DNA shape features (HelT, MGW, ProT, Roll) or sequences predict TF-DNA binding specificity across ENCODE ChIP-seq datasets, using test AUC from a trained DESSO CNN. Input is already a trained model and the goal is motif discovery rather than binding-specificity evaluation (use DESSO predict.py with cutoff scanning instead) Peak regions longer than 101 bp are needed — GCNN with peak_flank 500 (1001-bp peaks) is the appropriate DESSO mode, not the 101-bp CNN AUC setup The task is motif similarity assessment against JASPAR/TRANSFAC via TOMTOM rather than classification performance (AUC) measurement http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Evaluate TF-DNA binding specificity prediction by training DESSO CNN models on 101-bp ENCODE ChIP-seq peak regions (peak_flank 50) with either sequence (Seq) or DNA shape (HelT/MGW/ProT/Roll, DNAShape) inputs, and reading test-set AUCs from Test_result.txt as the performance metric. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz672
skills.summary: Evaluate TF-DNA binding specificity prediction by training DESSO CNN models on 101-bp ENCODE ChIP-seq peak regions (peak_flank 50) with either sequence (Seq) or DNA shape (HelT/MGW/ProT/Roll, DNAShape) inputs, and reading test-set AUCs from Test_result.txt as the performance metric.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a trained model and the goal is motif discovery rather than binding-specificity evaluation (use DESSO predict.py with cutoff scanning instead) Peak regions longer than 101 bp are needed — GCNN with peak_flank 500 (1001-bp peaks) is the appropriate DESSO mode, not the 101-bp CNN AUC setup The task is motif similarity assessment against JASPAR/TRANSFAC via TOMTOM rather than classification performance (AUC) measurement

skills.description: Use when you have BHi-Cect cluster output (named list of loci per cluster) plus TF ChIP-seq peaks for the same cell line and need a count matrix summarizing TF-binding content per bottom enclave.
skills.name: tf-enclave-contingency-table-construction
skills.search_text: tf-enclave-contingency-table-construction Use when you have BHi-Cect cluster output (named list of loci per cluster) plus TF ChIP-seq peaks for the same cell line and need a count matrix summarizing TF-binding content per bottom enclave. Your cluster output is not from BHi-Cect or lacks a named list of loci per cluster — there is no enclave hierarchy to intersect with the peaks. You need genome-wide regulatory summaries at the top-level domain scale rather than the leaf (bottom enclave) level — the CA finding applies specifically to bottom enclaves. TF ChIP-seq data for the same cell line as the Hi-C data is unavailable — cross-cell-line peaks would not reflect the epigenomic activity underlying those enclaves. http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Constructs a transcription-factor (TF) by bottom-enclave contingency table by intersecting BHi-Cect leaf-cluster locus membership (from IMR90 Hi-C) with ChIP-seq peak data for ten TFs (CEBP, RCOR1, MAZ, MXI, RFX5, MafK, FOS, USF2, NFE2L2, ELK1), enabling downstream correspondence analysis of regulatory regimes. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa004
skills.summary: Constructs a transcription-factor (TF) by bottom-enclave contingency table by intersecting BHi-Cect leaf-cluster locus membership (from IMR90 Hi-C) with ChIP-seq peak data for ten TFs (CEBP, RCOR1, MAZ, MXI, RFX5, MafK, FOS, USF2, NFE2L2, ELK1), enabling downstream correspondence analysis of regulatory regimes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your cluster output is not from BHi-Cect or lacks a named list of loci per cluster — there is no enclave hierarchy to intersect with the peaks. You need genome-wide regulatory summaries at the top-level domain scale rather than the leaf (bottom enclave) level — the CA finding applies specifically to bottom enclaves. TF ChIP-seq data for the same cell line as the Hi-C data is unavailable — cross-cell-line peaks would not reflect the epigenomic activity underlying those enclaves.

skills.description: Use when you have two or more sets of differentially bound calling cards peaks (e.g., female vs male GBM CC differential peaks, BED/qbed-derived) and need to find TF motif families enriched in one group but not another.
skills.name: tf-motif-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: tf-motif-enrichment-analysis Use when you have two or more sets of differentially bound calling cards peaks (e.g., female vs male GBM CC differential peaks, BED/qbed-derived) and need to find TF motif families enriched in one group but not another. Input is raw qbed/ccf insertions rather than called, differential peaks — motif calling should follow peak calling, differential peak analysis, and peak filtering (pp.call_peaks, pp.filter_peaks) first The goal is TF binding site discovery itself, not motif enrichment comparison — use the Pycallingcards peak callers (CCcaller, MACCs) instead Peaks are from ChIP-seq or RNA-seq data rather than calling cards assays; this skill's workflow is grounded in CC peak inputs http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 De novo and comparative TF motif enrichment on calling cards (CC) peaks, using Pycallingcards' tools module (call_motif via HOMER) to discover motifs in differentially bound peak sets and compare_motif to identify sex- or condition-specific motif families. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae070
skills.summary: De novo and comparative TF motif enrichment on calling cards (CC) peaks, using Pycallingcards' tools module (call_motif via HOMER) to discover motifs in differentially bound peak sets and compare_motif to identify sex- or condition-specific motif families.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw qbed/ccf insertions rather than called, differential peaks — motif calling should follow peak calling, differential peak analysis, and peak filtering (pp.call_peaks, pp.filter_peaks) first The goal is TF binding site discovery itself, not motif enrichment comparison — use the Pycallingcards peak callers (CCcaller, MACCs) instead Peaks are from ChIP-seq or RNA-seq data rather than calling cards assays; this skill's workflow is grounded in CC peak inputs

skills.description: Use when you have a gene set of interest (e.g. differentially expressed genes) and need to discover which TF motifs are overrepresented in the regulatory elements EpiRegio associates with those genes in a specific cell type or tissue.
skills.name: tf-motif-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: tf-motif-enrichment-analysis Use when you have a gene set of interest (e.g. differentially expressed genes) and need to discover which TF motifs are overrepresented in the regulatory elements EpiRegio associates with those genes in a specific cell type or tissue. When you already have TF ChIP-seq peak regions and only want to find which REMs and target genes they overlap — use EpiRegio's Region Query workflow instead of motif enrichment When you need to find TF binding sites within the REMs of a single gene of interest rather than motifs enriched across a ranked REM set — use the identifyTFBindingSites scenario When no meaningful ranking (e.g. Cell type score) separates high- from low-ranked sequences, since PASTAA compares high-ranked against low-ranked input sequences http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_3176 Identifies transcription factors whose binding motifs are significantly enriched in REM sequences of differentially expressed genes, ranked by EpiRegio's Cell type score, using PASTAA with a Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value cutoff of 0.05. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa382
skills.summary: Identifies transcription factors whose binding motifs are significantly enriched in REM sequences of differentially expressed genes, ranked by EpiRegio's Cell type score, using PASTAA with a Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value cutoff of 0.05.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you already have TF ChIP-seq peak regions and only want to find which REMs and target genes they overlap — use EpiRegio's Region Query workflow instead of motif enrichment When you need to find TF binding sites within the REMs of a single gene of interest rather than motifs enriched across a ranked REM set — use the identifyTFBindingSites scenario When no meaningful ranking (e.g. Cell type score) separates high- from low-ranked sequences, since PASTAA compares high-ranked against low-ranked input sequences

skills.description: Use when building a TF-target gene prior from open-chromatin data: e.g., you have an ATAC-seq peak atlas plus a gene expression matrix and need a binary {0,1} TF-by-gene matrix to constrain a model's TF-to-gene layer.
skills.name: tf-motif-scanning-open-chromatin-peaks
skills.search_text: tf-motif-scanning-open-chromatin-peaks Use when building a TF-target gene prior from open-chromatin data: e.g., you have an ATAC-seq peak atlas plus a gene expression matrix and need a binary {0,1} TF-by-gene matrix to constrain a model's TF-to-gene layer. You need directional TF-target relationships (activation vs. repression) — CITRUS explicitly does not represent directionality in the TF-target gene priors. You must resolve activities of individual TFs from the same family — TFs of the same family often share a similar motif and cannot be disambiguated, so motifs may encompass multiple TFs. Your input has no open-chromatin (ATAC-seq) peaks, since the prior is derived from TF binding motifs in open chromatin regions. http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Constructs a binary TF-target gene prior matrix by scanning pan-cancer ATAC-seq open-chromatin peaks for TF motif occurrences (FIMO vs. MEME-curated cis-BP motifs, P < 1e-5) and assigning motif-bearing peaks to nearest genes. This prior constrains the decoder's TF-to-gene connections in CITRUS. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkac881
skills.summary: Constructs a binary TF-target gene prior matrix by scanning pan-cancer ATAC-seq open-chromatin peaks for TF motif occurrences (FIMO vs. MEME-curated cis-BP motifs, P < 1e-5) and assigning motif-bearing peaks to nearest genes. This prior constrains the decoder's TF-to-gene connections in CITRUS.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need directional TF-target relationships (activation vs. repression) — CITRUS explicitly does not represent directionality in the TF-target gene priors. You must resolve activities of individual TFs from the same family — TFs of the same family often share a similar motif and cannot be disambiguated, so motifs may encompass multiple TFs. Your input has no open-chromatin (ATAC-seq) peaks, since the prior is derived from TF binding motifs in open chromatin regions.

skills.description: Use when a time-specific TF–pathway interaction network has been constructed (e.g., by TSMiner from time-series expression data) and you need to measure how many TFs are shared between consecutive-stage pathways to assemble a regulatory cascade.
skills.name: tf-overlap-set-comparison
skills.search_text: tf-overlap-set-comparison Use when a time-specific TF–pathway interaction network has been constructed (e.g., by TSMiner from time-series expression data) and you need to measure how many TFs are shared between consecutive-stage pathways to assemble a regulatory cascade. Expression data are not time-series (TSMiner constructs time-specific networks and cannot be applied to single-condition or static interaction data). The goal is TF–target binding prediction rather than quantifying overlap between already-predicted TF–pathway associations. Negatively correlated TF–TG interactions dominate the question of interest, since known repressors are limited and fewer results are obtained from negative interactions. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Compare the sets of transcription factors (TFs) significantly interacting with each pathway in a time-specific regulatory cascade to quantify shared regulators and infer which pathways belong to the same regulatory cascade, as demonstrated for the late-stage liver regeneration (LR) immune cascade built with TSMiner. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: Compare the sets of transcription factors (TFs) significantly interacting with each pathway in a time-specific regulatory cascade to quantify shared regulators and infer which pathways belong to the same regulatory cascade, as demonstrated for the late-stage liver regeneration (LR) immune cascade built with TSMiner.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Expression data are not time-series (TSMiner constructs time-specific networks and cannot be applied to single-condition or static interaction data). The goal is TF–target binding prediction rather than quantifying overlap between already-predicted TF–pathway associations. Negatively correlated TF–TG interactions dominate the question of interest, since known repressors are limited and fewer results are obtained from negative interactions.

skills.description: Use when you need to annotate a defined TF set with ssDNA-binding domains (OB, KH, RRM, sPC4-like clans) and compute the fraction of TFs having at least one direct interaction partner that carries such a domain.
skills.name: tf-partner-fraction-analysis
skills.search_text: tf-partner-fraction-analysis Use when you need to annotate a defined TF set with ssDNA-binding domains (OB, KH, RRM, sPC4-like clans) and compute the fraction of TFs having at least one direct interaction partner that carries such a domain. Your goal is to validate ChIP-seq peaks on HOT regions (e.g. motif or KO signal filtering) rather than to annotate TFs with ssDNA-binding domains The proteins of interest are not reviewed human Swiss-Prot entries, or you lack a curated physical-interaction source comparable to iRefWeb Quantifies how many transcription factors (TFs) occupying HOT regions can bind single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) directly or via direct interaction partners, combining HMMER3/PFAM domain scanning of Swiss-Prot sequences with physical-interaction filtering of iRefWeb PPI data. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz460
skills.summary: Quantifies how many transcription factors (TFs) occupying HOT regions can bind single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) directly or via direct interaction partners, combining HMMER3/PFAM domain scanning of Swiss-Prot sequences with physical-interaction filtering of iRefWeb PPI data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is to validate ChIP-seq peaks on HOT regions (e.g. motif or KO signal filtering) rather than to annotate TFs with ssDNA-binding domains The proteins of interest are not reviewed human Swiss-Prot entries, or you lack a curated physical-interaction source comparable to iRefWeb

skills.description: Use when time-series gene expression data (e.g. mouse LR RNA-seq across post-PH time points) must be converted into time-specific TF–pathway regulatory networks to identify which TFs regulate pathways at each stage.
skills.name: tf-pathway-interaction-network-extraction
skills.search_text: tf-pathway-interaction-network-extraction Use when time-series gene expression data (e.g. mouse LR RNA-seq across post-PH time points) must be converted into time-specific TF–pathway regulatory networks to identify which TFs regulate pathways at each stage. Expression data are not time-series — TSMiner captures dynamic TF–pathway events specific to time-course profiles; static clustering or single-condition differential analyses are the wrong fit. The goal is cluster/module detection alone — clustering methods cannot evaluate the temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways, which is exactly what this skill provides instead. Only negatively correlated TF–TG interactions are required and no repressor interaction data are available — results from negative interactions will be sparse because known repressors of many genes are limited. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Extract time-specific transcription factor (TF)–pathway interaction networks from time-series RNA-seq expression profiles using TSMiner, integrating TF–gene interaction data and KEGG/Reactome pathway gene sets to reconstruct regulatory cascades such as the late-stage mouse liver regeneration immune cascade. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: Extract time-specific transcription factor (TF)–pathway interaction networks from time-series RNA-seq expression profiles using TSMiner, integrating TF–gene interaction data and KEGG/Reactome pathway gene sets to reconstruct regulatory cascades such as the late-stage mouse liver regeneration immune cascade.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Expression data are not time-series — TSMiner captures dynamic TF–pathway events specific to time-course profiles; static clustering or single-condition differential analyses are the wrong fit. The goal is cluster/module detection alone — clustering methods cannot evaluate the temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways, which is exactly what this skill provides instead. Only negatively correlated TF–TG interactions are required and no repressor interaction data are available — results from negative interactions will be sparse because known repressors of many genes are limited.

skills.description: Use when you have time-series expression profiles plus TF–TG interactions and pathway gene sets (KEGG/Reactome) and must decide which pathways significantly interact with a time-specific TF.
skills.name: tf-pathway-mutual-interaction-scoring
skills.search_text: tf-pathway-mutual-interaction-scoring Use when you have time-series expression profiles plus TF–TG interactions and pathway gene sets (KEGG/Reactome) and must decide which pathways significantly interact with a time-specific TF. When you only have static (single-timepoint) expression data — TSMiner's MIM scoring is designed for time-series expression profiles When no TF–TG interaction information is available, since triple-gene blocks require known TF–target pairs When you need direct TF–TF or protein–protein regulatory events rather than TF-to-pathway interactions via target genes http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Scores whether a pathway is significantly correlated with a time-specific transcription factor using TSMiner's mutual interaction measure (MIM) computed on TF–TG–PG triple-gene blocks, with permutation-based significance testing to retain genuine TF–pathway regulatory interactions. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: Scores whether a pathway is significantly correlated with a time-specific transcription factor using TSMiner's mutual interaction measure (MIM) computed on TF–TG–PG triple-gene blocks, with permutation-based significance testing to retain genuine TF–pathway regulatory interactions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you only have static (single-timepoint) expression data — TSMiner's MIM scoring is designed for time-series expression profiles When no TF–TG interaction information is available, since triple-gene blocks require known TF–target pairs When you need direct TF–TF or protein–protein regulatory events rather than TF-to-pathway interactions via target genes

skills.description: Use when training or re-tuning CITRUS on TCGA pan-cancer SGA/GEP data and the decoder's TF layer must remain constrained by the TF-target gene matrix (tf_gene weights) while balancing embedding size, attention, and regularization.
skills.name: tf-target-prior-constrained-decoder-tuning
skills.search_text: tf-target-prior-constrained-decoder-tuning Use when training or re-tuning CITRUS on TCGA pan-cancer SGA/GEP data and the decoder's TF layer must remain constrained by the TF-target gene matrix (tf_gene weights) while balancing embedding size, attention, and regularization. Your input gene set is not filtered to top-variant genes that overlap the TF-target gene matrix — the tf_gene constraint requires GEP genes to be present in the prior matrix. You need directionality (activation vs. repression) or co-binding TF complexes (e.g. AP-1–IRF) in the prior — CITRUS TF–target priors do not represent these. You need to disambiguate TFs of the same family sharing similar motifs — the motif-based prior cannot distinguish them. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Configures and tunes the CITRUS decoder whose hidden nodes explicitly represent transcription factor (TF) states, constrained by a TF-target gene matrix derived from ATAC-seq motif analysis, so that gene-expression prediction and extracted TF activities are biologically interpretable. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkac881
skills.summary: Configures and tunes the CITRUS decoder whose hidden nodes explicitly represent transcription factor (TF) states, constrained by a TF-target gene matrix derived from ATAC-seq motif analysis, so that gene-expression prediction and extracted TF activities are biologically interpretable.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your input gene set is not filtered to top-variant genes that overlap the TF-target gene matrix — the tf_gene constraint requires GEP genes to be present in the prior matrix. You need directionality (activation vs. repression) or co-binding TF complexes (e.g. AP-1–IRF) in the prior — CITRUS TF–target priors do not represent these. You need to disambiguate TFs of the same family sharing similar motifs — the motif-based prior cannot distinguish them.

skills.description: Use when a time-series expression analysis must distinguish TFs that activate targets (positive TF–TG correlation) from TFs that repress targets (negative TF–TG correlation), producing separate activator and repressor networks per time point.
skills.name: tf-tg-correlation-stratified-analysis
skills.search_text: tf-tg-correlation-stratified-analysis Use when a time-series expression analysis must distinguish TFs that activate targets (positive TF–TG correlation) from TFs that repress targets (negative TF–TG correlation), producing separate activator and repressor networks per time point. The TF–TG interaction file lacks correlation-sign annotations (only undirected or unsigned interactions are available), so no positive/negative split can be made. The analysis goal is a single merged regulatory network regardless of activation/repression direction rather than separate time-specific activator and repressor networks. Input is not a time-series expression profile (e.g., static bulk or single-timepoint data), since TSMiner constructs time-specific networks from time-series expression profiles. http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 A TSMiner analysis strategy (introduced in v1.1.0) that processes positively and negatively correlated TF–TG interactions as separate input runs, so that time-specific transcriptional activators and transcriptional repressors are identified in distinct TF–pathway interaction networks rather than mixed in a single network. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: A TSMiner analysis strategy (introduced in v1.1.0) that processes positively and negatively correlated TF–TG interactions as separate input runs, so that time-specific transcriptional activators and transcriptional repressors are identified in distinct TF–pathway interaction networks rather than mixed in a single network.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The TF–TG interaction file lacks correlation-sign annotations (only undirected or unsigned interactions are available), so no positive/negative split can be made. The analysis goal is a single merged regulatory network regardless of activation/repression direction rather than separate time-specific activator and repressor networks. Input is not a time-series expression profile (e.g., static bulk or single-timepoint data), since TSMiner constructs time-specific networks from time-series expression profiles.

skills.description: Use when building time-specific TF-pathway regulatory networks from time-series RNA-seq (e.g. mouse liver regeneration data) plus a TF-gene interaction file and KEGG/Reactome pathway gene sets, and you need significant TF-pathway interaction scores.
skills.name: tf-tg-interaction-scoring
skills.search_text: tf-tg-interaction-scoring Use when building time-specific TF-pathway regulatory networks from time-series RNA-seq (e.g. mouse liver regeneration data) plus a TF-gene interaction file and KEGG/Reactome pathway gene sets, and you need significant TF-pathway interaction scores. Input is a static (non-time-series) expression matrix — TSMiner is designed for time-series expression profiles and cannot evaluate temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways from clustering-style inputs. No TF-gene interaction information is available for the organism/tissue — the MIM triple-gene block scoring depends on known TF–TG interactions. The goal is pathway enrichment on a single gene list — clustering methods with standard enrichment analysis (e.g. hclust, k-means, STEM, WGCNA) are the comparison approaches, not this MIM-based scoring. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Scoring TF–pathway and TF–TG regulatory interactions from time-series expression data using TSMiner's MIM-based triple-gene block (TF–TG–PG) construction with permutation-based significance testing, to retain only significant interactions for time-specific regulatory networks. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: Scoring TF–pathway and TF–TG regulatory interactions from time-series expression data using TSMiner's MIM-based triple-gene block (TF–TG–PG) construction with permutation-based significance testing, to retain only significant interactions for time-specific regulatory networks.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a static (non-time-series) expression matrix — TSMiner is designed for time-series expression profiles and cannot evaluate temporal dynamics of regulators or pathways from clustering-style inputs. No TF-gene interaction information is available for the organism/tissue — the MIM triple-gene block scoring depends on known TF–TG interactions. The goal is pathway enrichment on a single gene list — clustering methods with standard enrichment analysis (e.g. hclust, k-means, STEM, WGCNA) are the comparison approaches, not this MIM-based scoring.

skills.description: Use when you have patient-by-TF activity values from a CITRUS model output (e.g. 'hid_tmr' from output_dataset_CITRUS.pkl) plus tumor barcodes and cancer-type labels, and you need to identify which TFs are significantly activated or repressed in each of the 17 TCGA tumor types.
skills.name: tf-tumor-type-association-testing
skills.search_text: tf-tumor-type-association-testing Use when you have patient-by-TF activity values from a CITRUS model output (e.g. 'hid_tmr' from output_dataset_CITRUS.pkl) plus tumor barcodes and cancer-type labels, and you need to identify which TFs are significantly activated or repressed in each of the 17 TCGA tumor types. You only have raw gene expression (GEP) or somatic alteration (SGA) matrices but no CITRUS-inferred TF activities — the t-tests require the patient-specific 'hid_tmr' TF activity layer, not raw inputs. You want TF–somatic-alteration causal links rather than TF–tumor-type associations — that requires the in silico knock out analysis, not per-tumor-type t-tests. Your tumor labels are missing or misaligned with tumor barcodes in 'tmr' — the within-type vs. remainder contrast requires correctly paired 'can' labels per sample. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 Systematically associates CITRUS-inferred, patient-specific transcription factor (TF) activities with tumor types by running one SciPy two-sample t-test per TF–cancer-type pair, comparing each TF's activity within a cancer type against the remaining tumors. This converts the 'hid_tmr' TF-activity matrix into a TF-by-tumor-type association table analogous to Figure 3 / Supplementary Data 1 of the CITRUS paper. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkac881
skills.summary: Systematically associates CITRUS-inferred, patient-specific transcription factor (TF) activities with tumor types by running one SciPy two-sample t-test per TF–cancer-type pair, comparing each TF's activity within a cancer type against the remaining tumors. This converts the 'hid_tmr' TF-activity matrix into a TF-by-tumor-type association table analogous to Figure 3 / Supplementary Data 1 of the CITRUS paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have raw gene expression (GEP) or somatic alteration (SGA) matrices but no CITRUS-inferred TF activities — the t-tests require the patient-specific 'hid_tmr' TF activity layer, not raw inputs. skills.search_text: time-series-regulatory-network-construction Use when a time-series gene expression dataset (e.g., RNA-seq over a biological time course like mouse liver regeneration) must be converted into time-specific regulatory networks identifying when TFs and pathways become active. The expression data are not time-series (no temporal dimension), since TSMiner requires time-course profiles to assign TF activity to specific time points No TF–TG interaction data are available — TSMiner integrates three input types, and missing TF-gene interaction information prevents network construction The goal is only pathway enrichment of expression clusters without temporal dynamics of regulators — clustering tools (hclust, k-means, STEM, WGCNA) cannot evaluate temporal dynamics of regulators, but if temporal resolution is irrelevant a simpler clustering workflow suffices http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Constructs time-specific TF–pathway regulatory networks from time-series expression profiles using TSMiner, which integrates a time-series expression matrix, TF–TG interaction information, and KEGG/Reactome pathway gene sets to identify transcriptional activators and repressors at each time point. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab629
skills.summary: Constructs time-specific TF–pathway regulatory networks from time-series expression profiles using TSMiner, which integrates a time-series expression matrix, TF–TG interaction information, and KEGG/Reactome pathway gene sets to identify transcriptional activators and repressors at each time point.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The expression data are not time-series (no temporal dimension), since TSMiner requires time-course profiles to assign TF activity to specific time points No TF–TG interaction data are available — TSMiner integrates three input types, and missing TF-gene interaction information prevents network construction The goal is only pathway enrichment of expression clusters without temporal dynamics of regulators — clustering tools (hclust, k-means, STEM, WGCNA) cannot evaluate temporal dynamics of regulators, but if temporal resolution is irrelevant a simpler clustering workflow suffices

skills.description: Use when prioritizing non-coding GWAS variants in a tissue- or cell type-specific manner: you have per-variant SAD scores from DeepFun pre-trained models and need tissue-level aggregation plus a disease-by-tissue comparison such as a heatmap.
skills.name: tissue-specific-chromatin-profile-aggregation
skills.search_text: tissue-specific-chromatin-profile-aggregation Use when prioritizing non-coding GWAS variants in a tissue- or cell type-specific manner: you have per-variant SAD scores from DeepFun pre-trained models and need tissue-level aggregation plus a disease-by-tissue comparison such as a heatmap. The variant is coding or you need long-range (3D DNA contact) effects — DeepFun's model does not consider long-range interactions such as 3D DNA contact You require quantitative epigenomic signal magnitudes — DeepFun training binarized peaks and ignored quantitative information Input is already aggregated tissue-level enrichment data rather than variant-level SAD scores requiring the Basset sad.ipynb pipeline http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Aggregate per-variant SNP Activity Difference (SAD) scores from DeepFun/Basset across 1548 DNase I accessibility, 1536 histone mark and 4795 TF binding profiles (225 tissues/cell types) to test whether disease-associated non-coding variants show higher predicted chromatin impact in disease-relevant tissues. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkab429
skills.summary: Aggregate per-variant SNP Activity Difference (SAD) scores from DeepFun/Basset across 1548 DNase I accessibility, 1536 histone mark and 4795 TF binding profiles (225 tissues/cell types) to test whether disease-associated non-coding variants show higher predicted chromatin impact in disease-relevant tissues.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The variant is coding or you need long-range (3D DNA contact) effects — DeepFun's model does not consider long-range interactions such as 3D DNA contact You require quantitative epigenomic signal magnitudes — DeepFun training binarized peaks and ignored quantitative information Input is already aggregated tissue-level enrichment data rather than variant-level SAD scores requiring the Basset sad.ipynb pipeline

skills.description: Use when a differential alignment or ranking of genes across two tissue conditions needs biological validation against a curated set of known tissue-specific genes and GO terms.
skills.name: tissue-specific-gene-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: tissue-specific-gene-enrichment-analysis Use when a differential alignment or ranking of genes across two tissue conditions needs biological validation against a curated set of known tissue-specific genes and GO terms. Input is a raw alignment score matrix rather than a ranked gene list with per-gene P-values — enrichment testing requires the ranked differential output first The gene set under study has no prior tissue-specificity labels or GO annotation, making hypergeometric and GOrilla validation impossible Genes on chromosome Y should be excluded per the article's filter, so do not include them when counting top-ranked genes http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Validates chromatin-state-based differential alignment results (EpiAlign) by testing whether previously known tissue-specific genes are enriched among the top differentially aligned genes, using hypergeometric enrichment and GO term analysis (GOrilla, P < 0.0001). epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz287
skills.summary: Validates chromatin-state-based differential alignment results (EpiAlign) by testing whether previously known tissue-specific genes are enriched among the top differentially aligned genes, using hypergeometric enrichment and GO term analysis (GOrilla, P < 0.0001).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw alignment score matrix rather than a ranked gene list with per-gene P-values — enrichment testing requires the ranked differential output first The gene set under study has no prior tissue-specificity labels or GO annotation, making hypergeometric and GOrilla validation impossible Genes on chromosome Y should be excluded per the article's filter, so do not include them when counting top-ranked genes

skills.description: Use when you have a table of recurrent chromatin state patterns from EpiAlign horizontal alignment and need to determine which patterns carry cell-type-specific characteristics via tissue-specific gene overlap.
skills.name: tissue-specific-gene-set-annotation
skills.search_text: tissue-specific-gene-set-annotation Use when you have a table of recurrent chromatin state patterns from EpiAlign horizontal alignment and need to determine which patterns carry cell-type-specific characteristics via tissue-specific gene overlap. Motifs you are analyzing still contain the quiescent state 'o', which the authors exclude because it lacks a good biological interpretation. You need cross-sample similarity rather than within-epigenome recurrent patterns — vertical (cross-epigenome) alignment or clustering tasks need a different skill. Your epigenome annotation was not produced by a chromatin state method like ChromHMM; EpiAlign requires single-track chromatin state sequences as input. Annotates EpiAlign horizontal-alignment pattern tables (recurrent chromatin state motifs extracted from a single Roadmap epigenome, e.g. E071 brain) with tissue-specific gene sets and Roadmap sample metadata, so that each motif carries a tissue/cell-type association. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkz287
skills.summary: Annotates EpiAlign horizontal-alignment pattern tables (recurrent chromatin state motifs extracted from a single Roadmap epigenome, e.g. E071 brain) with tissue-specific gene sets and Roadmap sample metadata, so that each motif carries a tissue/cell-type association.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Motifs you are analyzing still contain the quiescent state 'o', which the authors exclude because it lacks a good biological interpretation. You need cross-sample similarity rather than within-epigenome recurrent patterns — vertical (cross-epigenome) alignment or clustering tasks need a different skill. Your epigenome annotation was not produced by a chromatin state method like ChromHMM; EpiAlign requires single-track chromatin state sequences as input.

skills.description: Use when you have single-cell Hi-C contact matrices plus per-cell TLD predictions (e.g. from deDoc2.w/deDoc2.s) and want to detect higher-order multi-TLD structures and test whether inter-TLD contacts within candidate cliques exceed genomic-distance-expectation.
skills.name: tld-clique-identification
skills.search_text: tld-clique-identification Use when you have single-cell Hi-C contact matrices plus per-cell TLD predictions (e.g. from deDoc2.w/deDoc2.s) and want to detect higher-order multi-TLD structures and test whether inter-TLD contacts within candidate cliques exceed genomic-distance-expectation. The goal is de novo TLD (domain boundary) prediction from raw single-cell Hi-C — deDoc2.w/deDoc2.s should be run first; this skill consumes existing TLD predictions, not raw contact matrices alone. Bulk (population-average) Hi-C data is the target where TADs are the unit of analysis — the pipeline is designed for per-cell TLDs and per-cell contact matrices. Cliques with 4 or fewer TLDs are the only candidates available — the pipeline explicitly retains only cliques containing more than 4 TLDs. http://edamontology.org/topic_3940 Identifies single-cell TLD-cliques — higher-level chromatin structures beyond nested TLDs — by adapting the Paulsen et al. TAD-clique pipeline to predefined single-cell TLDs, and quantifies whether cliques are genuine higher-order structures by measuring inter-TLD contact enrichment as observed/expected over 250 position-permuted control cliques. epigenomics/v2 10.1002/advs.202300366
skills.summary: Identifies single-cell TLD-cliques — higher-level chromatin structures beyond nested TLDs — by adapting the Paulsen et al. TAD-clique pipeline to predefined single-cell TLDs, and quantifies whether cliques are genuine higher-order structures by measuring inter-TLD contact enrichment as observed/expected over 250 position-permuted control cliques.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is de novo TLD (domain boundary) prediction from raw single-cell Hi-C — deDoc2.w/deDoc2.s should be run first; this skill consumes existing TLD predictions, not raw contact matrices alone. Bulk (population-average) Hi-C data is the target where TADs are the unit of analysis — the pipeline is designed for per-cell TLDs and per-cell contact matrices. Cliques with 4 or fewer TLDs are the only candidates available — the pipeline explicitly retains only cliques containing more than 4 TLDs.

skills.description: Use when comparing TLD/TAD predictor outputs on single-cell Hi-C contact matrices and you need quantitative, per-predictor quality metrics (2D structural entropy, modularity, AMI) to rank methods on raw, non-imputed data.
skills.name: tld-partition-ami-evaluation
skills.search_text: tld-partition-ami-evaluation Use when comparing TLD/TAD predictor outputs on single-cell Hi-C contact matrices and you need quantitative, per-predictor quality metrics (2D structural entropy, modularity, AMI) to rank methods on raw, non-imputed data. Input Hi-C data is bulk or already imputed/normalized — deDoc2 needs no normalization and this benchmark specifically targets raw single-cell data to test performance without imputation Predicted TLD counts are too sparse to compare (e.g., cells excluded when insufficient TLDs are identified, as with the '2n DNA' stage) You need fine-grained per-domain biological validation rather than genome-wide partition quality ranking http://edamontology.org/topic_3922 Benchmark TAD-like domain (TLD) predictions from multiple single-cell Hi-C predictors (deDoc2.w, deDoc2.s, deDoc, scHiCluster, deTOKI, Higashi, HiCS_de) on raw, non-imputed contact matrices by scoring 2D structural entropy, modularity, and adjusted mutual information (AMI). It quantifies which predictor yields well-defined TLDs without imputation. epigenomics/v2 10.1002/advs.202300366
skills.summary: Benchmark TAD-like domain (TLD) predictions from multiple single-cell Hi-C predictors (deDoc2.w, deDoc2.s, deDoc, scHiCluster, deTOKI, Higashi, HiCS_de) on raw, non-imputed contact matrices by scoring 2D structural entropy, modularity, and adjusted mutual information (AMI). It quantifies which predictor yields well-defined TLDs without imputation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input Hi-C data is bulk or already imputed/normalized — deDoc2 needs no normalization and this benchmark specifically targets raw single-cell data to test performance without imputation Predicted TLD counts are too sparse to compare (e.g., cells excluded when insufficient TLDs are identified, as with the '2n DNA' stage) You need fine-grained per-domain biological validation rather than genome-wide partition quality ranking

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a TLD predictor (e.g., deDoc2, scHiCluster, deTOKI, Higashi) preserves its domain calls when Hi-C contact matrices are perturbed by controlled noise levels such as 10%, 20%, or 40%.
skills.name: tld-prediction-robustness-benchmarking
skills.search_text: tld-prediction-robustness-benchmarking Use when evaluating whether a TLD predictor (e.g., deDoc2, scHiCluster, deTOKI, Higashi) preserves its domain calls when Hi-C contact matrices are perturbed by controlled noise levels such as 10%, 20%, or 40%. When the goal is absolute TLD prediction accuracy on ground-truth data rather than stability under perturbation — this skill compares noisy vs. original predictions, not predictions vs. known annotations When input matrices are already heavily processed or imputed (e.g., RWR-imputed), since deDoc2 is designed to decode TLDs from raw, unimputed single-cell Hi-C data and noise modeling assumes sparse downsampled inputs When binsize must be determined first — use the NDI-based binsize determination (deDoc2 -NDI flag) instead, as this skill assumes a fixed default 40 kb binsize http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 A benchmarking protocol for assessing how robust TAD-like domain (TLD) predictors are to arbitrary data noise, by adding controlled noise to downsampled Hi-C matrices and comparing TLD predictions via adjusted mutual information (AMI) and weighted similarity (WS). epigenomics/v2 10.1002/advs.202300366
skills.summary: A benchmarking protocol for assessing how robust TAD-like domain (TLD) predictors are to arbitrary data noise, by adding controlled noise to downsampled Hi-C matrices and comparing TLD predictions via adjusted mutual information (AMI) and weighted similarity (WS).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is absolute TLD prediction accuracy on ground-truth data rather than stability under perturbation — this skill compares noisy vs. original predictions, not predictions vs. known annotations When input matrices are already heavily processed or imputed (e.g., RWR-imputed), since deDoc2 is designed to decode TLDs from raw, unimputed single-cell Hi-C data and noise modeling assumes sparse downsampled inputs When binsize must be determined first — use the NDI-based binsize determination (deDoc2 -NDI flag) instead, as this skill assumes a fixed default 40 kb binsize

skills.description: Use when benchmarking multiple TLD predictors on scHi-C contact matrices (real or simulated, e.g., D = 750/1000 thresholds) and you need reproducible, fairness-preserving parameter settings per tool, including simulated-data overrides for Higashi.
skills.name: tld-predictor-parameter-configuration
skills.search_text: tld-predictor-parameter-configuration Use when benchmarking multiple TLD predictors on scHi-C contact matrices (real or simulated, e.g., D = 750/1000 thresholds) and you need reproducible, fairness-preserving parameter settings per tool, including simulated-data overrides for Higashi. Bulk Hi-C data with deep coverage — cell-level sparsity overrides (e.g., Higashi nbr = 0, no_nbr_epoch = 20) and deDoc2's no-imputation rationale apply to sparse single-cell inputs, not conventional population maps When the goal is TLD hierarchy analysis or downstream biology (cell-cycle dynamics, brain cortex cell types) rather than predictor configuration/benchmarking — deDoc2.w vs deDoc2.s level selection is out of scope here Input matrices already normalized or imputed — deDoc2 expects raw Hi-C data and performs its own optional RWR imputation (-rwr, rp = 0.5) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 Configures TAD-like domain (TLD) predictors (deDoc2, deDoc, deTOKI, scHiCluster, Higashi) for fair benchmarking on single-cell Hi-C contact matrices, e.g., ~100 simulated cells from the chr18:50–55 Mb 3D structure ensemble at 40 kb resolution. Key principle: run all predictors with default settings except for explicit, documented overrides on simulated data. epigenomics/v2 10.1002/advs.202300366
skills.summary: Configures TAD-like domain (TLD) predictors (deDoc2, deDoc, deTOKI, scHiCluster, Higashi) for fair benchmarking on single-cell Hi-C contact matrices, e.g., ~100 simulated cells from the chr18:50–55 Mb 3D structure ensemble at 40 kb resolution. Key principle: run all predictors with default settings except for explicit, documented overrides on simulated data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Bulk Hi-C data with deep coverage — cell-level sparsity overrides (e.g., Higashi nbr = 0, no_nbr_epoch = 20) and deDoc2's no-imputation rationale apply to sparse single-cell inputs, not conventional population maps When the goal is TLD hierarchy analysis or downstream biology (cell-cycle dynamics, brain cortex cell types) rather than predictor configuration/benchmarking — deDoc2.w vs deDoc2.s level selection is out of scope here Input matrices already normalized or imputed — deDoc2 expects raw Hi-C data and performs its own optional RWR imputation (-rwr, rp = 0.5)

skills.description: Use when raw nanopore FAST5 signals must be aligned to a reference at base-event resolution to extract per-position translocation times, because Albacore's fixed block strides are insufficient for timing analysis.
skills.name: tombo-resquiggle-signal-alignment
skills.search_text: tombo-resquiggle-signal-alignment Use when raw nanopore FAST5 signals must be aligned to a reference at base-event resolution to extract per-position translocation times, because Albacore's fixed block strides are insufficient for timing analysis. Input is already basecalled FASTQ or an event table without raw signal — re-squiggling requires raw FAST5 current data. The analysis only needs sequence calls, not per-base timing — Albacore's event table with fixed block strides suffices. No reference genome is available for the organism — Tombo re-squiggling is reference-guided and cannot proceed without a FASTA. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Re-squiggle Albacore-basecalled ONT FAST5 reads against the hg38 reference with Tombo, segmenting raw current into base-level events so per-base translocation times can be computed as measurement counts divided by the sampling rate. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad220
skills.summary: Re-squiggle Albacore-basecalled ONT FAST5 reads against the hg38 reference with Tombo, segmenting raw current into base-level events so per-base translocation times can be computed as measurement counts divided by the sampling rate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already basecalled FASTQ or an event table without raw signal — re-squiggling requires raw FAST5 current data. The analysis only needs sequence calls, not per-base timing — Albacore's event table with fixed block strides suffices. No reference genome is available for the organism — Tombo re-squiggling is reference-guided and cannot proceed without a FASTA.

skills.description: Use when comparing ranked TR lists from multiple TR-identification methods on the same epigenomic query region sets, to test whether top-ranked hits agree at top-k cutoffs (k = 10, 50, 100).
skills.name: top-k-rank-cutoff-sensitivity-analysis
skills.search_text: top-k-rank-cutoff-sensitivity-analysis Use when comparing ranked TR lists from multiple TR-identification methods on the same epigenomic query region sets, to test whether top-ranked hits agree at top-k cutoffs (k = 10, 50, 100). The goal is accuracy benchmarking against known perturbed TRs (e.g., five perturbed TRs in bulk datasets) — use mean reciprocal rank (MRR) instead of Jaccard overlap. Only one method's ranked list is available — pairwise Jaccard requires at least two methods run on the same query region sets. The input is raw epigenomic peaks rather than already-computed ranked TR tables — peak processing (MACS2 peak calling, blacklist removal, DAR filtering) must happen first. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies cross-method agreement among ranked transcriptional-regulator (TR) lists (BIT, BART, ChIP-Atlas, i-cisTarget, HOMER, WhichTF) by computing pairwise Jaccard indices of top-k TR sets at k = 10, 50, and 100, mirroring Supplementary Fig. 9 of the BIT paper. epigenomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-60269-4
skills.summary: Quantifies cross-method agreement among ranked transcriptional-regulator (TR) lists (BIT, BART, ChIP-Atlas, i-cisTarget, HOMER, WhichTF) by computing pairwise Jaccard indices of top-k TR sets at k = 10, 50, and 100, mirroring Supplementary Fig. 9 of the BIT paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is accuracy benchmarking against known perturbed TRs (e.g., five perturbed TRs in bulk datasets) — use mean reciprocal rank (MRR) instead of Jaccard overlap. Only one method's ranked list is available — pairwise Jaccard requires at least two methods run on the same query region sets. The input is raw epigenomic peaks rather than already-computed ranked TR tables — peak processing (MACS2 peak calling, blacklist removal, DAR filtering) must happen first.

skills.description: Use when preparing a gene-expression or methylation matrix (thousands of rows) for cola consensus partitioning and a feature-selection step is needed to pick rows that drive subgroup discovery, especially when comparing SD/MAD/CV against ATC.
skills.name: top-value-feature-selection
skills.search_text: top-value-feature-selection Use when preparing a gene-expression or methylation matrix (thousands of rows) for cola consensus partitioning and a feature-selection step is needed to pick rows that drive subgroup discovery, especially when comparing SD/MAD/CV against ATC. The input is already a low-dimensional or pre-filtered feature table where a top-n row selection would discard informative features The goal is single-cell clustering with thousands of cells, where cola's runtime/memory may be unacceptable and downsampling may miss small clusters Rows have not been preprocessed (missing values imputed, outliers adjusted, near-zero-variance rows removed), which would distort top-value scores http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Selects informative features (rows) for consensus partitioning in high-dimensional genomic data by scoring all rows with a top-value method — SD, MAD, CV, or cola's ATC (ability to correlate to other rows) — and retaining only the top-scoring rows before partitioning. epigenomics/v2 10.1093/nar/gkaa1146
skills.summary: Selects informative features (rows) for consensus partitioning in high-dimensional genomic data by scoring all rows with a top-value method — SD, MAD, CV, or cola's ATC (ability to correlate to other rows) — and retaining only the top-scoring rows before partitioning.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a low-dimensional or pre-filtered feature table where a top-n row selection would discard informative features The goal is single-cell clustering with thousands of cells, where cola's runtime/memory may be unacceptable and downsampling may miss small clusters Rows have not been preprocessed (missing values imputed, outliers adjusted, near-zero-variance rows removed), which would distort top-value scores

skills.search_text: topic-region-binarization Use when a fitted cisTopic object (e.g. the 30-topic 10X 5k PBMC model) must be reduced to per-topic region sets before running rGREAT GREAT() or topicsRcisTarget motif enrichment on hg19. skills.summary: Converts the continuous region-topic proportion scores of a cisTopic model into discrete per-topic sets of top regions (binarized cisTopics) so that downstream region-set analyses such as GREAT GO enrichment and RcisTarget motif enrichment can be run on each topic.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is cell-level analysis (e.g. cell state annotation or signatureCellEnrichment) rather than region-set-level enrichment, since binarization discards cell-topic and graded region-topic information No model has been selected yet — binarizecisTopics() requires a cisTopic object after runModels() and selectModel(), not raw fragment/peak inputs Working with the deprecated R cisTopic package for new analyses — the README states cisTopic is deprecated in favor of pycisTopic
